gaps: [mexico] No official tribal/nation history pages were found for the Mexican peoples (Mexico has no equivalent of the US tribal-government sites); sources are encyclopedic, reference and Wikipedia, so many items are 'medium' confidence.

[mexico] Britannica, many World History Encyclopedia pages (Mixtec, Siege of Tenochtitlan, Caste War) and several scholarly PDFs (Borah on the Tepehuán revolt, Letras Históricas on the Mixtón War, INAH Boletín on the Caste War) could not be read as text through nr.py and were not cited.

[mexico] Mixtec and Zapotec have thin dated claims: sources give no founding dates for Tilantongo or Monte Albán-era control within 1492-1900, and no Zapotec or Mixtec colonial uprisings (e.g. Tehuantepec 1660, Cajonos 1700) were sourced, so they are omitted.
[mexico] Mayo (Yoreme), Zacateco, Pame/Guamares, Opata and Otomí polities are not in the shared registry and were not added; they appear only inside Guachichil/Yaqui text.

[mexico] Purépecha: no source line found stating continued Purépecha self-government after 1530, so the Pátzcuaro and Tzintzuntzan homeland claims end in 1530 even though Purépecha communities remain around the lake.

[mexico] Maya Yucatán: only three claims (Mayapan, Maní, Sotuta); Cupul, Chikinchel, Chetumal, Tutul-Xiu and Cocom polities are not separately claimed. The 8 November 1546 eastern uprising has no single battle location in the source, so it is described in the Sotuta claim, not as its own event.
[mexico] Raramuri revolts of 1690-1698 (Tepóraca's execution 1690; war 1696-1698) are in the claim statement but not given separate events because the sources are one Wikipedia paragraph.
[mexico] Huastec evidence is limited to one Wikipedia article; the Pánuco claim is low confidence.

[mexico] Tlaxcala, Caxcan, Guachichil, Tepehuán, Rarámuri and Mixtec start dates for homelands are placeholders ('circa' 1492 or older) because the sources describe the situation at contact, not a founding date; each is flagged in notes.
[mexico] Items after 1900 (Cruzoob capital occupied 1901; Yaqui deportations from 1903; General May treaty 1935) are included only to show the end of the polity's control.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Tenochtitlan founding: Wikipedia 1325 (the date used); World History Encyclopedia c.1345.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Triple Alliance formation: 1428 (World History Encyclopedia, Wikipedia on the Tepanec War victory) vs a treaty in 1430 (Wikipedia Aztec Triple Alliance); used 1428.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Noche Triste: Wikipedia conquest timeline 30 June 1520; Wikipedia Noche Triste article says the army left on the night of 1 July 1520; used 30 June.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Nojpetén: assault dated 10 March 1697 (Nojpetén article) vs fall on 13 March 1697 (Spanish conquest of Petén, Chan Santa Cruz articles); used 13 March.

[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Caste War start: 30 July 1847 (Wikipedia, used); 30 June and mid-July also given elsewhere. Chan Santa Cruz occupied 3 May 1901 (Yucatán Today) vs war's end telegraphed 5 May 1901 (Wikipedia); month precision used.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Chichimeca War end: 1590 (Caxcan and Guachichil context) vs 1600 (infobox of the Chichimeca War article); 1590 used for claim end dates.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Mixtón War: 1540-1542 (Wikipedia) vs 1540-1541 (Schmal); Alvarado's attack dated June 1541 in both, Nochistlán captured 9 Nov 1541.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Yaqui battle name: Encyclopedia.com calls the 1886 defeat the Battle of Buatachive; Wikipedia describes El Añil falling on 12 May 1886.

[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Rarámuri rebellions: Wikipedia places Tepóraca's war after 1648 and his execution in 1690; a Spanish-language article seen in search results lists rebellions of 1648, 1652 and 1697.
[mexico] SOURCE CONFLICT: Mixtec conquest: Wikipedia gives both 1521 (Orozco in Oaxaca, 25 Nov 1521) and 1523 for the end of Mixtec independence.

[southwest] Pueblo peoples: only Taos, Pecos and Santa Fe are anchored; other Rio Grande pueblos (Tewa, Keres, Tiwa, Towa towns such as San Juan, Santo Domingo, Isleta, Jemez, Zia) have no verified claim lines. No official Pueblo Revolt or pueblo history pages (newmexicohistory.org, indianpueblo.org, NAU) could be fetched.

[southwest] Western Apache: no start date for homeland claims in sources fetched (San Carlos Apache and White Mountain Apache official sites returned 403 / certificate errors); claims use the 1870 and 1872 post/reservation dates. Cibecue, Tonto and Yavapai-Apache areas are only covered through the Battle of Cibecue Creek event.
[southwest] Chiricahua: Mimbres/Warm Springs (Chihenne) and Sonoran homelands, Mangas Coloradas and Victorio campaigns, and the Chiricahua Reservation of 1872-1876 are not given their own claims.

[southwest] Jicarilla and Lipan: no official Jicarilla Apache Nation history page found; Lipan claims rest on the Lipan Apache Tribe of Texas site and Wikipedia. The Texas-Lipan treaty of Live Oak Point (1838) lacks a Wikidata coordinate and was left out of events.
[southwest] Mescalero: homeland before 1700 has no dated source; Lipan and Chiricahua on the Mescalero reservation are covered only as relocations.

[southwest] Tohono O'odham: no source dates the Papagueria homeland or the creation of the reservation, so only San Xavier (1700), the Gadsden division (1853) and the Nation's capital Sells (1930s) are claimed. Hia-Ced O'odham and Sobaipuri are not covered.

[southwest] Quechan, Mohave: official Quechan Tribe pages could not be fetched; Quechan claims rest on NPS and Wikipedia. Cocopah, Maricopa (Piipaash), Yavapai and Hualapai (Pai) are not in this region's polity list.

[southwest] Ute: Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute homelands (Ignacio, Towaoc) have no dated source, so they are not claimed; Utah Ute bands (Pahvant, Sanpits, etc.) and the 1863 Conejos treaty are not covered. Navajo-Hopi land dispute (1882 Hopi reservation, 1974 act) not covered.
[southwest] Hopi: Second Mesa villages and the 1882 executive-order reservation are not claimed; the Oraibi split (1906) falls just outside the period of interest.
[southwest] WebSearch quota ran out partway through the run, so some tribal sites (Zuni, Hopi history pages, Quechan, Gila River, San Carlos, White Mountain) were not discovered through search.

[southwest] SOURCE CONFLICT: Acoma 1599: EBSCO says Vicente de Zaldivar reached Acoma on 11 January 1599; Wikipedia says 21 January (battle on 22 January). The original clash with Juan de Zaldivar is dated October 1598 (Wikipedia, Onate) or December 1598 (NPS). Used month precision.
[southwest] SOURCE CONFLICT: Mescalero reservation: tribal website says established 29 May 1873; Wikipedia says 27 May 1873. Used month precision (May 1873).

[plains] Not covered: Kaw (Kanza), Omaha, Iowa/Otoe-Missouria, Assiniboine/Nakoda of Montana, Plains Apache, Arikara as a separate polity (folded into the MHA Nation) and the 1823 Arikara War; no claims for Sisseton-Wahpeton or Hunkpapa exile in Canada.

Source access: Britannica (403/404 to automated fetch) and several tribal sites (Chickasaw Nation, Seminole Tribe, Muscogee, Pawnee, Comanche, Kiowa, Cheyenne-Arapaho, Haida Nation, Sealaska Heritage, Tlingit & Haida, Narragansett, Mohegan) could not be read, so many items rely on encyclopedia/NPS/Wikipedia sources; the WebSearch quota ran out in several regional passes. Mexican peoples have no tribal-government histories; sources are encyclopedic.

Method note: every quote was machine-checked as a verbatim contiguous span of the fetched page text and every coordinate checked against Wikidata P625 (approximate=true where a gazetteer/area point was used). Statements may still include details drawn from the cited page that are outside the 25-word quote; treat as unverified single-pass research.

Claims starting after 1900 and events dated after 1900 were dropped from the merge as out of scope: mexico-c-019, mexico-c-034, southwest-c-033, southwest-c-041, westernus-c-045, westernus-e-037. Claims with "time immemorial" occupation use from=1492 (map-window start) with precision circa, not a founding date.
Counts exceed the requested targets (claims and events): regional passes kept all well-sourced items rather than padding or pruning; trim by confidence or authority if a smaller catalogue is wanted.

claims.statement: Mexica (Tenochca) founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco and ruled from it as the dominant capital of the Triple Alliance until it fell to the Spanish-led coalition on 13 August 1521.

citations.title: Aztec Triple Alliance (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: founded their new city Tenochtitlan on this island in the year ōme calli (or "Two House", 1325 AD)

citations.title: Tenochtitlan (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: he was able to lay siege to the city which would eventually fall on the 13th of August 1521 CE.

claims.notes: Founding date differs: Wikipedia gives 1325 (Two House); World History Encyclopedia gives a traditional founding of 1345. Used 1325.

claims.statement: Tetzcoco (Texcoco), the Acolhua city-state on Lake Texcoco, was the second-ranking member of the Triple Alliance from 1428 and received two-fifths of the shared tribute.

citations.title: Tetzcoco (altepetl) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tetzcoco thereby became the second-most important city in the eventual Aztec empire, by agreement receiving two-fifths of the tribute collected while Tlacopan received one-fifth.

citations.title: Aztec Triple Alliance (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: These three city-states ruled that area in and around the Valley of Mexico from 1428 until the combined forces of the Spanish conquistadores

claims.notes: Wikipedia notes the three cities' treaty is also dated 1430 in some accounts.

claims.statement: Tlacopan (Tacuba), a Tepanec city-state on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, was the third and junior partner of the Triple Alliance, receiving a fifth of joint tribute.

citations.title: Tlacopan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Throughout its existence, Tlacopan was to remain a minor polity within the Triple Alliance.

citations.title: Tlacopan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1428, after its successful conquest of Azcapotzalco, Tlacopan allied with the neighbouring city-states of Tenochtitlan and Texcoco

claims.notes: Coordinate is the modern Tacuba neighbourhood of Mexico City, which Wikipedia identifies as the site of Tlacopan.

claims.statement: Cortés's expedition entered Tenochtitlan on 8 November 1519; control of the city was then contested through the war until the Mexica surrendered on 13 August 1521.

citations.title: Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés' expedition arrived at Tenochtitlan on November 8, 1519

citations.title: Siege of Tenochtitlan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Aztec forces were destroyed and the Aztecs surrendered on 13 August 1521, Julian Date.

claims.statement: The Tlaxcalteca drove out the Chichimecas around 1350 and set up an autonomous Tlaxcalan state; the Tlaxcalan people were allowed to survive and keep their culture after the Spanish conquest.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Sometime around A.D. 1350, the present-day inhabitants of the area, the Tlaxcalans, drove out the Chichimecas.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Defeating the opposition, the Tlaxcalans moved into the Cholula region and set up an autonomous Tlaxcalan state.

citations.title: Tlaxcallan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tlaxcala was allowed to survive and preserve its pre-Columbian culture.

claims.notes: Date is the source's approximate 'around 1350'. The 'to' is open because Tlaxcala remained a Tlaxcalteca polity into the colonial period and today.

claims.statement: By 1519 Tlaxcalan government was a confederation of four republics, each with its own ruling lord; Tizatlan was one of the four seats (with Ocotelolco, Tepeticpac and Quiahuiztlan).

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: had evolved into a "confederation of four republics," each with its own ruling lord, judges and other officials.

citations.title: Tlaxcallan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: These fiefdoms were Ocotelolco, Quiahuiztlan, Tepeticpac, and Tizatlan.

claims.notes: The four-seat structure is described for 1519 by Schmal; Wikipedia's list of the four señoríos dates to the 1545 Spanish reorganisation. 'to' 1545 is the year the Spanish corregidor reorganised Tlaxcala into four señoríos (the same four seats continued under Spanish recognition).

claims.statement: Tlaxcallan was never conquered by the Aztec Empire but was surrounded by it, subjected to 'Flower Wars' and an embargo from the reign of Motecuhzoma I, until its lords allied with Cortés on his entry into the capital on 18 September 1519.

citations.title: Tlaxcallan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tlaxcala was never conquered by the Aztec Empire, but was engaged in a state of perpetual war, the so-called "flower wars" or "garland wars".

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: As the Spaniards entered the Tlaxcalan capital on September 18, they were welcomed into the town as if they were heroes.

claims.notes: Start decade is inferred from the 'reign of Motecuhzoma I' (1440-1469 in World History Encyclopedia's chronology); the sources give no exact start for the Flower Wars.

claims.statement: Taríakuri's Wakúsecha (Uacúsecha) lineage made Pátzcuaro its first capital around 1325, the beginning of the Purépecha state that grew to control the lake basin.

citations.title: Tarascan Civilization (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: whose chief Taríakuri established the first capital at Pátzcuaro around 1325 CE.

citations.title: Purépecha Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The kingdom was centered around the Lake Pátzcuaro basin.

claims.notes: 'to' 1530 is the year the Purépecha state lost its independence (execution of Tangaxuan II); Purépecha communities continued around the lake.

claims.statement: Tzintzuntzan on Lake Pátzcuaro was the capital of the Purépecha Empire and seat of the king (the Irecha, called Cazonci by the Spanish) from about 1350 until the state lost its independence in 1530.

citations.title: Tarascan Civilization (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the Tarascan capital and largest settlement was at Tzintzúntzan on the northeast arm of Lake Pátzcuaro.

citations.title: Purépecha Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The kingdom was founded in the early 14th century and lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530.

claims.notes: World History Encyclopedia dates the Tzintzuntzan-capital phase 1350-1520; Wikipedia gives a foundation in the early 14th century.

claims.statement: After Cristóbal de Olid's 1522 expedition, Tangaxuan II submitted without battle and kept wide autonomy, so that for years both Cortés and the Cazonci claimed to rule Michoacán, until Nuño de Guzmán had him executed on 14 February 1530.

citations.title: Tangaxuan II (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: This resulted in a strange arrangement where both Cortés and Tangáxuan considered themselves rulers of Michoacán for the following years

citations.title: Tangaxuan II (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He was executed by burning by Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán on February 14, 1530.

claims.statement: Mayapan, walled capital of the Maya of Yucatán, was the political and cultural capital from the 1220s until a Xiu-led revolt against the Cocom rulers in 1441, after which it was sacked, burned and abandoned.

citations.title: Mayapan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Mayapan was the political and cultural capital of the Maya in the Yucatán Peninsula during the Late Post-Classic period from the 1220s until the 1440s.

citations.title: Mayapan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1441, Ah Xiu Xupan of the powerful noble family of Xiu became resentful of the political machinations of the Cocom rulers

citations.title: Mayapan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Mayapan was sacked, burned, and abandoned

claims.notes: Ethnohistoric sources on Mayapan are described by Wikipedia as 'confusing, chronologically implausible'; dates follow Wikipedia.

claims.statement: The Tutul-Xiu Maya moved their capital to Maní in the 13th century and were the dominant power in western Yucatán after Mayapan fell; their lord allied with the Spanish in 1542 and Maní has been continuously occupied.

citations.title: Maní, Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: it was home to the Tutul-Xiu Maya dynasty, which moved their capital here from Uxmal in the 13th century.

citations.title: Maní, Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Xiu were the dominant power in the western Yucatán after the fall of Mayapan in 1441.

citations.title: Maní, Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Xiu of Maní allied themselves with the Spanish and assisted in the conquest of the rest of the peninsula.

citations.title: Maní, Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Maní has been continuously occupied for approximately 4000 years.

claims.notes: '13th century' rendered as circa 1200.

claims.statement: Cocom Maya of Sotuta remained independent of the Spanish and among the main enemies of the conquest of Yucatán, which ran from Montejo's 1527 landing to the defeat of the 1546 eastern uprising in which Sotuta took part.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: while the Cocom Maya of Sotuta became the implacable enemies of the European colonisers.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The provinces of Cupul, Cochua, Sotuta, Tazes, Uaymil, Chetumal and Chikinchel united in a concerted effort to drive the invaders from the peninsula

claims.notes: End year is the defeat of the 1546-47 eastern uprising, which the article describes as the final conquest of northern Yucatán.

claims.statement: The Itza Maya king (Kan Ek') ruled from the island capital Nojpetén in Lake Petén Itzá, reportedly founded after the Itza left Mayapan around 1441-1446, until its fall to Spanish forces in March 1697.

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: These relate that Nojpetén was founded when the Itza fled south around 1441-1446

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697

claims.notes: Assault date: Nojpetén article says the assault began 10 March; Spanish conquest of Petén article says it fell 13 March 1697. Used 13 March.

claims.statement: From the first Franciscan missions of 1618 and the failed 1622 Spanish expedition, the independent Itza kingdom resisted Spanish rule for almost eighty years.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: set out from Mérida in Yucatán on a mission to attempt the peaceful conversion of the still pagan Itza

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: this expedition was a disaster, and the Spanish were massacred by the Itza.

claims.statement: After the Spanish bombardment of the island, the Itza defenders were forced to abandon Nojpetén (place is where people were driven from).

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Spanish bombardment of the island caused heavy loss of life among the Itza defenders, who were forced to abandon the city.

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: it was the capital of the last Maya kingdom to fall to the conquerors.

claims.notes: Day follows the 13 March date; the same article gives 10 March for the start of the assault.

claims.statement: Cecilio Chi's attack on Tepich on 30 July 1847 opened the Caste War; by spring 1848 the Maya forces held most of Yucatán except the walled cities of Campeche and Mérida.

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cecilio Chi, the Maya leader of Tepich, with Jacinto Pat attacked Tepich on 30 July 1847.

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the spring of 1848, the Maya forces had taken over most of the Yucatán, except the walled cities of Campeche and Mérida

claims.notes: Start date varies: Wikipedia 30 July 1847; other accounts give 30 June or mid-July 1847 for the outbreak.

claims.statement: Chan Santa Cruz (Noj Kaaj Santa Cruz Balam Naj), founded in October 1850 around the Talking Cross shrine, was the capital of the independent Cruzoob Maya state until federal troops occupied it in May 1901.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: From its founding in October 1850 until the end of the war, Noj Kaaj Santa Cruz was considered the capital

citations.title: Chan Santa Cruz (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Chan Santa Cruz was occupied by the Mexican army in 1901.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: hostilities are generally considered to have officially ceased on May 3, 1901, when federal army troops took the Maya capital

claims.notes: Fall date: Yucatán Today says federal troops took the capital on 3 May 1901; Wikipedia's Caste War article says General Bravo telegraphed the war's end on 5 May 1901. Month precision used. Yucatán Today is a regional magazine, so kind 'reference' is generous.

claims.statement: Mitla (Lyobaa) became the most important Zapotec city after the decline of Monte Albán and remained inhabited up to the Spanish conquest.

citations.title: Mitla (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Gaining prominence from the early Post-Classic period (c. 700-900 CE)

citations.title: Mitla (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Mitla became the most important Zapotec city following the decline of the long-time capital Monte Albán.

citations.title: Mitla (World History Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: continued to be inhabited up to the Spanish conquest.

claims.notes: Sources show Mixtec influence and, by the Spanish arrival, Mixtec presence at Mitla; the site is shared in the late period. 'circa 900' is the end of the source's c. 700-900 CE range for Mitla's rise to prominence. DATE CAVEAT: one of the from/to years is not stated in the attached quotes or cited pages (inferred from related events); treat that bound as approximate.

claims.statement: Zaachila, named for the Zapotec ruler Zaachila Yoo of the late 14th and early 15th centuries, became the final Zapotec capital after Monte Albán fell, until the Mexica conquered it in 1495.

citations.title: Zaachila (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Zaachila became the final Zapotec capital after Monte Albán fell.

citations.title: Zaachila (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The city is named after Zaachila Yoo, the Zapotec ruler, in the late 14th and early 15th century.

citations.title: Zaachila (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Zaachila was conquered by Ahuitzotl in 1495

claims.notes: Wikipedia says the history of the pre-Hispanic city is unclear (flourishing 1100-1521, or founded 1399); circa 1400 used. Mixtecs also took control of the capital before the Spaniards arrived.

claims.statement: Zapotec of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec fought the Mexica under Ahuitzotl at the fortified city of Guiengola; this was the last battle between the Aztecs and the Zapotecs.

citations.title: Zapotec civilization (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The last battle between the Aztecs and the Zapotecs occurred between 1497-1502, under the Aztec ruler Ahuizotl

claims.notes: Single source; dates as given (1497-1502).

claims.statement: Tilantongo in the Mixteca Alta was the ancient Mixtec capital; Mixtec kingdoms governed La Mixteca until subdued by the Spanish and their allies in 1521-1523.

citations.title: Mixtec (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Important ancient centers of the Mixtec include the ancient capital of Tilantongo

citations.title: Mixtec (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: However, they would be subdued by the Spanish and their central Mexican allies led by Francisco de Orozco in 1521.

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. no source gives a founding date for Tilantongo. Wikipedia gives 1521 and 1523 for the end of Mixtec independence.

claims.statement: After Aztec armies defeated the Mixtecs in 1458, the Mexica built a fort on the hill of Huaxyácac in 1486 to collect tribute from Mixtecs and Zapotecs, until Francisco de Orozco's Spanish force reached the Valley of Oaxaca on 25 November 1521.

citations.title: Mixtec (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Aztec forces triumphed over the Mixtecs in 1458.

citations.title: Mixtec (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1486, the Aztecs established a fort on the hill of Huaxyácac (now called El Fortín)

citations.title: Mixtec (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: which allowed the Aztecs to enforce tribute collection from the Mixtecs and Zapotecs.

citations.title: Zapotec civilization (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 25, 1521, Francisco de Orozco arrived in Valley of Oaxaca

claims.notes: Not all Mixtec towns became Aztec vassals (Wikipedia).

claims.statement: Caxcanes lived in the Nochistlán and Juchipila area of southern Zacatecas, having driven out the Tecuexes in the twelfth century, until Viceroy Mendoza's army captured Nochistlán on 9 November 1541.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Caxcanes lived in the northern part of the present-day Mexican state of Jalisco, in southern Zacatecas, and Aguascalientes.

citations.title: The Caxcanes of Nochistlán: Defenders of Their Homeland (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: In the Twelfth Century, the Caxcanes had driven out another indigenous group, the Tecuexes, using armed force.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 9, 1541, he captured the city of Nochistlán and Tenamzaztle, but the indigenous leader later escaped.

claims.notes: Start is 'twelfth century' (Schmal). Wikipedia's Mixtón War article says Nochistlán fell 9 Nov 1541 and the Mixtón stronghold fell in early 1542.

claims.statement: In the Mixtón War (1540-1542) the Caxcanes, led by Tenamaztle of Nochistlán, rose against Spanish encomienda rule and repulsed Pedro de Alvarado's attack on the Mixtón stronghold in June 1541; the stronghold fell in early 1542.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the most prominent leader who emerged among them was Tenamaztle of Nochistlán, Zacatecas.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The first attack of the Spanish was repulsed with 10 Spaniards and many indigenous allies killed.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In early 1542 the stronghold of Mixtón fell to the Spaniards and the rebellion was over.

citations.title: The Caxcanes of Nochistlán: Defenders of Their Homeland (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Eventually the abuse of the encomienda system led to a violent uprising of the Caxcanes and Tecuexes and other Indians throughout the region.

claims.notes: Some accounts date the war 1540-1541.

claims.statement: After the defeat of the Mixtón rebellion many surviving Caxcanes, especially around Juchipila, were enslaved and sent to Guadalajara or transported from their homelands to work on Spanish farms and haciendas (place is Juchipila, a Caxcan centre they were taken from).

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: many of the survivors (mostly women and children) were transported from their homelands to work on Spanish farms and haciendas.

citations.title: The Caxcanes of Nochistlán: Defenders of Their Homeland (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Many of the surviving Caxcanes around Apozol and Juchipila were enslaved and sent to Guadalajara.

claims.notes: Date is the year the rebellion ended (early 1542); the removals continued over following years. Some survivors returned after about a decade (Schmal).

claims.statement: Before and at European contact the Guachichiles ranged over the most extensive territory of the Chichimeca peoples, centred on the area that became San Luis Potosí.

citations.title: Guachichil (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Prior to European contact, they occupied the most extensive territory of all the Indigenous Chichimeca tribes in pre-Columbian central Mexico.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Guachichiles' territory centered on the area around what would become the city of San Luis Potosí.

claims.notes: Start 1492 is a placeholder for 'prior to European contact' (no founding date exists); 'to' is the start of the Chichimeca War, after which the range was contested.

claims.statement: From the Chichimeca War (1550 to about 1590) the Guachichiles and the allied Chichimeca nations raided the silver roads and fought Spanish expansion into their lands around San Luis Potosí.

citations.title: Who Were the Chichimecas? (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: The Guachichile Indians were the most populous Chichimeca nation, occupying perhaps 100,000 square kilometers

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Living in close proximity to the silver road between Querétaro and Zacatecas, they were the most feared of the native raiders.

claims.notes: End year: Wikipedia's Chichimeca War article says 1550-1600 and the Caxcan article says 1550-1590; 1590 used (peace by purchase from the 1590s).

claims.statement: After natives near the Cerro de la Bufa showed silver ore to a Spaniard on 8 September 1546, Spanish mining towns spread into the Gran Chichimeca, and the Chichimeca nations resented the intrusion and resisted, fighting the Chichimeca War from 1550.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Spanish soldiers soon began raiding native territory trying to acquire slaves for the mines.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 8, 1546, natives near the Cerro de la Bufa in what would become the city of Zacatecas

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Chichimeca nations resented the intrusions by the Spanish on their sovereign ancestral lands.

claims.notes: Place is shared Zacatecos/Guachichil territory; eastern Zacatecas is within Guachichil range per Schmal.

claims.statement: The Yoeme (Yaqui) lived in rancherías along the lower Río Yaqui in Sonora before European arrival and were a distinct united people by 1414; Vícam became one of their Eight Pueblos.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: Sometimes they even lived among these groups, but by 1414 they had become a distinct and united tribe.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: These eighty rancherias were spread over a distance of approximately sixty miles

citations.title: Yaqui (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Jesuits persuaded the Yaqui to settle into eight towns: Bácum, Benem, Cócorit, Huiribis, Pótam, Rahum, Tórim, and Vícam.

claims.notes: Encyclopedia.com (Gale) gives 1414 as the date they were a distinct tribe; the Yoeme homeland continues on the Río Yaqui.

claims.statement: After their 1610 peace with Spain the Yoeme welcomed Jesuit missionaries and, from about 1617, settled into eight towns around mission churches, the Eight Pueblos (Cócorit is one), which remain their towns.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: Soon the Catholics built missions, creating the "Eight Towns."

citations.title: Who are the Yoeme (Yaqui)? (Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: they did welcome Jesuit missionaries in 1617 to come into their land and teach them about Christ.

citations.title: Yaqui (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Jesuits persuaded the Yaqui to settle into eight towns: Bácum, Benem, Cócorit, Huiribis, Pótam, Rahum, Tórim, and Vícam.

claims.notes: Indigenous Mexico dates the Jesuits' welcome to 1617 and Encyclopedia.com says 'soon' after the 1610 peace, so circa 1617 used. Encyclopedia.com and some other accounts report three Spanish attacks in 1609-10 that the Yoeme repelled.

claims.statement: From 1876 José María Leyva (Cajemé) led an independent Yaqui republic whose fortification El Añil stood near Vícam; El Añil fell on 12 May 1886 and Cajemé was executed on 23 April 1887.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1876 the Yaqui leader José Maria Leyba Peres, or Cajemé, established a small independent republic in Sonora.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On April 23, 1887, Cajemé was executed at Tres Cruces de Chumampaco.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: El Añil was located near the village of Vícam

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: El Añil was captured on May 12, 1886.

claims.statement: The Tepehuán lived on the eastern slopes and valleys of the Sierra Madre Occidental, mainly in Durango; Jesuit missions at Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes (from 1596) and Santiago Papasquiaro were founded in their country.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Tepehuán people lived on the rugged eastern slopes and valleys of the Sierra Madre Occidental, primarily in the future state of Durango.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Jesuits began missionary work among the Tepehuan in 1596, establishing missions at Santiago Papasquiaro and Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes

claims.notes: Start 1492 is a placeholder for 'before Spanish settlement' (Spanish settlers arrived in the 1570s); the Tepehuán survive in three groups today.

claims.statement: In the Tepehuán Revolt of 1616-1620 the Tepehuán, under six war chiefs including Francisco Gogoxito, attacked Spanish missions and settlements; about a hundred people died in Santiago Papasquiaro and a similar number at El Zape.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: 100 people were killed in a church at El Zape and a similar number died in Santiago Papasquiaro.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Tepehuán attack on the Spaniards, under six war chiefs, most notably Francisco Gogoxito, was well coordinated

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The revolt was officially declared at an end in 1620

claims.notes: Jesuit sources date the first killings to 16-20 November 1616. Wikipedia reports about 4,000 Tepehuán dead, mainly of hunger and disease.

claims.statement: At Spanish contact the Rarámuri (Tarahumara) lived across much of central and western Chihuahua; they retreated to the high sierras and canyons of the Sierra Madre Occidental and were never conquered by the Spanish conquistadors.

citations.quote: wintered on the Exploits River or at Red Indian Lake and resorted to the coast in Notre Dame Bay

citations.title: Shawnadithit - Dictionary of Canadian Biography
citations.quote: Shawnadithit was the last known survivor of the Beothuk, the First Nations inhabitants of Newfoundland

claims.notes: 'From' is the approximate formation of Beothuk culture (about AD 1500, Wikipedia); their ancestors had been on the island since about AD 1. Mi'kmaq oral histories reject the claim that Shanawdithit was the last Beothuk, and some oral histories suggest survivors joined Mi'kmaq and other peoples.

claims.statement: Red Indian Lake (Beothuk Lake) in the interior of Newfoundland was a wintering place of the Beothuk, who retreated inland from European settlement; in 1819 settlers killed the chief Nonosabasut and captured Demasduit there.

citations.title: Beothuk
citations.quote: wintered on the Exploits River or at Red Indian Lake and resorted to the coast in Notre Dame Bay

citations.title: Shawnadithit - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Shawnadithit observed European traders capture her aunt Demasduit and murder her uncle, Beothuk chief Nonosabasut, at Red Indian Lake

citations.title: Shawnadithit - The Canadian Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the Beothuk increasingly found themselves forced onto smaller areas of land

citations.title: Beothuk
citations.quote: The Beothuks avoided Europeans in Newfoundland by moving inland from their traditional settlements.

claims.notes: The interior retreat is described in the sources as a response to European settlement; the Beothuk themselves left no written record, and Shanawdithit's drawings and accounts made in St. John's in 1828-29 are the main source.

claims.statement: Bonavista Bay on Newfoundland's northeast coast was part of the core Beothuk coastal range.

citations.title: Beothuk
citations.quote: The Beothuk lived throughout the island of Newfoundland, mostly in the Notre Dame and Bonavista Bay areas.

claims.notes: Single-source. Beothuk lost access to coastal resources as the English fishery expanded.

claims.statement: Facing encroachment on their lands, the Nanticoke bought a 3,000-acre tract on Broad Creek (now in Sussex County, Delaware) in 1707 and held it as a reservation until they sold it in 1768.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: in 1707 the tribe purchased a 3,000-acre tract on Broad Creek in Somerset County, Maryland (now Sussex County, Delaware).

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: They sold the reservation on Broad Creek in 1768.

claims.notes: Only Wikipedia was readable for this nation; no tribal source could be fetched. The Nanticoke's older homeland lay in Dorchester, Somerset and Wicomico counties, Maryland, where in 1684 the Nanticoke and English governments defined a reservation near Vienna, Maryland (not separately claimed here for lack of an end date).

claims.statement: The Nanticoke sold their reservation on Broad Creek in 1768.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: They sold the reservation on Broad Creek in 1768.

claims.notes: A sale by the Nanticoke rather than a treaty cession; the circumstances (pressure from colonists) are not detailed in the source.

claims.statement: In 1778 about two hundred Nanticoke moved north to Fort Niagara because of their alliance; the British later resettled them with the Haudenosaunee at the Six Nations Reserve near Brantford, Ontario.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: In 1778, two hundred Nanticoke moved north to Fort Niagara in present-day Canada because of their alliance.

citations.title: Nanticoke people
citations.quote: Later the British resettled them at the Six Nations Reserve with Iroquois peoples, near Brantford, Ontario, Canada.

claims.notes: Place is the Nanticoke reserve area they left (approximate); the sources do not say the move was from Broad Creek specifically.

claims.statement: The Ojibwe (Anishinaabe) lived at Bawating (Sault Ste. Marie), where the Anishinaabe were established before sustained European contact.

citations.title: Sault Tribe of Chippewa Indians (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: who arrived there before Europeans showed up in the mid-to-late 16th century

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The Ojibwa (Ojibwe), or "To-roast-till-puckered-up," went northwest to Sault Ste Marie.

claims.notes: Start date is approximate (the source says only that the Anishinaabe were there before European arrival in the 16th century).

claims.statement: Madeline Island (La Pointe) in Chequamegon Bay was the longtime capital and cultural and religious centre of the Ojibwe nation in the western Lake Superior country.

citations.title: History - Bad River Tribe
citations.quote: longtime capital and cultural/religious center of the Ojibwe AKA Chippewa Nation

citations.title: History - Bad River Tribe
citations.quote: the French explorers Radisson and Groseilliers encountered the Ojibwe people here in the mid-1600's

claims.notes: Start date is the first documented French contact (mid-1600s); the Bad River Tribe states the Ojibwe were in the area well before that.

place.name: Upper Peninsula of Michigan (ceded Ojibwe lands, 1842)

claims.statement: By the Treaty of La Pointe (4 October 1842) the Ojibwe ceded extensive lands in what is now northern Wisconsin and the Upper Peninsula of Michigan to the United States.

citations.title: Treaty of La Pointe (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By this treaty, the Ojibwa ceded extensive tracts of land that are now parts of the states of Wisconsin and Michigan

citations.title: Treaty of La Pointe (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: on October 4, 1842 and proclaimed on March 23, 1843

claims.notes: Place is the centroid of the Upper Peninsula, used as an anchor for a ceded area that also included northern Wisconsin. Only Wikipedia was readable for this treaty.

claims.statement: The Treaty of La Pointe, finalized on 30 September 1854 on Madeline Island, set aside the Bad River Reservation on Lake Superior and Chequamegon Bay, which remains the Bad River Band's homeland.

citations.title: History - Bad River Tribe
citations.quote: This treaty was finalized on September 30, 1854 at Lapointe on Madeline Island

citations.title: History - Bad River Tribe
citations.quote: The Bad River Reservation was established by the 1854 Treaty of Lapointe with the U.S. government

claims.notes: The 1854 treaty also created reservations at Red Cliff, Lac du Flambeau and Lac Courte Oreilles.

claims.statement: The Odawa made their principal settlements near Michilimackinac at the Straits of Mackinac, where the Three Fires divided and met; they returned there in 1671 after fleeing the Beaver Wars west.

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: They located their principal settlements near the French fort at Michilimackinac

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the Wyandot and Odawa fled first to Chequamegon on Lake Superior and in 1671 back to Michilimackinac

claims.notes: Odawa presence at the Straits is older; 1671 is the date of the documented return after the western flight following 1649.

claims.statement: L'Arbre Croche (Waganakising), a string of Odawa villages along the Lake Michigan shore south of the Straits of Mackinac, was the largest settlement in the Great Lakes in the mid-18th century.

citations.title: L'Arbre Croche (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: L'Arbre Croche, also known by the Odawa name Waganagisi, was the largest settlement in the Great Lakes at the time

claims.notes: The page ties 'the time' to the Jesuit mission of summer 1741; use circa. Only Wikipedia was readable for this item.

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Washington (signed 28 March 1836) the Odawa and Ojibwe ceded about 13.8 million acres of northwestern Lower Michigan and the eastern Upper Peninsula to the United States.

citations.title: Treaty of Washington (1836) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty was concluded and signed on March 28, 1836 in Washington D.C.

citations.title: L'Arbre Croche (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1836, the Odawa gave up land across most of the Eastern Upper Peninsula and Northern Lower Peninsula

claims.notes: Month precision used although the signing day is known (28 March 1836); the treaty was proclaimed 27 May 1836.

claims.statement: After the destruction of Wendake the Odawa returned to Manitoulin Island within about two decades; the eastern end of the island at Wiikwemkoong has never been ceded.

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: After two decades they were back on Manitoulin Island

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the eastern section of the island, at Wikwemikong, remains unceded land

claims.notes: 'After two decades' after 1649-50 is approximated as circa 1670. Wiikwemkoong is a community of Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi peoples.

place.name: Twin Lakes, near Plymouth, Indiana (Menominee village)

claims.statement: Chief Menominee's Potawatomi village at Twin Lakes, on the reserve granted in the 1832 Treaty of Tippecanoe, was held until the militia removal of September 1838.

citations.title: Potawatomi Trail of Death (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: refused to sign the Treaty of Yellow River (1836) that would have relinquished the reserve granted to him in the Treaty of Tippecanoe (1832)

citations.title: Citizen Potawatomi (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: More than 756 Potawatomi were rounded up by Gen. John L. Tipton in Twin Lakes, Indiana

claims.notes: Counts of those removed vary (756 in the Oklahoma encyclopedia; about 859 in Wikipedia).

claims.statement: In the Trail of Death the Potawatomi at Twin Lakes were forced by militia to leave Indiana on 4 September 1838 and marched about 660 miles to the Osage River in Kansas; more than 40 died, most of them children. Place is the departure point.

citations.title: Potawatomi Trail of Death (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The journey from Twin Lakes, Indiana, to Osawatomie, Kansas, began on September 4, 1838

citations.title: Citizen Potawatomi (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: the forced removal of the Potawatomi from the Great Lakes occurred between September and November 1838

claims.notes: Departure point removal; the march ended near Osawatomie, Kansas on 4 November 1838.

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Chicago (agreed 26-27 September 1833) the Potawatomi, with the Ojibwe and Odawa, ceded their remaining roughly 5,000,000 acres in Illinois and Michigan Territory and agreed to move west of the Mississippi.

citations.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: An initial version of the treaty was agreed to on September 26, 1833.

citations.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: required them to cede to the United States government their 5,000,000 acres

claims.notes: Supplementary articles were agreed the next day (27 September).

claims.statement: Under Leopold Pokagon the Pokagon Band negotiated to stay in southwestern Michigan and were the only Michigan Potawatomi band that did not remove west; their government is at Dowagiac.

citations.title: Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They were the only Potawatomi band from Michigan that did not remove west of the Mississippi River.

citations.title: Pokagon Band of Potawatomi Indians (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Chief Leopold Pokagon negotiated to keep his Potawatomi band of 280 people in southwestern Michigan.

claims.notes: The year 1833 is the date of the Treaty of Chicago provision allowing the band to stay; the band regained federal recognition in 1994.

claims.statement: The Citizen Potawatomi, removed to Kansas in 1838, moved to Indian Territory in 1870-71 where their reservation covered almost all of present Pottawatomie County, Oklahoma.

citations.title: Citizen Potawatomi (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: relocated south to the Indian Territory to escape non-Indian land depredation in 1870-71

citations.title: Citizen Potawatomi (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: included almost all of Pottawatomie County, half of Cleveland County, and a portion of Oklahoma County

claims.notes: Reservation allotted in 1890 and opened to non-Indian settlement in 1891; the Citizen Potawatomi Nation remains in Pottawatomie County.

claims.statement: Michilimackinac, where the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi are said to have divided, was the preferred meeting place of the Council of Three Fires.

citations.title: Council of Three Fires (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Michilimackinac became the preferred meeting place due to its central location.

citations.title: Odawa (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The division of the Upper Great Lake Algonquians apparently took place at Michilimackinac

claims.notes: 796 is the traditional date given by Potawatomi elder Shup-Shewana from Midewiwin scrolls (reported on Wikipedia); it is not independently dated by archival sources. The council was long-standing and its other meeting places are not listed.

claims.statement: Wendake (Huronia), between Lake Simcoe and Georgian Bay, was the homeland of the Wendat confederacy until the Haudenosaunee defeat and dispersal in 1649.

citations.title: Huronia (region) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: whose country it was from prehistoric times until 1649

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The "Bear" and the "Cord Makers" were the original inhabitants of what is now northern Simcoe County in Ontario.

claims.notes: Start date approximates the late-16th-century formation of the five-nation alliance; Wendat occupation is far older.

claims.statement: Armed with Dutch firearms, the Haudenosaunee defeated and dispersed the Wendat in 1648-49 and the Wendat abandoned Wendake; survivors went to Christian Island and Quebec, among the Petun and Haudenosaunee, and west as the Wyandot.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: In 1648 and 1649, armed with Dutch firearms, they defeated and dispersed the Wendat

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: Defeated in 1649, the Wyandotte fled westward and took shelter with the Ottawa and Illinois tribes.

claims.notes: Epidemics of 1634-42 had already reduced the Wendat from perhaps 20,000-25,000 to about 9,000.

claims.statement: After years of exile near Quebec the Wendat who had survived settled for good at Lorette (now Wendake, Quebec) in 1697, where the Huron-Wendat Nation lives today.

citations.title: Wendake (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They finally settled for good in the village of Lorette in 1697.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: then to Lorette where their descendants still live

claims.notes: Wikipedia's account also lists earlier stops (Ile d'Orleans 1651, Quebec City 1668).

claims.statement: The Wyandot (Wendat descendants) settled around Sandusky, Ohio about 1745 and held the Wyandot Reserve at Upper Sandusky until their removal to Kansas in 1843.

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: A large party moved from the Detroit vicinity to the present Sandusky, Ohio, area around 1745.

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: A twelve square-mile tract was designated the Wyandotte Reserve at Upper Sandusky, Ohio.

claims.notes: Wikipedia dates the move to Sandusky Bay at 1738-1748; the Oklahoma encyclopedia says around 1745.

claims.statement: By a treaty of 1842 the Wyandot ceded all their land in Ohio and Michigan and were removed west, buying land in present Kansas in 1843.

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In 1842 a treaty was signed which ceded all Wyandotte land in Ohio and Michigan to the United States.

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The Wyandotte were removed west, and the remainder of their Ohio land was sold.

claims.notes: Place is the community removed from; the destination in 1843 was Delaware reservation land in eastern Kansas.

claims.statement: In 1867 the Wyandotte were removed from Kansas and received a reservation of 20,000 acres in northeastern Indian Territory; the Wyandotte Nation is centred on Wyandotte, Oklahoma today.

citations.title: Wyandotte (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In 1867 the Wyandotte were removed from Kansas and received a reservation of twenty thousand acres

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the remaining approximately 200 Wyandot were forced to a reservation in Oklahoma with their former enemies, the Seneca

claims.notes: Allotted to 241 tribe members by 1893.

claims.statement: The Neutral Confederacy (Attawandaron), whose heartland lay along the Grand River and the Niagara peninsula, had about 40 villages in 1616 and was dispersed by Haudenosaunee attacks about 1651.

citations.title: Neutral Confederacy (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Its heartland was along the Grand River and the eastern end of Lake Ontario in what is now Ontario, Canada.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: followed by the Tionontati in 1649-50, the Neutral by 1651 and the Erie by 1656

claims.notes: Start date is the first documented population estimate (1616). Place is a river anchor for a broad territory; the confederacy's name in French sources (Neutral) was given because they were not at war with the Wendat or Haudenosaunee in the early 1600s.

place.name: Chautauqua County, New York (Erie country, southeast of Lake Erie)

claims.statement: The Erie (Eriehronon) lived southeast of Lake Erie in what is now western New York and northwestern Pennsylvania until Haudenosaunee warfare ended them as a political entity in the mid-1650s.

citations.title: Erie people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Their territory was located southeast of Lake Erie in what is now western New York and northwestern Pennsylvania.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: followed by the Tionontati in 1649-50, the Neutral by 1651 and the Erie by 1656

claims.notes: Start is the first European record (1624, via the Wendat). Place is a county anchor; Wikipedia notes European contact with the Erie was exceptionally limited and the largest Erie 'capital', Rigue, was attacked in 1654.

place.name: Petun country, south of Nottawasaga Bay (Georgian Bay)

claims.statement: The Petun (Tionontati), closely related to the Wendat, lived south of Georgian Bay; the Haudenosaunee virtually destroyed them in 1649-50 and survivors joined refugee Wendat to form the Wyandot.

citations.title: Petun (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Their traditional homeland was south of Lake Huron's Georgian Bay, in what is today's Canadian province of Ontario.

citations.title: Wendat (Huron) (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: followed by the Tionontati in 1649-50, the Neutral by 1651 and the Erie by 1656

claims.notes: Start (1616) is Champlain's recorded visit to a Petun village. Place is an anchor on Nottawasaga Bay.

claims.statement: Kekionga, at the confluence of the St. Joseph and St. Marys rivers that form the Maumee (now Fort Wayne), was the Miami capital and principal village from the early 1700s until the Treaty of Greenville.

citations.title: Miami (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: During the early 1700s they dwelled near present Fort Wayne, Indiana, where Kekionga, their principal village, was located.

citations.title: Kekionga (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was the capital of the Miami people

claims.notes: Miami presence in the region goes back further (Green Bay c. 1650, then south in the 1650-1750 migration).

claims.statement: Wayne's Legion arrived at Kekionga on 17 September 1794 and built Fort Wayne there; then by the Treaty of Greenville (3 August 1795) the Miami lost control of the long portage.

citations.title: Kekionga (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Miami lost control of the long portage by the Treaty of Greenville (1795)

citations.title: Kekionga (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Legion arrived at Kekionga on 17 September 1794

claims.notes: The Miami retained unceded land west and south of the Greenville line until 1818-1840 treaties.

place.name: Miami reservation lands, Wabash River, Indiana

claims.statement: In October 1846 the United States forced the Miami rank-and-file to leave their Indiana lands; removal began on 6 October by canal boat to Kansas, while several major families were exempted and stayed in Indiana.

citations.title: Miami people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1846, the government forced the tribe's rank-and-file to leave

citations.title: Miami (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: Forced removal in 1846 resulted in half of the tribe remaining in Indiana, and approximately five hundred relocated to Kansas.

claims.notes: Place is the Wabash River valley, where the Miami reservations lay; exact embarkation point not confirmed from a source. The Oklahoma encyclopedia and Wikipedia differ on how many stayed.

claims.statement: The Western Miami agreed in 1867 to move to northeastern Indian Territory (present Ottawa County, Oklahoma), where the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma is now based.

citations.title: Miami (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: agreed to move to northeastern Indian Territory (present Ottawa County, Oklahoma) in 1867

citations.title: Peoria (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: By the Omnibus Treaty of 1867 the Confederated Peorias, now joined by the Miami, sold all properties in Kansas

claims.notes: Incorporated as the Miami Tribe of Oklahoma in 1940.

place.name: Pickaway Plains / Scioto River Shawnee towns (Chillicothe), Ohio

claims.statement: The Chalahgawtha (Chillicothe) Shawnee and other Shawnee divisions lived in towns on the Scioto River and Pickaway Plains in central Ohio from 1758 until American attacks in 1787.

citations.title: Chalahgawtha (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The next Chillicothe (1758-1787) was one of seven Shawnee villages developed on the west bank of the Scioto River

citations.title: Pickaway Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: This area was inhabited most recently by the Shawnee, who founded at least three villages here

claims.notes: Most Shawnee in Ohio lived at the Scioto Chillicothe in the 1760s; the Chillicothe name moved with the principal village (Old Chillicothe 1774-80, later Miami River sites). Wikipedia sources only.

place.name: Pickaway Plains / Scioto River Shawnee towns (Chillicothe), Ohio

claims.statement: In Lord Dunmore's War, Virginia's army marched to the Scioto towns on the Pickaway Plains and by the Treaty of Camp Charlotte (19 October 1774) the Shawnee agreed to cease hunting south of the Ohio.

citations.title: Lord Dunmore's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the terms of the Treaty of Camp Charlotte (October 19, 1774), the Shawnee agreed to cease hunting south of the Ohio

citations.title: Pickaway Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cornstalk agreed to honor the Treaty of Fort Stanwix of 1768, ceding the Shawnee hunting lands of present-day Kentucky to Virginia

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Fort Meigs (1817) the Ohio Shawnee ceded their remaining lands in exchange for reservations at Wapakoneta, Hog Creek and Lewistown, which they kept until the early 1830s.

citations.title: Shawnee (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1817, the Ohio Shawnee signed the Treaty of Fort Meigs, ceding their remaining lands in exchange for three reservations in Wapaughkonetta

claims.notes: End date approximate: Lewistown group left July 1831; Wapakoneta and Hog Creek Shawnee surrendered after Black Hoof's death in 1831 (move 1832-33).

claims.statement: After Black Hoof's death the remaining 400 Ohio Shawnee at Wapakoneta and Hog Creek surrendered their lands and moved to the Shawnee Reserve in Kansas; the Lewistown Seneca-Shawnee left for Indian Territory in July 1831.

citations.title: Shawnee (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the remaining 400 Ohio Shawnee at Wapaughkonetta and Hog Creek surrendered their lands and relocated to the Shawnee Reserve in Kansas

citations.title: Shawnee (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In July 1831, the Lewistown group of Seneca-Shawnee departed for Indian Territory

claims.notes: Exact date of the Wapakoneta departure not given on the page (1831-33).

claims.statement: By 1840 many Shawnee had settled along the Canadian River in Indian Territory after scattering through Arkansas, Texas and Louisiana; the Absentee Shawnee Tribe is headquartered at Shawnee, Oklahoma.

citations.title: Shawnee, Absentee (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: many of those scattered groups had migrated to the Indian Territory (present Oklahoma), and dwelled along the Canadian River

claims.notes: Absentee Shawnee ancestors left Ohio for Spanish Louisiana during the American Revolution; the Eastern Shawnee and Shawnee Tribe (Loyal Shawnee) are the other two federally recognized Shawnee tribes.

place.name: Starved Rock, Illinois River (Grand Kaskaskia Village)

claims.statement: The Grand Kaskaskia Village on the Illinois River at Starved Rock, with 351 dwellings in 1677, was the principal Kaskaskia (Illinois Confederation) village until it was abandoned in 1680.

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The principal Kaskaskia village was located at Starved Rock on the Illinois River

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The town contained 351 Indian dwellings in 1677.

claims.notes: Start date is Marquette's 1673 visit; the village is older.

claims.statement: The Kaskaskia moved about 1703 to the mouth of the Kaskaskia River, where they joined the Michigamea, and stayed near the French settlements there until 1832.

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: About 1703 the Kaskaskia joined the Michigamea at the mouth of the Kaskaskia River, and they remained until 1832.

citations.title: Kaskaskia - Oklahoma Historical Society
citations.quote: There, near French settlements, their population fell from an estimated six hundred in 1764 to 210 in 1778.

claims.notes: Population fell from about 600 in 1764 to 210 in 1778 through warfare, disease and liquor.

claims.statement: In 1803 the Kaskaskia, recognized as representing the Michigamea, Cahokia and Tamaroa, surrendered all but about 1,600 acres of their land in Illinois to the United States.

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In that year the Kaskaskia surrendered all but about sixteen hundred acres of their land in present Illinois.

claims.notes: Treaty of Vincennes, 1803 (day not given in the source cited).

claims.statement: In 1832 the Kaskaskia united with the Peoria and exchanged their remaining Illinois lands for a reservation in present Kansas.

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In 1832 they united with the Peoria and exchanged their remaining lands for a reservation in present Kansas.

claims.notes: A treaty exchange rather than a military expulsion; the Peoria source gives the treaty as 1832 and their prior home as Missouri.

place.name: Ottawa County, Oklahoma (Peoria and Miami lands)

claims.statement: Under the Omnibus Treaty of 1867 the Confederated Peoria (Kaskaskia, Peoria, Wea, Piankashaw) moved from Kansas to northeastern Indian Territory, now Ottawa County, Oklahoma; the Peoria Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma is based there.

citations.title: Kaskaskia (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: which was assigned a new home in northeast Indian Territory (present Ottawa County, Oklahoma) in 1867

citations.title: Peoria (tribe) (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: By the Omnibus Treaty of 1867 the Confederated Peorias, now joined by the Miami

claims.notes: The Peoria Tribe was dissolved by termination in 1956 and federally restored by Congress in April 1978.

claims.statement: The Meskwaki controlled the Fox River system in eastern and central Wisconsin; they fought the French in the Fox Wars to defend it until their warriors were largely killed in September 1730.

citations.title: Meskwaki (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Meskwaki gained control of the Fox River system in eastern and central Wisconsin.

citations.title: Meskwaki (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 9, 1730, most of the Meskwaki warriors were killed

claims.notes: Start date is the first French population estimate (1698). The Fox Wars span 1701-1742 in Wikipedia; the Wisconsin Historical Society (not readable here) gives 1712-1730. The 1730 battle took place in Illinois during a breakout, not on the Fox River.

claims.statement: The Meskwaki pooled their treaty annuities and bought their first 80 acres of land along the Iowa River in 1857, founding the Meskwaki Settlement at Tama, Iowa, with the permission of the Iowa legislature.

citations.title: The Meskwaki Nation's Story of Survival, Land and Sovereignty in Iowa (Iowa PBS)
citations.quote: the Meskwaki Nation used their own funds to purchase land along the Iowa River in 1857

citations.title: Sac and Fox (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The Meskwaki have resided on the Meskwaki Settlement in central Iowa since 1856

claims.notes: Sources differ: 1856 (Iowa law allowing residence) versus 1857 (land purchase). The 1857 purchase date was used.

claims.statement: Under the Black Hawk Purchase (treaty signed at Davenport, 21 September 1832) the Sauk and Meskwaki were forced to give up about 6 million acres along the Mississippi in eastern Iowa after the Black Hawk War.

citations.title: Black Hawk Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Sauk and Meskwaki were forced to relinquish another 6 million acres

citations.title: Black Hawk Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The purchase was made for $640,000

claims.notes: Month precision; the Wikipedia page gives the date as 21 September 1832.

claims.statement: Saukenuk, at the mouth of the Rock River, was the Sauk principal village from about 1750, with an estimated 4,800 Sauk living there and nearby in 1826.

citations.title: Black Hawk State Historic Site / Saukenuk (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Sauk had arrived by 1750, probably after the Fox Wars (1712-1733).

citations.title: Sac and Fox (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The settlement was known as the great town of Sâkînâke, the Saukenuk of history.

claims.notes: The disputed 1804 Treaty of St. Louis transferred the land to the United States in the U.S. view; the Sauk rejected it and stayed.

claims.statement: In June 1831, faced with U.S. troops and about 1,500 Illinois militia, Black Hawk's band abandoned Saukenuk, recrossed the Mississippi and promised on 30 June to remain west of it.

citations.title: Black Hawk War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Black Hawk and his followers had abandoned the village and recrossed the Mississippi.

citations.title: Sac and Fox (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
