claims.notes: Place = Nanih Waiya as the homeland removed from; later waves occurred 1832-34, 1838 and 1844-55 and groups were still being removed until 1903 (Choctaw Nation).

claims.statement: In the new homeland in Indian Territory the Choctaw Nation built a council house it named Nanih Waiya after the mother mound of the homeland; the council house stood near Tuskahoma, which the Nation made its permanent capital in 1882.

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: They also built a council house in the new capitol, which they named Nanih Waiya after the Mother Mound of the homeland.

citations.title: Tuskahoma, Oklahoma - Wikipedia
citations.quote: an Act of the Choctaw Nation dated October 20, 1882, established the community as the permanent seat of government

claims.notes: Start year is approximate: the Nation passed its first post-removal constitution on 3 June 1834 and then built the council house (date not given). The capital moved among Doaksville, Skullyville, Fort Towson and Boggy Depot in between (Wikipedia); the first capital was two miles east of Tuskahoma. Coordinates are those of Tuskahoma.

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

claims.statement: The Chickasaw homeland lay in northeastern Mississippi, where de Soto's expedition wintered most likely near Tupelo in 1540-41 and where the Chickasaw National Council House stood at Pontotoc Creek.

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: When Europeans first encountered them, the Chickasaw were living in villages in what is now northeastern Mississippi.

citations.title: Hernando de Soto - Wikipedia
citations.quote: He moved into inland Mississippi, most likely near present-day Tupelo, where they spent the winter.

citations.title: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek - Wikipedia
citations.quote: assembled at the National Council House on Pontotoc Creek in Pontotoc, Mississippi

claims.notes: De Soto's wintering place "most likely near present-day Tupelo" is Wikipedia's phrasing; the Chickasaw identification of that camp rests on the next paragraph of the article. Start year marks first documented European contact.

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek (20 October 1832), signed after Mississippi had extended its laws over them, the Chickasaw ceded their remaining homeland east of the Mississippi in exchange for a promise to find suitable land to the west.

citations.title: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1832 (Treaty of Pontotoc Creek) - Chickasaw.tv
citations.quote: relinquished Chickasaw lands east of the Mississippi River in exchange for a promise to find suitable land west of the Mississippi River

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: ceding their remaining Mississippi territory to the U.S.

claims.notes: The Chickasaw Nation notes that settlers rushed in despite Article 15 of the treaty. A supplement was signed two days later.

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

claims.statement: The Chickasaw gathered at Memphis on 4 July 1837 and began their removal to Indian Territory, the last of the Five Tribes to leave the East; they settled within the Choctaw Nation under a treaty signed at Doaksville in 1837.

citations.title: Chickasaw - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Chickasaw gathered at Memphis, Tennessee, on July 4, 1837, with all of their portable assets

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: Chickasaws were the last of the Five Tribes to leave their homeland in the East for Indian Territory.

citations.title: A New Chahta Homeland: A History by the Decade, 1830-1840 - Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma
citations.quote: Choctaws and Chickasaws signed a treaty at Doaksville (near Fort Towson) to create a Chickasaw District within Choctaw Nation

claims.notes: Place = Pontotoc, the homeland removed from; removal continued through 1847 in several groups. The Chickasaw were separated from the Choctaw by treaty in 1855-56.

claims.statement: After a treaty signed in Washington in 1856 the Chickasaw Nation became independent in Indian Territory, with its capital at Tishomingo in what is now Oklahoma.

citations.title: Chickasaw Nation Capitols - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Nation became independent in 1856 when a treaty was signed in Washington giving the Chickasaw Nation full ownership of 4,707,903 acres of land

citations.title: Chickasaw Nation Capitols - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Tishomingo became the Nation's capital at this time

claims.notes: Wikipedia only for the capital date; the Chickasaw Nation remains headquartered in Oklahoma. A first constitution dates to 1848 and officers were elected in 1857 (same source).

place.name: Ackia and Ogoula Tchetoka (Chickasaw villages), Tupelo area, Mississippi

claims.statement: In 1736 French forces from Louisiana, with Choctaw and other allies, attacked fortified Chickasaw villages near present Tupelo, Mississippi, and were repulsed at Ogoula Tchetoka and Ackia.

citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Both attacks were bloodily repulsed

citations.title: Battle of Ackia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Ackia (in present-day south Tupelo, Mississippi) was attacked by the Southern force.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only. French and Chickasaw hostility continued after 1736. Coordinates are Tupelo (approximate; battle sites are in the Tupelo area).

place.name: Grand Village of the Natchez (Fatherland Site), Mississippi

claims.statement: The Grand Village (Fatherland Site) at present Natchez, Mississippi, was the main ceremonial and political centre of the Natchez and the home of the Great Sun from the time of La Salle's visit in 1682 until the Natchez abandoned it in 1730.

citations.title: Grand Village of the Natchez - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Between 1682 and 1729, the Natchez people used the village as their main ceremonial center, as noted in contemporary French accounts.

citations.title: Natchez Indians - 64 Parishes
citations.quote: A small mound center, Grand Village was the residence of chiefs known as "Great Sun" and "Tattooed Serpent."

claims.notes: Site construction began about 1200 CE by Plaquemine peoples (Wikipedia). Natchez settlements were a loose confederation (64 Parishes).

claims.statement: The French built Fort Rosalie in 1716 among the Natchez, anchoring a growing French settlement in Natchez country until, after the revolt of 1729, French and Choctaw reprisals in early 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort.

citations.title: History & Culture - Natchez National Historical Park (NPS)
citations.quote: Established by the French among the Natchez people on the eastern bank of the Mississippi River in 1716

citations.title: Fort Rosalie - Wikipedia
citations.quote: French and allied Choctaw military reprisals in early 1730 forced the Natchez to abandon the fort, which was in ruins.

claims.notes: Fort Rosalie lies in the present city of Natchez; it was rebuilt by the French in the early 1730s.

place.name: Grand Village of the Natchez (Fatherland Site), Mississippi

claims.statement: After the 1729 revolt the French defeated the Natchez in 1730 and by 1731 had killed, captured or dispersed most of them; the Natchez abandoned the Grand Village and their homeland, ending the Natchez as a unified nation.

citations.title: Grand Village of the Natchez - Wikipedia
citations.quote: After suffering a military defeat by French settlers in 1730, the Natchez abandoned the site and moved away.

citations.title: Natchez Indians - 64 Parishes
citations.quote: The war ultimately led the Natchez to abandon their homeland.

citations.title: Fort Rosalie - Wikipedia
citations.quote: killing, capturing, or dispersing most of the Natchez, resulting in the end of the Natchez people as a unified political nation

claims.notes: Many were sold into slavery in Saint-Domingue; survivors took refuge among the Chickasaw, then the Creek and Cherokee, and their descendants live today within the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and Cherokee Nation in Oklahoma (64 Parishes).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Catawba (Ye Iswa) occupied the Catawba River valley astride the present North Carolina-South Carolina border; the first recorded European contact was by Hernando de Soto in 1540.

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: Historically, the American Indian people who came to be called "Catawba" occupied the Catawba River Valley above and below the present-day North Carolina-South Carolina border.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The first recorded contact with these people was by Hernando de Soto in 1540.

claims.notes: Coordinates are the Catawba Indian Nation reservation area (Wikidata point for the Catawba people); the original valley extended over a much larger area. The Catawba Nation absorbed refugees of about thirty other peoples after 1715 (NCpedia).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Catawba held a reservation fifteen miles square (about 144,000 acres) on the Catawba River in South Carolina, confirmed by the 1763 Treaty of Augusta, until the Treaty of Nation Ford in 1840.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the 1763 Treaty of Augusta ceded the Catawba tribe of South Carolina a tract of land "fifteen miles square" comprising approximately 144,000 acres

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: negotiated a land deal with South Carolina that established clear title to a reservation 15 miles square

claims.notes: NCpedia dates the land deal with South Carolina to 1759; the South Carolina Encyclopedia dates the confirming grant to the 1763 Treaty of Augusta. By the early 1800s almost all of the reservation had been leased to settlers (SCE).

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Nation Ford, made with South Carolina in March 1840, the Catawba gave up their reservation lands, though accounts differ on the terms: a $5,000 pledge to buy land elsewhere, or about 300 acres in North Carolina with $5,000 only if none could be found, plus $2,500 and nine years of $1,500 payments. Another account has them keeping one square mile and calls the treaty void from the start, the right to make it being federal.

citations.title: Catawba People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Catawba agreed to give up their lands in exchange for a government pledge to spend $5,000 to purchase land for them elsewhere.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: In 1840 the Catawba Nation and the state of South Carolina entered into the Treaty of Nation Ford

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1840, by the Treaty of Nation Ford with South Carolina, the Catawba sold to the state all but one square mile

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The treaty was invalid ab initio because the state did not have the right to make it

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: in return for a tract of land of approximately three hundred acres in North Carolina; if no such tract could be procured to their satisfaction, they were to be given $5,000 by the state.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: the state would pay the Catawbas $2,500 at or immediately after the time of their removal and $1,500 each year thereafter for the space of nine years.

claims.notes: Sources differ on the replacement land (300 acres in North Carolina, SCE; none, NCpedia) and on whether any land was retained. The Catawba returned to the ceded land and the state withheld payments (SCE). Wikipedia says the treaty was invalid ab initio (no Congressional approval). Statement now gives the differing terms, attributed as accounts, and the invalidity claim; the 144,000-acre figure and the 630-acre tract of 1843 stay here.

place.name: Catawba River Valley / Catawba Indian Reservation, South Carolina

claims.statement: A tract of 630 acres near the centre of the old reservation was secured for the Catawba in 1843; the Catawba Indian Nation, federally recognized again in 1993, is headquartered at Rock Hill.

citations.title: Catawbas - South Carolina Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Joseph White in 1843 to secure for them a tract of 630 acres near the center of the "Old Reservation."

citations.title: Catawba people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1993 they regained federal recognition and won a $50 million Indian land claims settlement

claims.notes: The Catawba were federally recognized in 1941, terminated in 1959, and regained recognition in 1993.

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

claims.statement: The Tuscarora occupied the inner Coastal Plain of North Carolina; their Lower Towns, on the lower Neuse River and Contentnea Creek under Chief Hancock, fought the war of 1711-13, and Fort Neoheroka (Greene County) fell in March 1713.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Tuscarora American Indian people occupied much of the North Carolina inner Coastal Plain at the time of the Roanoke Island colonies in the 1580s.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Lower Towns, on the lower Neuse River and the Catechna (now Contentnea) Creek, led by Chief Hancock

claims.notes: Start is "circa" (1580s). Upper Towns lay on the upper Neuse, Tar and Roanoke rivers (NCpedia). Place = Fort Neoheroka (Greene County) standing for the Lower Towns; the Upper Towns lay further inland.

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

claims.statement: After the defeat at Fort Neoheroka (20-23 March 1713) the Tuscarora who had fought the colonists left North Carolina, migrating north over many years and joining the Five Nations (Haudenosaunee), who accepted them as the sixth nation in 1722.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: The Tuscaroras who had opposed the settlers removed to Niagara County, N.Y., to join the Five Nations, thereafter the Six Nations.

citations.title: Tuscarora people - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1722, sponsored by the Oneida, the Tuscarora were accepted as the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

claims.notes: Date is approximate: the northward migration took place over about 90 years (Wikipedia) and the Haudenosaunee admission is dated 1722.

place.name: Indian Woods Reservation, Bertie County, North Carolina

claims.statement: Tom Blount's Upper Town Tuscarora, who had aided the colonists, were given a reservation (Indian Woods) on the Roanoke River in Bertie County, North Carolina, in 1717.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: Lands on the north side of the Roanoke River between Quitsna Swamp and Deep Creek in southwestern Bertie County were secured in 1717

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: were rewarded with a reservation

claims.notes: Coordinates are the Bertie County point (approximate). End year 1831 is the deed extinguishing Tuscarora title.

place.name: Indian Woods Reservation, Bertie County, North Carolina

claims.statement: In 1831 the Tuscarora executed a deed to North Carolina extinguishing their title and interest in the Indian Woods lands.

citations.title: Tuscarora People - NCpedia
citations.quote: the Tuscarora executed a deed to the state in 1831 extinguishing their title, right, and interest in the North Carolina land

claims.notes: About 645 families remained in the South and later re-formed communities in and around Robeson County; four Tuscarora communities there were not officially recognized by North Carolina as of the early 2000s (NCpedia).

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

claims.statement: The Yamasee settled near the Savannah River in the 1680s and built towns including Pocotaligo, the main Upper Yamasee town, in what is now Beaufort County, South Carolina.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They established several villages, including Pocotaligo, Tolemato, and Topiqui, in Beaufort County.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The Yamasee became prominent in the history of South Carolina when they settled near the Savannah River in the 1680s.

citations.title: Yamasee War - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the main Upper Yamasee town of Pocotaligo

claims.notes: Start is approximate: Wikipedia places the move in 1687 and "the 1680s". Coordinates are the community of Pocotaligo, SC (approximate; near Yemassee).

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

claims.statement: After the Yamasee War began in April 1715 and the Yamasee were defeated, they were driven from South Carolina across the Savannah River into Spanish Florida; by spring 1716 most had settled in Florida.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Eventually, Craven was able to drive the Yamasees across the Savannah River back into Spanish Florida.

citations.title: Yamassee War - NCpedia
citations.quote: By the spring of 1716, most of the Yamassee had settled in Florida.

claims.notes: Place = the Yamasee towns around Pocotaligo they were driven from.

claims.statement: After the war many Yamasee settled in the region around St. Augustine and Pensacola in Spanish Florida; some remained near St. Augustine until Spain gave up the city to Britain in 1763.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: After the war, the Yamasees migrated southwards to the region around St. Augustine and Pensacola, where they formed an alliance with the Spanish colonial administration.

citations.title: Yamasee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Still others remained near St. Augustine until the Spanish relinquished control of the city to the British in 1763.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; smallpox and raids in 1727 led many Yamasee to disperse, some joining the Seminole or Creek, and about 90 evacuated to Havana in 1763.

place.name: Anhaica / Mission San Luis de Apalachee, Tallahassee, Florida

claims.statement: The Apalachee lived in Apalachee Province in the Florida Panhandle, one of the most powerful and wealthy chiefdoms in Florida, whose capital Anhaica lay at present Tallahassee, later the site of Spain's Mission San Luis.

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Apalachee Province was one of the most powerful and wealthy chiefdoms or provinces in Florida

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: capital of Apalachee Province

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1528, Pánfilo de Narváez is the first recorded European presence in Apalachee

claims.notes: Start year is the first European record (Narváez, 1528); Apalachee lived there long before. De Soto wintered at Anhaica in 1539-40.

place.name: Anhaica / Mission San Luis de Apalachee, Tallahassee, Florida

claims.statement: In January 1704 Carolina colonists under James Moore and their Muscogee allies raided the Apalachee missions; Mission San Luis was evacuated and destroyed that year, and most Apalachee were killed, captured, fled, or resettled near the Savannah and Ocmulgee rivers.

citations.title: Mission San Luis de Apalachee - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The mission lasted until 1704 when it was evacuated and destroyed to prevent its use by an approaching militia of Creek Indians and South Carolinians.

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: most of their population were either killed, captured, fled to larger Spanish and French outposts, or voluntarily joined the English

citations.title: Apalachee massacre - Wikipedia
citations.quote: They were resettled near the Savannah and Ocmulgee Rivers, where living conditions proved to be only slightly better.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only. The Apalachee population in 1680 was about 8,000 across 14 missions.

place.name: Fort Caroline area (Saturiwa Timucua), St. Johns River, Florida

claims.statement: The Timucua, independent chiefdoms of northeast Florida, included the Saturiwa near the St. Johns River at present Jacksonville, where the French built Fort Caroline in 1564; slave raids and disease reduced the Timucua to about 1,000 people by 1700.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: European contact with the Eastern Timucua began in 1564 when the French Huguenots under René Goulaine de Laudonnière established Fort Caroline in Saturiwa territory.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: By 1700, the population of the tribe had been reduced to an estimated 1,000 due to slave raids from Carolinian settlers and their Indian allies.

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; start year is the first documented French contact with the Saturiwa, not the beginning of Timucua presence (earlier Spanish contact 1513-1528). The Timucua were never a single political unit.

place.name: Fort Caroline area (Saturiwa Timucua), St. Johns River, Florida

claims.statement: When Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 the Spanish took the fewer than 100 surviving Timucua and other native people to Cuba.

citations.title: Timucua - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1763, when Spain ceded Florida to Great Britain, the Spanish took the less than 100 Timucua and other natives to Cuba.

claims.notes: The source does not name the Timucua departure point; the Fort Caroline area is used only as a Timucua anchor. Research on possible Timucua descendants in Cuba is under way (Wikipedia).

place.name: Mound Key (Calos, Calusa capital), Estero Bay, Florida

claims.statement: The Calusa kingdom of southwest Florida was ruled from its capital Calos, probably at Mound Key in Estero Bay, when the Spanish first explored the coast in the early 1500s.

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: The capital of the Calusa, and from where the rulers administered, was Mound Key, near present day Estero, Florida.

citations.title: Mound Key Archaeological State Park - Florida State Parks
citations.quote: Mound Key is believed to have been the ceremonial center of the Calusa Indians when the Spaniards first explored Southwest Florida in the early 1500s.

claims.notes: Start year is the 1566 eyewitness account of the king's house; the Calusa had held the coast for over 2,000 years (Florida State Parks). End year is the final removal to Cuba in 1763; survivors had already left their capital earlier under disease and slave raids.

place.name: Mound Key (Calos, Calusa capital), Estero Bay, Florida

claims.statement: In 1711 the Spanish evacuated about 270 people, including many Calusa, from the Florida Keys to Cuba, and after Spain ceded Florida to Britain in 1763 the Spanish relocated the remaining south Florida peoples to Cuba, completing their removal.

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the remaining tribes of South Florida were relocated to Cuba by the Spanish, completing their removal from the region

citations.title: Calusa - Wikipedia
citations.quote: In 1711, the Spanish helped evacuate 270 Indians, including many Calusa, from the Florida Keys to Cuba

claims.notes: Wikipedia only for the removal; place = the Calusa capital.

place.name: Coosa capital (Little Egypt site), Coosawattee River area, Murray County, Georgia

claims.statement: The Coosa paramount chiefdom, centred on the Coosawattee River in northwest Georgia (the "Little Egypt" site), dominated several smaller chiefdoms and was inhabited from at least 1400 until about 1600, when most of its core area was abandoned.

citations.title: Coosa chiefdom - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It was inhabited from at least 1400 until about 1600 CE, and dominated several smaller chiefdoms.

citations.title: Coosa chiefdom - Wikipedia
citations.quote: By the close of the 16th century, most of the core area of the Coosa was abandoned.

citations.title: Cherokee Indians - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: With the arrival of Spanish explorers and Old World diseases, the chiefdoms collapsed

claims.notes: Dates approximate. Coordinates are Murray County, Georgia (approximate; the capital site is on the Coosawattee River in Gordon/Murray counties). Coosa is also the name of one of the four Muscogee mother towns.

claims.statement: Cahokia, a Mississippian city near present St. Louis, existed from about 1050 to 1350 and may have had 10,000-20,000 people at its peak between 1050 and 1150.

citations.title: Cahokia - Wikipedia
citations.quote: is the site of a Native American city which existed c. 1050 - c. 1350 AD

citations.title: Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site - UNESCO World Heritage Centre
citations.quote: This agricultural society may have had a population of 10-20,000 at its peak between 1050 and 1150.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. UNESCO dates occupation to the Mississippian period (800-1400). The later Cahokia tribe (Illiniwek) was not necessarily descended from the earlier inhabitants (Wikipedia).

claims.statement: Moundville on the Black Warrior River in Alabama was founded around 1120 and gradually ceased to be a town between 1300 and 1450 as its mounds fell out of use and most inhabitants left.

citations.title: Moundville Archaeological Park - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: The Moundville site was founded around 1120 by Native American peoples of the Mississippian period

citations.title: Moundville Archaeological Park - Encyclopedia of Alabama
citations.quote: Between 1300 and 1450, the mounds gradually fell out of use, and most of Moundville's inhabitants left the great town.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. The Encyclopedia of Alabama says the site was abandoned in the sixteenth century.

claims.statement: Etowah, on the Etowah River near present Cartersville, Georgia, was a Mississippian mound town settled by the twelfth century (perhaps two centuries earlier) and occupied, with brief abandonments, into the seventeenth century.

citations.title: Etowah Mounds - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: The town was settled by the twelfth century; many archaeologists date the settlement at least two centuries earlier.

citations.title: Etowah Mounds - New Georgia Encyclopedia
citations.quote: Its occupation continued, with brief periods of abandonment, into the seventeenth century.

claims.notes: Pre-1492 background. Dates approximate; occupation was intermittent.

place.name: Mabila (site uncertain; Marengo County, Alabama region)

claims.statement: Mabila was a fortified town of the paramount chief Tuskaloosa in central Alabama; in October 1540 it was the scene of a major battle with de Soto's Spanish expedition, in which the town was burned.

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: was a small fortress town under a polity led by Tuskaloosa in 1540, in a region of present-day central Alabama

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: On October 18, 1540, de Soto and the expedition arrived at Mabila, a heavily fortified village situated on a plain.

citations.title: Battle of Mabila - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Armed with guns, the Spaniards eventually burned down the village and killed most of the warriors.

claims.notes: The exact location of Mabila is unknown; coordinates are the centre of Marengo County, Alabama, where 2021 archaeology located the province of Mabila (approximate).

place.name: xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam), mouth of the Fraser River

claims.statement: The Musqueam (xʷməθkʷəy̓əm), a hən̓q̓əmin̓əm̓-speaking Coast Salish people, have lived and moved through their territory at the mouth of the Fraser River (Point Grey, Vancouver) for thousands of years and remain there on the Musqueam Indian Reserve.

citations.title: Musqueam's Story - Musqueam Indian Band
citations.quote: We have always moved throughout our territory using the resources it provides for fishing, hunting, trapping and gathering

citations.title: Musqueam Indian Band - Wikipedia
citations.quote: have lived in the Point Grey area (today part of Vancouver), around the mouth of the Fraser River, for at least 4,000 years

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. the source states continuous presence for thousands of years. Coordinate is the Wikidata point for Musqueam First Nation (reserve), not a single village.

place.name: Burrard Inlet and Howe Sound (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh Úxwumixw, Squamish Nation)

claims.statement: The Squamish (Sḵwx̱wú7mesh) have lived across Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet for thousands of years; reserves there were allotted and surveyed at village and food-gathering sites between 1876 and 1888.

citations.title: Our History - Squamish Nation
citations.quote: Our rich history spans millennia, evidenced by an archaeological site dating back 8,600 years

citations.title: Our History - Squamish Nation
citations.quote: 1876 - 1888 Creation of Reserves Reserve lands along Howe Sound and Burrard Inlet were allotted and surveyed

claims.notes: from=1492 is the start of the map window, NOT a founding date: sources describe occupation since time immemorial / long before 1492. the source states continuous presence for thousands of years. The 1876-1888 reserve allotment left 'all remaining land' claimed as Crown land per the Nation's own timeline; there was no treaty.

claims.statement: In April 1850 James Douglas met leaders of the Lekwungen (now the Songhees and Esquimalt First Nations) and made verbal agreements, the first of the fourteen land purchases known as the Douglas Treaties (1850-1854) on Vancouver Island.

citations.title: Douglas Treaties - Wikipedia
citations.quote: Douglas met first in April 1850 with leaders of the Lekwungen people (now Songhees and Esquimalt First Nations), and made verbal agreements

citations.title: Douglas Treaties - Wikipedia
citations.quote: made a series of fourteen land purchases from First Nations

claims.notes: Wikipedia only; the later written terms of the treaty were recorded separately from the verbal agreement. Whether the First Nations understood the transactions as cessions of title is disputed in the literature.

place.name: Medicine Creek treaty lands (Nisqually delta to Mount Rainier)

claims.statement: By the Treaty of Medicine Creek (26 December 1854) the Nisqually, Puyallup, Steilacoom, Squaxin Island and related bands ceded some 2.5 million acres of south Puget Sound, keeping three small reservations and fishing and hunting rights.

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: cede nearly all their lands, retaining three tiny reservations and access to traditional hunting and fishing grounds

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: encompassed some 2.5 million acres extending from south Puget Sound to the slopes of Mount Rainier

claims.notes: Coordinate is the Nisqually Reservation point (Wikidata) as a stand-in for the treaty ground on the Nisqually delta.

claims.statement: After the armed conflict that followed the 1854-55 treaties, in August 1856 Governor Isaac Stevens agreed with Puyallup and Nisqually leaders to significantly larger reservations for both tribes than the treaty had provided.

citations.title: South Puget Sound tribes sign Treaty of Medicine Creek on December 26, 1854 - HistoryLink
citations.quote: in August 1856 Stevens will meet with Puyallup and Nisqually leaders and agree to significantly larger reservations for both tribes

citations.title: Puyallup Tribe of Indians - Wikipedia
citations.quote: the reservation was established in 1854 in the Treaty of Medicine Creek

claims.notes: Homeland-on-reservation claim from the 1856 enlargement; the Puyallup lived on the Puyallup River long before.

place.name: Lummi Reservation (Lummi Peninsula, mouth of the Nooksack River)

events.title: Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan formed
events.statement: The death of the Tepanec king Tezozomoc in 1426 set off a civil war. In 1427 Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan and Huexotzinco went to war against Azcapotzalco and won in 1428. Huexotzinco then withdrew, and the other three cities formed the Triple Alliance, dated 1428 by some accounts and 1430 by others, dividing the Tepanec lands and agreeing to cooperate in future conquests. They ruled in and around the Valley of Mexico until 1521.

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1426, the Tepanec king Tezozomoc died

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the resulting succession crisis precipitated a civil war between potential successors

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1427, Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan, and Huexotzinco went to war against Azcapotzalco, emerging victorious in 1428.

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: After the war, Huexotzinco withdrew, and, in 1430

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Tepanec lands were carved up among the three cities, whose leaders agreed to cooperate in future wars of conquest.

citations.title: Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: These three city-states ruled that area in and around the Valley of Mexico from 1428 until the combined forces of the Spanish conquistadores and their native allies who ruled under Hernán Cortés defeated them in 1521.

citations.title: Aztec Civilization (World History Encyclopedia)

events.notes: Sources differ on the treaty's year: World History Encyclopedia's timeline and Wikipedia's lead give 1428; Wikipedia's Tepanec War section gives 1430.

events.title: Tlaxcala allies with Cortés
events.statement: Moving inland in August 1519, Cortés's army met a Tlaxcalan force on the 31st and fought a run of battles against it. The Tlaxcalans, long at war with the Aztecs and eager for revenge, soon became allies instead, and in September they welcomed the Spanish into their capital. During twenty days there, senior leaders including Maxixcatzin and Xicotencatl the Elder were won over, and provisions and men were promised. They stayed loyal even after the Spanish were driven from Tenochtitlan.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (John Schmal, Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: On August 31, at a point ten miles into Tlaxcalan territory, Cortés’ army encountered a hostile force of at least 30,000 Tlaxcalans.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (John Schmal, Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: As the Spaniards entered the Tlaxcalan capital on September 18, they were welcomed into the town as if they were heroes.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (John Schmal, Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Xicotenga agreed to provide necessary provisions and manpower to the Spaniards.

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (John Schmal, Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: Xicotenga saw in Cortés a powerful ally who could help the Tlaxcalans destroy the Mexica and undermine the power of the Aztec Empire.

citations.title: Tlaxcala (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Due to protracted warfare between the Aztecs and the Tlaxcalteca, the latter were eager to exact revenge, and soon became loyal allies of the Spanish. Even after the Spanish were expelled from Tenochtitlan, the Tlaxcalteca continued their support.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On 23 September 1519, Cortés arrived in Tlaxcala and was greeted with joy by the rulers, who saw the Spanish as an ally against the Aztecs.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés seems to have won the true friendship and loyalty of the senior leaders of Tlaxcala, among them Maxixcatzin and Xicotencatl the Elder

citations.title: Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés stayed twenty days in Tlaxcala

citations.title: Indigenous Tlaxcala: The Allies of the Spaniards (John Schmal, Indigenous Mexico)
citations.quote: In the next battle, Cortés claimed that he faced a Tlaxcalan army

events.notes: Dated to the month: sources give the entry into the capital as 18 September (Schmal) and 23 September (Wikipedia), and the alliance was negotiated over the following twenty days. Schmal calls Xicotenga a king; Wikipedia's Tlaxcallan article has a confederation with several rulers, so the card names senior leaders. Schmal's 'at least 30,000' is left off as a single author's figure with no stated origin. Editor's pass: the two dates for the entry (18 and 23 September) are folded into 'in September'; Schmal's Xicotenga is not named separately.

events.title: La Noche Triste
events.statement: With the city in arms against them, Cortés's army and its Tlaxcalan allies were driven out of Tenochtitlan by the Mexica, leaving at night along the western causeway to Tlacopan. All the artillery and most of the horses were lost. Estimates of the dead run from about 150 to 450 Spaniards and from 1,000 to 4,000 allies. The Spanish name means the Night of Sorrows; in Mexico it is officially the Victorious Night.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Hernán Cortés and his army of Spanish conquistadors, including their native allies were driven out of the Mexica capital, Tenochtitlan.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés and his native allies, the Tlaxcaltecs, were increasingly unwelcome guests in the capital.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés selected the western causeway to Tlacopan, needing the quickest route out of Tenochtitlan with all his provisions and people.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cortés himself claimed that 154 Spaniards were lost along with over 2,000 native allies.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Francisco López de Gómara, who was not himself an eyewitness, estimated that 450 Spaniards and 4,000 allies died.

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)

citations.title: La Noche Triste (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Date conflict: Wikipedia's conquest timeline gives 30 June; the Noche Triste article's narrative says the army left on the night of 1 July, and its infobox gives 30 June to 1 July 1520. A further figure (Thoan Cano, 1,170 Spaniards) is judged probably too high by the same article and is left off. Casualty figures are known here through Wikipedia's summary of the chroniclers. Figures moved from the card: Cortés 154 Spaniards and over 2,000 allies; Díaz del Castillo (eyewitness) around 450 and 1,000; López de Gómara 450 and 4,000.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic in the Valley of Mexico
events.statement: Smallpox spread to Tepeaca and Tlaxcala from May to September 1520 and reached Tenochtitlan by that fall, as Cortés was returning after the Noche Triste. Its introduction has been attributed to an enslaved African with the Spanish, though this is disputed. Cuitláhuac, ruler for only 80 days, perhaps died of it. Suzanne Austin Alchon's estimates of mortality run from a quarter to a half of central Mexico's people, and it contributed to the collapse of Aztec resistance.

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: From May to September, smallpox spread slowly to Tepeaca and Tlaxcala, and to Tenochtitlán by the fall of 1520. At this time, Cortes was returning to conquer the city after being thrown out on the Noche Triste.

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: has been attributed to an African slave trafficked by the Spanish colonizers (by the name of Francisco Eguía, according to one account), but this has been disputed.

citations.title: Cuitláhuac (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cuitláhuac ruled just 80 days, perhaps dying from smallpox

citations.title: History of smallpox in Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Estimates of mortality range from one-quarter to one-half of the population of central Mexico.

citations.title: Smallpox Kills Thousands of Indigenous Americans (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: it contributed to the collapse of Aztec resistance against the Spanish, facilitating Cortés's conquest of Tenochtitlán by 1521.

events.notes: The mortality range is footnoted in Wikipedia to Alchon, A Pest in the Land (2003); known only through that footnote, the book itself not read. Wikipedia's smallpox article says flatly that Cuitláhuac died of smallpox while his own article says 'perhaps'; the card uses the weaker. Also in the source: the eyewitness Motolinia said more than half died in most provinces. Cortés names only one ruler who died of it, Maxixcatzin.

events.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
events.statement: Cortés came back with a coalition made up mainly of Tlaxcalan men and besieged Tenochtitlan from 26 May 1521. The Mexica surrendered on 13 August, after more than two months of fighting. Cuauhtémoc, caught fleeing by water with his family and treasure, was tortured over the gold lost on the Noche Triste. Estimates of the dead run from 100,000 to 240,000, and with the city's fall the Aztec Empire came to an end.

citations.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: May 26 – August 13, 1521

citations.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Spanish-led coalition, which was composed mainly of Tlaxcaltec men

citations.title: Fall of Tenochtitlan (Wikipedia)

Hassig (by footnote) gives 50,000 to 200,000 Native allies, left off the card. 'Julian Date' is the source's note on the calendar. Confidence set to high under the 2026-10-31 definition: the fall is established, only its toll is rough. Figures: Björnson and Jonassohn 100,000 (by footnote); Schmal's 'Aztec historians' 240,000.

events.title: Tangaxuan II executed; end of Purépecha independence
events.statement: Tangaxuan II, the last cazonci of the Purépecha, had made peace with Cortés and kept wide autonomy, his people paying tribute to both. Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán, marching northwest with a large force, found him still de facto ruler and allied himself against him with a Purépecha noble, Don Pedro Panza Cuinierángari. Tried for plotting rebellion, withholding tribute, sodomy and heresy, he was tortured and burned on 14 February 1530, his ashes thrown into the Lerma. Puppet rulers followed.

citations.quote: He was baptized Francisco when his realm made a peace treaty with Hernán Cortés.

Guzmán's force is left unnumbered: 5,000 to 8,000 is uncited on the Tangaxuan page, and the Mixtón War article gives 300-400 Spaniards and 5,000 to 8,000 Aztec and Tlaxcalan allies.

events.title: Mixtón War begins
events.statement: In spring 1540 the Caxcanes and their allies rose against Spanish rule in Nueva Galicia, emboldened perhaps by Coronado's departure north with over 1,600 Spaniards and allies. From the hill of Mixtón they beat off Pedro de Alvarado, who died after a horse fell on him in June 1541. Viceroy Mendoza took Nochistlán and Tenamaztle that November, and Mixtón fell in early 1542. Thousands were sent to the mines, in Peter Gerhard's words, and many captives were executed.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In spring 1540, the Caxcanes and their allies struck back, emboldened perhaps by the fact that Governor Francisco Vásquez de Coronado had taken more than 1,600 Spaniards and indigenous allies from the region northward

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Subsequent attacks by Alvarado were also unsuccessful and on June 24 Alvarado was injured when a horse fell on him. He died on July 4.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 9, 1541, he captured the city of Nochistlán and Tenamzaztle, but the indigenous leader later escaped.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In early 1542 the stronghold of Mixtón fell to the Spaniards and the rebellion was over.

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: thousands were dragged off in chains to the mines

citations.title: Mixtón War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: many of those captured after the fall of Mixtón were executed, some by cannon fire, some torn apart by dogs, and others stabbed

events.notes: Peter Gerhard's words are known here through Wikipedia's footnote, which cites him as quoted in Schmal; not read directly. Mendoza's force (450 Spaniards and 30,000-60,000 native troops) and the 15,000 defenders are left off: the first has a weak web footnote, the second is a Spanish estimate. Tenamaztle stayed at large until 1550. The point is Nochistlán, Tenamaztle's home, a stand-in: no page read locates the start of the rising, and the Mixtón hill is elsewhere in Zacatecas.

events.title: Xiu lord of Maní allies with the Spanish at Mérida
events.statement: On 6 January 1542 the Spanish under Francisco de Montejo the Younger founded the colonial town of Mérida at T'ho. On 23 January Tutul-Xiu, lord of Maní, the most powerful province of northern Yucatán, came to the encampment in peace with sorely needed food. He converted, was baptised Melchor and stayed two months for instruction. The Xiu alliance encouraged the western lords to accept Spanish rule, while the Cocom of Sotuta became implacable enemies.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On 6 January 1542, he founded the second permanent town council, calling the new colonial town Mérida. On 23 January, Tutul-Xiu, the lord of Maní, approached the Spanish encampment at Mérida in peace, bearing sorely needed food supplies.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: he was baptised as Melchor and stayed with the Spanish at Mérida for two months, receiving instruction in the Catholic faith. Tutul-Xiu was the ruler of the most powerful province of northern Yucatán

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: his submission to Spain and conversion to Christianity encouraged the lords of the western provinces to accept Spanish rule.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Xiu Maya of Maní allied themselves with the Spanish, while the Cocom Maya of Sotuta became the implacable enemies of the European colonisers.

citations.title: Francisco de Montejo the Younger (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a Spanish conquistador , who in 1542 founded the city of Mérida

events.notes: The founder follows Wikipedia's Montejo the Younger article; the conquest article's 'he founded' follows a sentence on the Younger's cousin, and may mean the cousin. Dates and the Xiu material are from the conquest article, a long referenced page.

events.title: Cocoliztli epidemic of 1545-1548
events.statement: The cocoliztli of 1545-1548, a major epidemic of the post-conquest population collapse, preferentially though not exclusively struck native people. Rodolfo Acuña-Soto and colleagues estimate 5 to 15 million dead; Christina Warinner and colleagues about 800,000 in the Valley of Mexico. Its cause is debated: ancient DNA from a cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca points to a Salmonella serotype, Paratyphi C, while Acuña-Soto's team argue for an indigenous viral hemorrhagic fever. A second large outbreak came in 1576.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Around 800,000 died in the Valley of Mexico

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cocoliztli seemed to preferentially, but not exclusively, target native people.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: recent bacterial genomic studies have suggested that Salmonella, specifically a serotype of Salmonella enterica known as Paratyphi C, was at least partially responsible for this initial outbreak.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Contact-era site has the only cemetery to be conclusively linked to victims of the outbreak of 1545–1548.

citations.title: Cocoliztli epidemics (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A second large outbreak of cocoliztli occurred in 1576, lasting until about 1580.

citations.title: Acuna-Soto et al., Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico (Emerging Infectious Diseases, 2002)
citations.quote: killed an estimated 5 million to 15 million people, or up to 80% of the native population of Mexico

citations.title: Acuna-Soto et al., Megadrought and Megadeath in 16th Century Mexico (Emerging Infectious Diseases, 2002)
citations.quote: appear to have been hemorrhagic fevers caused by an indigenous viral agent and aggravated by unusual climatic conditions

events.notes: Acuna-Soto et al. (2002) was read directly for the 5-15 million and the viral theory. Warinner et al. (2012) is known only through Wikipedia's footnote on the 800,000; not read directly. The point stands for the Valley of Mexico; the epidemic was wider. Caxcan removed from the participants: nothing read supports them.

events.title: Chichimeca War begins
events.statement: After a silver strike in 1546 drew Spaniards to Zacatecas, in the heart of La Gran Chichimeca, Zacatecos attacked supply routes in late 1550, and Guachichiles and Guamares joined in 1551. The war became the longest and most expensive Spanish campaign against Indigenous peoples in Aridoamerica. A war of fire and blood failed, and from 1590 the Spanish turned to a "Purchase for Peace", sending goods north and settling Tlaxcalan families among the Chichimecas.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 8, 1546, natives near the Cerro de la Bufa in what would become the city of Zacatecas showed the Spaniard Juan de Tolosa several pieces of silver-rich ore.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The first outbreak of hostilities was in late 1550 when Zacatecos attacked supply routes of Purépecha.

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1551 the Guachichile and Guamares joined in

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Chichimeca War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: to persuade 400 families of Tlaxcalan Indians, old allies of the Spanish, to establish eight settlements in Chichimeca areas.

events.notes: End date varies by source (1590 or 1600); Wikipedia uses 1550-1600 and records a Chichimeca military victory with the Spanish suing for peace. Zacatecos attacked Purépecha supply routes first, not Spanish ones, in the source's wording.

events.title: Tepehuán Revolt
events.statement: In 1616 Quautlatas, a baptised messianic leader, preached that the Tepehuán must kill or expel the Spaniards. On 16 November a wagon train was attacked outside Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes, with nearly simultaneous attacks on missions and settlements across the region. By the revolt's official end in 1620, according to Charlotte Gradie, over 200 Spaniards, 10 missionaries and perhaps 4,000 Tepehuán had died, many of hunger and disease. Missions and settlements were afterwards better protected by soldiers.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: a messianic leader named Quautlatas who had been baptized as a Christian

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: they must kill or expel all Spaniards, especially the missionaries, from their lands.

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 16, 1616, a wagon train traveling to Mexico City was attacked by the Tepehuán just outside Santa Catarina de Tepehuanes

citations.title: Tepehuán Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: nearly simultaneous attacks at missions and Spanish settlements occurred throughout the region

Jesuit writers blamed the devil and denied Spanish responsibility; the Tepehuán blamed baptism and disease, per the same article. Replaced the devotional jesuit.org.sg source.

events.title: Rarámuri war of 1648 and destruction of San Francisco de Borja mission
events.statement: The Parral mines' discovery in 1631 brought slave raids and more Jesuit missionaries into Rarámuri lands. In 1648 the Rarámuri went to war against the Spanish, gathered at Fariagic and destroyed the mission of San Francisco de Borja. Two leaders were captured and executed, and the Spanish founded Villa de Aguilar in the upper country. The Rarámuri then split: those in the lower missions moved into the Catholic population, while upper groups fought on under Tepóraca.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The discovery of the mines of Parral, Chihuahua, in 1631 increased Spanish presence in Rarámuri lands, bringing more slave raids and Jesuit missionaries.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)

citations.quote: From then on, the Rarámuri split into two groups. Those in the lower missions continued to move into the general Catholic population and largely lost their tribal identity.

citations.title: Rarámuri (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Those in the upper areas went to war under the leadership of Tepóraca

events.notes: One Wikipedia source only; no independent account read, so the card follows it closely.

events.title: Fall of Nojpetén to the Spanish
events.statement: Nojpetén, the island capital of the Itza kingdom on Lake Petén Itzá, had held out more than 150 years after the rest of Yucatán fell. When the friar Avendaño failed to persuade King Kan Ekʼ to convert and surrender, Martín de Ursúa reached the lake in February 1697 with 235 soldiers, by Grant Jones's account. His bombardment caused heavy loss of life and the defenders abandoned the city, the last independent native kingdom in the Americas to fall.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697, more than 150 years after the conquest of the rest of the Yucatán Peninsula

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Avendaño tried to convince Kan Ekʼ to convert to Christianity and surrender to the Spanish crown, without success.

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Martín de Ursúa y Arismendi arrived at the western shore of Lake Petén Itzá in February 1697 with 235 Spanish soldiers and 120 native labourers.

citations.title: Nojpetén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Spanish bombardment of the island caused heavy loss of life among the Itza defenders, who were forced to abandon the city.

citations.title: Spanish conquest of Petén (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: With the defeat of the Itza, the last independent and unconquered native kingdom in the Americas fell to European colonisers.

events.notes: Date conflict: the Petén conquest article gives 13 March 1697; the Nojpetén article has Ursúa launching the assault on 10 March. Jones is known here through Wikipedia's footnote (Jones 2009, p. 59); that footnote also pairs Schwartz 1990. Not read directly.

events.title: Caste War of Yucatán begins at Tepich
events.statement: The cacique Manuel Antonio Ay, accused of plotting an uprising, was executed on 26 July 1847. Yucatecan forces hunting his accomplices then burned Tepich. On 30 July Cecilio Chi, its Maya leader, attacked it with Jacinto Pat. Yucatán Today says he killed several white families; another account has him ordering all non-Maya killed after an indiscriminate massacre of Maya. The act is widely taken as the war's start, and by spring 1848 Maya forces held most of Yucatán.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: Manuel Antonio Ay was executed on July 26, 1847

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Searching for other insurgents, Méndez burned the town of Tepich and repressed its residents.

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cecilio Chi, the Maya leader of Tepich, with Jacinto Pat attacked Tepich on 30 July 1847. In reaction to the indiscriminate massacre of Maya that had taken place, Chi ordered that all the non-Maya population be killed.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: This act of retaliation is widely considered the official start of the Caste War of Yucatán.

citations.title: Caste War of Yucatán (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the spring of 1848, the Maya forces had taken over most of the Yucatán, except the walled cities of Campeche and Mérida and the southwest coast.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatán (Yucatán Today)
citations.quote: seized the town and killed several white families.

citations.title: The Caste War or Maya Social War of Yucatan - Yucatan Today

events.notes: Start date varies: 30 June, 13 July and 30 July 1847 appear in different accounts; Wikipedia's Caste War article gives 30 July. Yucatán Today's 600 men is left off. Who burned Tepich: Wikipedia names Méndez, Yucatán Today the Yucatecan army. The Cruzob are removed from the participants: they did not exist yet in 1847. Added a quote for the uprising Ay was accused of planning.

events.title: Fall of El Añil, the Yaqui fortress
events.statement: In 1876 the Yaqui leader Cajemé set up a small independent republic in Sonora, defended by El Añil, a moated fortress near Vícam. In May 1886 Mexican troops took it: on the 5th by the Texas Band of Yaqui Indians' history, the 12th by another account. That history places the 12 May fight at Buatachive, where General Ángel Martínez's troops killed 200 Yaqui and captured hundreds of women and children, while Cajemé escaped. Cajemé was executed in 1887.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1876 the Yaqui leader José Maria Leyba Peres, or Cajemé, established a small independent republic in Sonora.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: El Añil was located near the village of Vícam, in the middle of a thick forest and on the left bank of the Yaqui river. The fortification consisted of a wide moat.

citations.title: Yaqui Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: El Añil was captured on May 12, 1886. Only a few Yaqui soldiers escaped by fleeing deep into the mountains, leaving 200 dead, and some 2,000 people, consisting primarily of the elderly, children, and the sick.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: Cajemé was apprehended and executed in 1887, and the Mexican army occupied Yaqui land.

citations.title: History (Texas Band of Yaqui Indians)
citations.quote: On May 5, the fortified site of Anil was captured after a pitched battle.

citations.title: History (Texas Band of Yaqui Indians)
citations.quote: On May 12, after a four-day siege, Mexican troops under General Angel Martinez, attacked Buatachive. In a three-hour battle, the Mexican forces killed 200 Yaqui soldiers, while capturing hundreds of women and children.

citations.title: History (Texas Band of Yaqui Indians)
citations.quote: Cajeme and a couple thousand Yaquis managed to escape the siege.

citations.title: Yaqui (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: In 1886 almost four thousand Yaquis were captured during the Battle of Buatachive.

events.notes: Dated to the month because Wikipedia's Yaqui Wars merges two fights: it has El Añil falling on 12 May with 200 dead, while the Texas Band of Yaqui Indians gives El Añil 5 May and Buatachive 12 May. Wikipedia's force sizes (1,200 and 1,500) are footnoted to Francisco P. Troncoso (1905), known only through that footnote, and left off since they sit in the merged passage. Encyclopedia.com has almost four thousand captured at Buatachive.

events.title: Coronado's army takes Hawikuh (Cibola)
events.statement: Coronado's entrada came north in search of gold, drawn by Fray Marcos de Niza's claim that Hawikuh was one of the Seven Cities of Cibola. It met Zuni warriors near Hawikuh in July 1540, inflicted casualties and captured the village. Women, children and most provisions had already been moved to the sacred mesa of Dowa Yalanne, and the men soon followed. The Spanish found no gold.

citations.title: Zuni (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Hawikuh was claimed by Niza to be one of the Seven Cities of Cibola

citations.title: Zuni (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Spanish met 600 Zuni warriors near Hawikuh in July 1540, inflicting several casualties, and capturing the village.

citations.title: Zuni (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: Coronado and his party defeated the Zuni at Hawikkuh but found that women, Children, and most provisions had been removed to the sacred stronghold mesa, Dowa Yalanne. The men escaped and soon followed.

citations.title: Zuni (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: having found no gold.

events.notes: The 600 warriors and the force of 230 horse and 70 foot are left off: Wikipedia's passage names no giver, and those figures can only be a part of the 1,600 who went north (see na-e-007). Encyclopedia.com spells the town Hawikkuh. No Zuni account of the fight was read; both sources draw on the Spanish side.

events.title: Oñate's colony is founded at Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)
events.statement: Juan de Oñate's expedition left in March 1598, and on 30 April he claimed the land across the Rio Grande for Spain. It reached the Tewa pueblo of Ohkay Owingeh on 11 July, where the people were recorded as hospitable, and next day he renamed Caypa pueblo San Juan de los Caballeros. It was the first capital of the new province; the capital moved to Santa Fe in 1610. Oñate let colonists demand tribute from Native peoples.

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: accompanied by a caravan of Catholic missionaries, a thousand soldiers, colonists, and Tlaxcalans.

citations.title: Juan de Oñate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Oñate led the party in prayer, as he claimed all of the territory across the river for the Spanish Empire.

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: arrived at Yúngéh (place of the mockingbird) in present-day Ohkay Owingeh on July 11, 1598.

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was recorded that the people who met him that day were hospitable and offered Yuque Yunque pueblo as guest quarters to Oñate and his party.

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: he baptized and renamed Caypa pueblo (present-day Ohkay Owingeh) as San Juan de los Caballeros

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: San Juan de los Caballeros became the first capital of the New Spanish region of Santa Fe de Nuevo Méjico.

citations.title: Juan de Oñate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Oñate granted land to colonists on the expedition, and empowered them to demand tribute from Native Americans.

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Dated to the arrival, 11 July 1598; the renaming was 12 July. The Oñate article's reference list names San Gabriel de Yunque-Ouinge, which most histories put as the seat between San Juan and Santa Fe; the card keeps to what was read. The 'thousand soldiers' in that article looks too high and stays off the card.

events.title: Acoma massacre
events.statement: In December 1598 Juan de Zaldívar, nephew of New Mexico's colonizer Juan de Oñate, demanded food at Acoma; refused, his men reportedly took it by force. The Acoma killed him and eleven to fourteen others. The Spanish reprisal began on 22 January 1599, and estimates of the Acoma dead run from about 800 to 1,500. Oñate sentenced some 500 prisoners: men over twenty-five were to be enslaved for twenty years and lose a foot, and twenty-four suffered the amputation.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Spanish envoy demanded food and shelter for himself and his sixteen men.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Acoma resisted and a fight ensued, leaving Zaldívar and eleven of his men dead.

citations.title: Acoma Pueblo: Ancient City in the Sky (National Park Service)
citations.quote: residents lured Captain Juan de Zaldívar, one of Oñate's officers, into the pueblo and murdered him and fourteen of his men.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The main battle between the Acoma and the Spaniards began the following morning, January 22.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: An estimated 500 men were killed in the battle, along with about 300 women and children.

citations.title: Acoma Pueblo: Ancient City in the Sky (National Park Service)
citations.quote: A bitter battle resulted in the sacking and burning of much of the pueblo and the death of approximately 1,500 residents.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some 500 prisoners were taken and later sentenced by Oñate to a variety of punishments after a trial was held at San Juan Pueblo.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Oñate ordered that every male above the age of twenty-five would have his right foot cut off and be enslaved for a period of twenty years. Twenty-four men suffered amputation.

citations.title: Acoma Massacre (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Sources differ on: the first clash (Wikipedia's Oñate article: October 1598; massacre article and NPS: December 1598); Spanish dead (12, 13 or 15); and the day Vicente de Zaldívar arrived (EBSCO: 11 January; Wikipedia: 21 January). Wikipedia's estimate of 500 men and 300 women and children names no giver, so the card credits Wikipedia with its 800. EBSCO says only 'more than five hundred' prisoners. Men twelve to twenty-five and women over twelve were also sentenced to twenty years. No Acoma account was read; the detail looks to come from the Spanish side. Moved from the card: the National Park Service has fourteen men killed, 'lured' into the pueblo, and about 1,500 Acoma dead; Wikipedia has eleven and about 800.

events.title: Pueblo Revolt
events.statement: Spanish rule, and cruelties such as Acoma, had stoked Pueblo anger. Popé of Ohkay Owingeh planned a rising, and runners carried knotted maguey cords to count down the days. Informants told Governor Otermín it would come on 13 August 1680, but Popé moved it up to the 10th. The Pueblos killed about 400 settlers and 21 of 33 priests and besieged Santa Fe. On 21 August Otermín led over a thousand settlers south, reaching El Paso on 29 September.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: Runners were sent out bearing knotted maguey cords, each knot representing one day.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: Governor Antonio de Otermín was told by informants that the revolt would occur on August 13, but Popé had advanced the day to August 10

citations.title: Ohkay Owingeh, New Mexico (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Po'pay was a local man

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (EBSCO Research Starters)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (EBSCO Research Starters)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)

The Hopi villages, without the change of date, rose on the original schedule. Wikipedia's Vargas article says the Spanish stayed in exile 16 years, counting differently.

events.title: Vargas retakes Santa Fe
events.statement: The Spanish came back twelve years later. Diego de Vargas reached Santa Fe on 13 September 1692 with soldiers, native auxiliaries and seven cannons, promised clemency, and next day proclaimed repossession, often called a bloodless reconquest. When he returned with settlers in December 1693 the town opposed him, and he retook it by force. Seventy participants in the revolt were executed and about 400 women and children sentenced to ten years' servitude. Fourteen pueblos attempted another revolt in 1696.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: De Vargas, with only sixty soldiers, one hundred Indian auxiliaries or native soldiers, seven cannons (which he used as leverage against the Pueblo inside Santa Fe), and one Franciscan priest, arrived at Santa Fe on September 13.

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Diego de Vargas (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Pueblo Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: This time, however, 70 Pueblo warriors and 400 family members within the town opposed his entry.

events.notes: Date conflict: Wikipedia's Pueblo Revolt article says 14 September 1692; its Vargas article says 12 September. Force sizes differ (Pueblo Revolt: sixty soldiers; Vargas: 150 soldiers and pro-Spanish Pueblo warriors; about 100 soldiers on the return of 1693), with no named giver, so they are left off. Lamadrid is known only through Wikipedia; not read directly. Confidence set to high: the event is established; only one of its dates differs by a day or two.

events.title: Destruction of Awatovi
events.statement: The Spanish rebuilt the mission of San Bernardo de Aguatubi at the Hopi town of Awatovi after 1692, and tension grew there between converted Hopis and traditionalists. About 1700 the extreme hostility of most Hopis to the converts led to the pueblo's destruction. In accounts drawing on Hopi tradition, the attackers killed the men and scattered the women and children among other villages. The site was never reoccupied and remains a ruin.

citations.title: Awatovi (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Not long afterward, the Spaniards rebuilt the mission of San Bernardo de Aguatubi.

citations.title: Awatovi (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1700, tensions began to grow in the pueblo of Awatovi between the converted Hopis and traditionalists.

citations.title: Awatovi (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the end of 1700, the extreme hostility of most Hopis to Christian converts at Awatovi led to the destruction of the pueblo.

citations.title: Awatovi (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The attackers killed all the men at Awatovi, and scattered the women and children among the other villages. The site was never reoccupied.

citations.title: Hopi Tribe (EBSCO Research Starters)

events.notes: Kept short because both sources are brief outside summaries; no Hopi oral account was read, and neither gives a death toll or names the attacking villages. Sources give 'about the year 1700' and 'by the end of 1700', so the date is circa. The label of tradition rests on Awatovi's footnotes to Ekkehart Malotki, Hopi Tales of Destruction (2002), not read directly. The event was internal to the Hopi.

events.title: Taos Revolt
events.statement: On 19 January 1847 Hispano and Pueblo insurgents rose against the US occupation at Taos and Taos Pueblo, led by Pablo Montoya and Tomás Romero of Taos Pueblo. Romero's force killed Governor Charles Bent in Taos. US troops and volunteers beat back some 1,500 insurgents, in Wikipedia's account, who took refuge in the church at Taos Pueblo. By Lewis Garrard's 1850 memoir, cannon fire killed about 150 there and 400 men were captured; Wikipedia has at least 28 hanged.

citations.title: Taos Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On the morning of January 19, 1847, the insurrectionists began the revolt in Don Fernando de Taos, present-day Taos, New Mexico and nearby Taos Pueblo.

citations.title: Taos Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They were led by Pablo Montoya, a Hispano with Taos Pueblo ancestry, and Tomás Romero from Taos Pueblo

citations.title: Taos Pueblo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tomás Romero led a group of Taos Puebloans to Charles Bent's house in the town of Taos. The governor was shot with arrows, scalped, and killed.

citations.title: Taos Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the combined forces beat back a force of some 1,500 Hispanos and Puebloans at Santa Cruz de la Cañada and Embudo Pass. The insurgents retreated to Taos Pueblo, where they took refuge in the thick-walled adobe church.

citations.title: Taos Revolt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the U.S. breached a wall of the church and directed cannon fire into the interior, inflicting many casualties and killing about 150 rebels. They captured 400 more men after close hand-to-hand fighting.

citations.title: Taos Revolt (Wikipedia)

events.notes: The 150 and 400 are footnoted in Wikipedia to Lewis Garrard's Wah-to-yah and the Taos Trail (1850), an American memoir, known here only through that footnote; the page presents him as eyewitness of the trials, not the church fight. The infobox has about 367 rebels killed overall. Wikipedia's Taos Revolt article has Bent left alive when the attackers moved on, then dying next door; Taos Pueblo's article compresses this. Mexico removed from the participants: nothing read supports it as a party.

events.title: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo

place.name: Villa de Guadalupe Hidalgo (Basilica of Guadalupe)

events.statement: The Mexican–American War ended with the treaty signed on 2 February 1848, which transferred northern Mexico, Ute territory among it, to the United States for $15 million. Article XI bound the Americans to prevent and punish Indian raids into Mexico, since Mexicans believed they had encouraged the Comanche and Apache raids that devastated the north. It proved unenforceable: Mexico filed 366 claims for raid damage by 1853, when Article XI was annulled.

citations.title: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: officially ended the Mexican–American War (1846–1848). It was signed on the 2nd of February 1848 in the town of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

events.title: The Gadsden Purchase (Treaty of La Mesilla)
events.statement: The United States wanted one more strip of Mexico, for a southern transcontinental railroad. At the close of 1853 James Gadsden and Santa Anna signed a first draft at $15 million; it was cut to 29,640 square miles of southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico for $10 million and took effect on 8 June 1854. The Tohono O'odham Nation records that this split O'odham land almost in half and that they were never told of the sale.

events.title: Bascom affair
events.statement: After raiders took livestock and young Felix Ward from a Sonoita ranch, Lt. George Bascom met the Chiricahua leader Cochise at Apache Pass. Cochise denied knowing of the raid. Bascom tried to hold him and his family hostage, but he escaped. Cochise then tortured and killed nine Mexican teamsters and seized three Americans, and on 19 February 1861 the army hanged his brother and nephews. His war of vengeance began the Apache Wars. Coyotero Apaches had taken the boy.

citations.title: Bascom Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Tonto Apache parties raided the ranch of John Ward at Sonoita Creek, stealing several head of livestock and kidnapping Ward's 12-year-old stepson Felix Ward.

citations.title: Bascom Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: At the meeting Cochise claimed he knew nothing of the raid.

citations.title: Bascom Massacre (Wikipedia)

events.notes: The same article first says Tonto Apache parties raided, then that Coyotero Apaches were responsible; the card uses the later determination. The NPS Fort Bowie page says the army hanged Cochise's family, while Wikipedia names his brother and nephews. The Americans held by Cochise were killed on his flight to Sonora.

events.title: Battle of Apache Pass
events.statement: On 15 July 1862 Capt. Thomas Roberts's California Column detachment, with two mountain howitzers, entered Apache Pass low on water. Cochise, who had recruited Mangas Coloradas and his bands, attacked with about 150 warriors by the National Park Service's reckoning; other counts run higher. Capt. John Cremony later quoted an unnamed Apache who put 63 killed by artillery. The memory of the Bascom Affair was a key motive for Cochise, and the army then built Fort Bowie in the pass.

citations.quote: supply wagons, livestock, and two mountain howitzers

events.notes: Strength differs three ways: NPS about 150; Wikipedia's text about 500; its infobox about 200, none of the last two with a named giver. The 63 is Cremony's report, as Wikipedia gives it; his book was not read directly. Roberts's report via Carleton has about 10 Apache killed. NPS dates the fight 15-16 July and describes the Apache ambushing the column's rear.

events.title: Carson's campaign in Canyon de Chelly
events.statement: Under General Carleton's orders, Colonel Kit Carson used a scorched-earth policy to starve the Diné out of their homeland. In January 1864 parties under Carson and Captain Albert Pfeiffer went through the Canyon de Chelly area from Fort Canby, killing 23 people, seizing sheep and destroying hogans and peach orchards. The canyon's ledges stayed relatively safe, but the crops and herds did not. Starving and freezing, Diné followed the troops back to Fort Canby in great numbers to surrender.

citations.quote: used a scorched earth policy to starve the Navajo out of their traditional homeland and force them to surrender.

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajos (EBSCO Research Starters)
citations.quote: In January, 1864, scouting parties led by Carson and Captain Albert Pfeiffer left Fort Canby, taking parallel routes through the Canyon de Chelly area north of the fort.

citations.title: Long Walk of the Navajos (EBSCO Research Starters)

events.notes: Wikipedia's Canyon de Chelly article dates the sweep 1863; EBSCO and Wikipedia's Long Walk article date the assault to January 1864. EBSCO agrees on twenty-three killed. Sources use 'Navajo'; the card uses Diné as the catalogue title does.

events.title: The Long Walk to Bosque Redondo begins
events.statement: By March 1864 six thousand Diné had gathered at the forts, and the US Army began marching them to Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico, some as far as 300 miles. In all about 10,000 Navajo and 500 Mescalero Apache were driven there. Between one in five and one in four of the Navajo died on the journey, and their oral tradition recounts soldiers shooting those who could not keep up. They would not go home until 1868.

Wikipedia's Long Walk gives up to 3,500 deaths over the four years, and 2,500 to 3,500 in the infobox, footnoted to the same blog and to M. Annette Jaimes (1992), not read directly; left off because the blog itself gives only the proportion. EBSCO counts more than eight thousand held at Bosque Redondo. Wikipedia has 53 marches from August 1864, EBSCO the first in March 1864. The Mescalero were already held there by some accounts.

events.title: The Treaty of Bosque Redondo
events.statement: Four years after the Long Walk, General William Sherman and Samuel Tappan reached Fort Sumner on 28 May 1868 to meet Barboncito and ten headmen. Sherman first proposed moving the Diné to Indian Territory; Barboncito refused. Twenty-nine made their mark on 1 June, on a treaty that ended the Navajo Wars and let those interned go home. It effectively established Navajo sovereignty, yet to the historian Jennifer Nez Denetdale it marks the loss of their freedom and autonomy.
