events.title: Camp Grant massacre

place.name: Camp Grant massacre site (San Pedro River)

events.statement: Lt. Royal Whitman had given nearly 500 Aravaipa and Pinal Apaches a refuge near Camp Grant. After Apaches ran off livestock from San Xavier, in Wikipedia's account six Americans, 48 Mexican Americans and 92 Tohono O'odham, organised by William Oury and Jesús María Elías, surrounded it at dawn on 30 April 1871, most men away hunting. All but eight of the dead, it says, were women and children. Twenty-seven captured children were enslaved. A Tucson jury acquitted in 19 minutes.

events.title: Brunot Agreement takes the San Juan Mountains from the Ute
events.statement: After the Utes refused a cession in 1868, a new commission under Felix Brunot negotiated with the Confederated Utes at the Los Pinos Agency, signing on 13 September 1873. The Southern Ute Tribe records that the Utes were led to believe they would allow mining only in the San Juan Mountains, but ended up forcibly relinquishing the lands. Utes most often remember it as the agreement when their land was fraudulently taken. A 2009 memorandum secured hunting rights there.

events.title: Meeker Massacre and Battle of Milk Creek (White River War)
events.statement: White River agent Nathan Meeker angered the Utes by withholding supplies to force farming and plowing a field they used for horses. His panicked telegrams brought cavalry, though the Utes had been promised no troops would enter their reservation; the historian Charles Marsh describes an armed force bearing down on a peaceful camp. On 29 September 1879 the Utes ambushed the column at Milk Creek and attacked the agency, killing Meeker. Colorado Newsline counts about two dozen dead each side.

The war cost the Utes most of their Colorado lands and removed the White River and Uncompahgre Utes. Title and date cover both Milk Creek and the agency.

events.title: Battle of Cibecue Creek
events.statement: Nock-ay-det-klinne, a respected Cibecue Apache medicine man, had been holding ghost dances at Cibecue over corruption and bad conditions on the Fort Apache reservation. On 30 August 1881 soldiers arrested him and were ambushed taking him to the fort. They killed him, and most of the 23 Apache scouts mutinied, the largest such action in US history. The soldiers retreated to Fort Apache, and in the unrest White Mountain warriors left to join Geronimo.

events.title: Geronimo's final surrender at Skeleton Canyon
events.statement: Worn down by Capt. Henry Lawton's pursuit and persuaded by Lt. Charles Gatewood, Geronimo and his small band returned to the United States and surrendered to General Miles at Skeleton Canyon on 4 September 1886. One condition was that they would see their families in Florida, but Miles decided all terms were void. They went by train from Fort Bowie to prison at Fort Pickens, not reunited as promised. The Chiricahua were kept as prisoners of war.

events.title: Quechan rising at the Yuma Crossing
events.statement: Anza established friendly relations with the Quechan, who controlled the Yuma Crossing, in 1774, but as Spanish use of the crossing grew, Spain felt it had to control it, straining relations. From 17 to 19 July 1781 the Quechan rose, killing four priests and thirty soldiers and damaging the mission settlements of San Pedro y San Pablo de Bicuñer and Purísima Concepción. Spain retaliated the next year, but never again tried to control the Quechan or the crossing.

events.title: Mohave War
events.statement: When the Rose-Baley emigrants camped at Beale's Crossing, in Mohave territory, they cut the Mohaves' valuable cottonwoods and clashed over stolen cattle, and the Mohave and Walapai attacked. William Hoffman's first expedition fought Cairook's men at Beaver Lake in January 1859, ten to twelve falling by his own account. In April a force of over 600 reached the Colorado, founding Fort Mohave. Hoffman pressed the chiefs to accept roads, forts and immigrants, and the Mohave made peace that year.

events.notes: Mostly one Wikipedia article. The Fort Mojave Indian Tribe's site dates the post to 1859 and calls it Camp Colorado, soon renamed Fort Mojave. Dropped the earlier 'Beale Road' cause as a simplification: the article ties the first fight to cattle and cottonwoods at the crossing, and the Beale Road served the emigrants.

events.title: Battle of Cieneguilla
events.statement: Lieutenant John Davidson's 60 dragoons fought Jicarilla Apaches, possibly with Ute allies, near Pilar on 30 March 1854. Accounts differ: an unauthorized attack on their camp, an ambush by about 250 Apaches and Utes (Homer Davidson's figure), or, in a modern version, dragoons taunted into attacking; Davidson reported simply coming upon them. After two to four hours 22 soldiers were dead and 36 wounded, forcing a retreat. Native dead are put at about 20, or by Will Gorenfeld about 50.

Davidson, Black Jack Davidson (1974), known only through Wikipedia's footnote; Will Gorenfeld (Wild West, 2008, footnote) gives 200 to 300 warriors and about 50 killed, while the Jicarilla War article says about 20. The Cieneguilla article itself also says the Apache and Ute laid an ambush, against 'unauthorized attack'. Battle lasted two or four hours per survivor James Bennett, in another article. To fit the three accounts, the trim dropped two lesser points: the Jicarilla War article and the battle's infobox name the leader Flechas Rayadas or Rayada (not Homer Davidson's attribution), and the Santa Fe Weekly Gazette called it 'one of the severest battles that ever took place between American troops and Red Indians' (citation removed with it).

events.title: The Fort Laramie (Horse Creek) Treaty of 1851

place.name: Mouth of Horse Creek, near Morrill, Nebraska
place.note: Wikidata's point for the mouth of Horse Creek on the North Platte; the exact treaty ground isn't marked.

events.statement: In September 1851 thousands gathered at the mouth of Horse Creek, 30 miles below Fort Laramie, whose own surroundings lacked food for the horses. The treaty signed there on the 17th set out territories for the Cheyenne, Sioux, Arapaho, Crow, Assiniboine, Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara and allowed roads and forts in exchange for $50,000 a year for fifty years. The Senate cut that to ten years, only the Crow refusing, and several nations never received what was promised.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty was negotiated and signed at the mouth of Horse Creek, 30 miles (48 km) downriver from Fort Laramie, because the area around Fort Laramie lacked food for the horses.

citations.quote: The treaty council was attended by thousands of Sioux men and their families

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Laramie (1851) (Wikipedia)

events.notes: The North Dakota Studies point that there were too few interpreters is in the citations but left off the card for length. Its 'did not establish a reservation' is also useful context. The point is now the creek's mouth (Wikidata, Q128927906); it was Fort Laramie's, under that site's qid.

events.title: Grattan fight (Grattan massacre)

place.name: Grattan massacre site, east of Fort Laramie

events.statement: In August 1854 about 4,000 Sichangu and Oglala, by Wikipedia's account, were camped under the 1851 treaty when a visiting Miniconjou, High Forehead, killed a Mormon emigrant's stray cow. On 19 August John Grattan's contingent entered the camp to seize him, though such matters were the Indian agent's. A soldier fatally shot Chief Matȟó Wayúhi (Conquering Bear), and the Lakotas returned fire, killing 29 to 31 by its figures, including Grattan and an interpreter. It began the First Sioux War.

citations.title: Grattan massacre (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Grattan massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: strayed and was killed by a visiting Miniconjou (Sioux) named High Forehead.

citations.title: Grattan massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A small contingent of soldiers entered a large Sioux camp to apprehend an individual accused of killing a settler's cow, despite the fact that such issues were supposed to be resolved by the US Indian agent according to treaty agreements.

citations.quote: Start of the First Sioux War

events.notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives 31 US killed; its lead 29 soldiers including the interpreter. One Wikipedia source only; the card gives both. Coordinates are those of the event's Wikidata item.

events.title: U.S.-Dakota War of 1862 begins
events.statement: By summer 1862 Dakota people on the reservation were starving; annuities were late and traders refused credit. On 17 August four Dakota hunters killed five settlers at Acton Township. That night a group of Mdewakanton men persuaded a reluctant Ta Oyate Duta (Little Crow) to all-out war, while others argued for peace. The next day his party attacked the Lower Sioux Agency and homesteads, beginning a war of five or six weeks.

events.title: Mankato mass execution of 38 Dakota men
events.statement: A military commission tried 392 Dakota prisoners, sentencing 303 to death by 5 November 1862. President Lincoln and government lawyers reviewed the transcripts, and when only two men were found guilty of rape he widened the criteria to those in massacres of civilians. He sent a list of 39 names; one man was reprieved. On 26 December 38 Dakota men were hanged together at Mankato, before an estimated 4,000 spectators, the largest mass hanging in US history.

events.notes: A mass execution after trials.

events.title: The Sand Creek massacre

place.name: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site

events.statement: At the army's command Black Kettle settled his people, around 750 Cheyenne and Arapaho, at Big Sandy Creek. On 29 November 1864 Colonel John Chivington's Colorado troops attacked; Captain Silas Soule and Lieutenant Joseph Cramer told their men to hold fire. Chivington claimed 500 to 600 warriors killed, but estimates of the dead run from about 70 to 230, mostly women, children and the elderly. A congressional committee later said it could hardly find fitting terms to describe his conduct.

events.title: Fetterman Fight (Battle of the Hundred in the Hands)
events.statement: On 21 December 1866, during Red Cloud's War, a group of ten warriors including Crazy Horse lured Captain William Fetterman's detachment from Fort Phil Kearny into an ambush by Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters. All 81 men were killed, then the army's worst disaster on the Great Plains. The ground, on the Bozeman Trail, was Crow land under the 1851 treaty, taken by these traditional enemies of the Crow without Crow consent.

citations.title: Fetterman Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a battle during Red Cloud's War on December 21, 1866, between a confederation of the Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho tribes and a detachment of the United States Army, based at Fort Phil Kearny, Wyoming.

citations.title: Fetterman Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A group of ten warriors, including Crazy Horse, acted to lure a detachment of U.S. soldiers into an ambush.

events.title: The Medicine Lodge treaties
events.statement: In October 1867 a US Indian Peace Commission signed three treaties at Medicine Lodge Creek, Kansas: with the Kiowa and Comanche, with the Plains Apache, and with the Arapaho and Cheyenne. The United States promised peace and protection in return for relocation to reservations in western Indian Territory, and neither side honoured all the articles. Article Twelve required three-fourths of adult men to approve later cessions; a 1900 allotment without such consent led to Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock.

citations.title: Medicine Lodge Treaty (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In October 1867 a U.S. Indian Peace Commission signed three treaties at Medicine Lodge Creek near Medicine Lodge, Kansas. One treaty was made with the Kiowa and Comanche, a second confederated the Plains Apache with the Kiowa and Comanche

events.notes: One reference source, the Oklahoma Historical Society's encyclopedia. The Senate ratified the treaties in July 1868. The source dates Lone Wolf to 1901, an error (it was decided in 1903); the card gives no year.

events.title: The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868
events.statement: Red Cloud's Lakota had fought the army over the Bozeman Trail forts on Sioux treaty land. The treaty signed from 29 April 1868 by Lakota, Yanktonai, Santee and Arapaho leaders ended that war: it recognized the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation, and the government promised to close the trail and its forts. No later cession would be valid unless three-fourths of adult Sioux men signed. In 1874 Custer's expedition found gold there, and miners moved in.

citations.quote: Yanktonai, Hunkpapa, Blackfeet, Cuthead, Two Kettle, Sans Arcs, and Santee) and the Arapaho.

citations.title: Fort Laramie Treaty (National Archives)

events.title: The Battle of the Washita River (Washita massacre)
events.statement: When the Medicine Lodge treaty failed to end raids, General Philip Sheridan planned a winter campaign. On 27 November 1868 Lieutenant Colonel George Custer's 7th Cavalry attacked a Southern Cheyenne camp of perhaps 250 people on the Washita, under the Peace Chief Black Kettle, the survivor of Sand Creek. He was killed trying to cross the river. Estimates of the dead range from 13 to 150, military figures running higher than Cheyenne ones, and 53 women and children were captured.

events.title: Red River War begins: Second Battle of Adobe Walls
events.statement: Angered by delayed rations and white buffalo hunters on the Texas Panhandle, the Quahadas under Quanah and the medicine man Isa-tai formed a multitribal alliance. On 27 June 1874 some 700 warriors, Cheyennes, Arapahoes, Kiowas and Comanches by the Handbook of Texas's count, attacked 28 hunters and one woman at Adobe Walls. The hunters' superior weapons fended them off, and the raid was a disaster for the attackers. It may be considered the official beginning of the Red River War.

citations.title: Red River War (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: continued delays and shortages in rations, fears of white encroachment on Indian land, and, especially, the movement of white buffalo hunters onto the plains of the Texas Panhandle

citations.quote: the Quahadas, under the guidance of Quanah and a medicine man named Isa-tai, formed a multitribal alliance dedicated to expelling the hunters from the plains.

citations.title: Parker, Quanah (Handbook of Texas Online)

citations.title: Red River War (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)

events.notes: Wikipedia estimates about 30 killed on the attacking side, 4 among the hunters. Its article describes only Comanche forces in the lead, though its infobox lists Comanche, Cheyenne and Kiowa. The war's decisive engagement was at Palo Duro Canyon in September 1874.

events.title: The Battle of the Little Bighorn (Greasy Grass)
events.statement: Lakota leaders such as Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse rejected the reservation system, and the army's 1876 campaign aimed to force the nonreservation Lakota and Cheyenne to capitulate. On 25 and 26 June, along the river the Lakota know as the Greasy Grass, Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors fought the 7th Cavalry and its Crow and Arikara scouts. They forced Major Reno to retreat, then converged on Custer's command, whose last men were cornered and killed.

events.notes: Battle spanned two days; dated to 25 June, the day of Custer's fight. Wikipedia's infobox gives 268 US killed and 31 to 100 Native killed with no author traced for either, so both tolls are left off.

events.title: The Black Hills taken
events.statement: In 1876 Congress denied the Sioux their treaty annuities until they gave up the Black Hills. A commission's "agreement" was signed by only 10% of adult Sioux men, far short of the 1868 treaty's three-fourths, and on 28 February 1877 Congress enacted it. In 1980 the Supreme Court held that the Sioux had never received just compensation. They refused the award, the Sioux Nation stating that its goal was the land's return.

events.notes: Wikipedia says the award was worth over $1 billion as of 2011. An act of Congress implementing a disputed agreement, not a treaty. The point is the centre of the Black Hills, in round figures.

events.title: The Wounded Knee massacre
events.statement: Alarm over the Ghost Dance at Pine Ridge brought the 7th Cavalry to Chief Spotted Elk's (Big Foot's) band near Wounded Knee Creek. On 29 December 1890 the soldiers surrounded them and demanded their weapons. A fight broke out and a shot was fired, from which side is unclear. Estimates of the Lakota dead run from about 150 to about 300, many of them women and children. Twenty-five soldiers died, and nineteen soldiers were awarded the Medal of Honor.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1837 on the Upper Missouri
events.statement: Smallpox spread across the Great Plains from 1836 to 1840, peaking after spring 1837, when the steamboat St. Peter's carried infected people upriver. In 1839 the Indian Affairs Commissioner, conceding the dead could not be counted, gave 17,200 on the upper Missouri and thought double that not too large east of the Rockies. The National Park Service says the Mandan fell to as few as 125, survivors joining the Hidatsa and Arikara; trader Francis Chardon wrote both twenty-three and twenty-seven.

citations.quote: Between 1836 and 1840, smallpox became widespread across the Great Plains. The epidemic reached its height following the spring of 1837, when an American Fur Company steamboat, the SS St. Peter's, carried infected people and supplies up the Missouri River

Reworded the Commissioner's figure: the report gives 17,200 for the upper Missouri Indians and thought twice that not too large for all east of the Rockies. Statement now says the 17,200 are deaths and keeps the Commissioner's caveat.

events.title: Spanish-Comanche peace treaty (Anza)
events.statement: Comanche raids on Taos drew Governor Juan Bautista de Anza north in 1779 with Spanish troops and Ute and Apache allies; on Greenhorn Creek he won a decisive victory in which Chief Cuerno Verde and other leaders died. After a further campaign in 1783 the Comanche were suing for peace by 1784, and a formal treaty followed at Pecos Pueblo on 28 February 1786, opening the Comanchero trade. In Texas, a separate Spanish-Comanche treaty dates from 1785.

No Comanche account in either source. Handbook of Texas gives the Texas treaty; Anza's is New Mexico's.

events.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Dull Knife and Little Wolf)
events.statement: Placed on the Southern Cheyenne reservation in Indian Territory, about 300 Northern Cheyenne men, women and children headed north in September 1878. In Nebraska they split into two groups of about equal numbers. One reached Montana; the other was captured and held at Fort Robinson. In January 1879 those prisoners escaped, and most were captured or killed in the pursuit. Those who survived were allowed to remain in the north.

citations.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: after being placed on the Southern Cheyenne reservation in the Indian Territory

citations.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In September 1878, about 300 Cheyenne men, women, and children headed north from their reservation

citations.title: Northern Cheyenne Exodus (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Kept shorter because only Wikipedia was read and the group's size and tolls vary inside it: lead about 300; infobox 297; the page's own 353 left. Infobox gives about 50 Cheyenne killed. The names Little Wolf and Dull Knife are in the title and the catalogue participants.

events.title: Ponca removal to Indian Territory
events.statement: The United States ceded Ponca land to the Sioux in 1868 and, rather than renegotiate, removed the Ponca to Indian Territory in 1877. It neither obtained the chiefs' consent nor provided an adequate reservation. The Oklahoma Historical Society reports estimates of nearly 158, almost a third of the tribe, dying in the first years. After his son's death subchief Standing Bear returned to Nebraska, and Standing Bear v. Crook (1879) held Indians to be persons who could sue.

citations.title: Ponca (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)

events.notes: Months of the removal vary by source and are omitted. The decision split the Ponca into northern and southern bands.

events.title: Battle of Seven Oaks (Victory of the Frog Plain)
events.statement: In the Pemmican War between the Hudson's Bay and North West companies, some 60 or 70 Métis under Cuthbert Grant, by the Dictionary of Canadian Biography's count, were bringing pemmican for the NWC brigade on 19 June 1816. HBC governor Robert Semple met them at Seven Oaks with about 25 men. A verbal altercation led to a skirmish in which he and about 20 of his party died. It helped bring about the two companies' merger in 1821.

citations.quote: was a violent confrontation of the Pemmican War between the Hudson's Bay Company (HBC) and the North West Company (NWC) which occurred on 19 June 1816

citations.title: Semple, Robert (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)

events.notes: Wikipedia's infobox: 65 against 28, with 1 and 21 killed. Fort Douglas surrendered the next day. Two of Grant's party were tried for murder and acquitted. Replaced The Canadian Encyclopedia, whose page refused the fetch (403). Wikipedia also calls it the Seven Oaks Massacre.

events.title: Selkirk Treaty (Peguis and Lord Selkirk)
events.statement: On 18 July 1817 Peguis and four other Saulteaux and Cree chiefs signed a treaty with Lord Selkirk to provide land for settlement, including a strip two miles wide on each side of the Red and Assiniboine rivers from their confluence, for an annual rent of tobacco. Peguis had helped both the Company and the settlers. In 1860, protesting settlers on unsurrendered land, he said the tobacco was only a goodwill token and no formal surrender had been made.

citations.title: Peguis (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)

citations.title: Peguis (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)

The signing place is not given; the point marks the confluence at which the ceded strip began, and Fort Garry was not yet built in 1817. The qid and coordinates are Fort Garry's, a stand-in.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1781-82 on the Hudson Bay and western plains
events.statement: According to historian Michael Payne, thousands died in the winter of 1781-82 as smallpox spread quickly through fur trade posts and Native encampments of western Canada. Samuel Hearne, in his journals, speculated that perhaps as many as nine in ten of the Chipewyan trading at Hudson's Bay Company posts died that year.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Three (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: The winter of 1781-82 proved horribly devastating to the Aboriginal people of western Canada.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Three (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: According to historian Michael Payne, thousands died from a smallpox epidemic that quickly spread through the fur trade posts and native encampments.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Three (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: he speculates that perhaps as many as 9 out of every 10 people died over that year

events.notes: Kept to about 50 words: the one readable source is a short radio-script summary, and The Canadian Encyclopedia's Chipewyan page refused the fetch (403). Hearne's guess is known through Payne's quoted remark, not his journals. The catalogue's Denesuline are the Chipewyan of this source. The point is a stand-in: the source names only Hudson's Bay Company posts and western Canada.

events.title: Smallpox epidemic of 1837-38 on the northern plains
events.statement: In 1837 several passengers on the American Fur Company steamboat St. Peter's, bound for Fort Union, contracted smallpox, and a smaller vessel carried supplies on to posts among the Niitsitapi. They caught the disease, and the deaths ended their dominance over the Plains. Historian Michael Payne describes a significant outbreak in 1837-38 carried along the Mississippi and Missouri into the West, reaching Plains peoples who crossed the border to trade.

citations.title: Blackfoot Confederacy (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In one instance in 1837, an American Fur Company steamboat, the St. Peter's, was headed to Fort Union and several passengers contracted smallpox on the way.

citations.title: Blackfoot Confederacy (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They continued to send a smaller vessel with supplies farther up the river to posts among the Niitsitapi.

citations.title: Blackfoot Confederacy (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Niitsitapi contracted the disease and eventually 6,000 died, marking an end to their dominance among tribes over the Plains.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Five (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemics: Part Five (Alberta Online Encyclopedia, archived)
citations.quote: groups of Plains Indians who, of course, crossed the border to trade with American traders

events.notes: Wikipedia's 'eventually 6,000 died' is left off: neither it nor Payne names a giver. Place is Fort Union, the steamboat's destination. Overlaps with na-e-051, which covers other nations.

events.title: Marias Massacre (Baker Massacre)
events.statement: To punish Mountain Chief's band of Piegan Blackfeet, General Sheridan ordered Major Eugene Baker's Second Cavalry to strike hard. On 23 January 1870 they attacked a different band, led by Chief Heavy Runner, to whom the United States had promised protection. Most of the dead were women, children and older men. A rough count by Baker's men gave 173; his scout Joe Kipp later said 217. Public outrage led to a long-term shift towards President Grant's "Peace Policy".

events.notes: Baker's and Kipp's figures are as Wikipedia reports them. The page also holds survivors' accounts (Spear Woman, Bear Head). The Canadian Encyclopedia's figure (about 220) could not be re-read (403).

events.title: Treaty 1 signed at Lower Fort Garry
events.statement: A year later came the first of the Numbered Treaties. After eight days of treaty-making, Treaty 1 was concluded on 3 August 1871 between the Crown and the Anishinaabe and Swampy Cree. Its text has them cede all the land in southern Manitoba for annuities and goods, though Indigenous delegates and leaders did not intend any cession. Within a year they were complaining of unfulfilled "Outside Promises", which a federal order of 1875 made part of the treaty.

events.notes: MHS lists signatories: Brokenhead, Long Plain, Peguis, Roseau River, Sagkeeng, Sandy Bay, Swan Lake. Wikipedia also says the accord has been held to be essentially about peace and friendship.

events.title: Cypress Hills Massacre
events.statement: Horses lost near Fort Benton sent a party of American wolfers and Métis freighters under Thomas Hardwick and John Evans north to Abe Farwell's post. On 1 June 1873, George Hammond led them to Little Soldier's Assiniboine camp over a missing horse; by Abe Farwell's account he fired first, and the party shot from a riverbank. Donald Graham, with them, said 13 died. The Office of the Treaty Commissioner says some historians put it near 20, survivors closer to 300.

citations.title: Cypress Hills massacre (Wikipedia)

events.notes: One wolfer died (Ed Legrace). The killings prompted Canada to speed the North-West Mounted Police's deployment. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan's Fort Walsh entry, seen only in a search result, has nearly 30 Assiniboine killed; CBC at least 23. Abe Farwell's testimony is the source of Hammond firing first.

events.title: Treaty 4 (Qu'Appelle Treaty)
events.statement: Treaty 4, also called the Qu'Appelle Treaty, was first signed at Fort Qu'Appelle on 15 September 1874 between the Crown and Cree and Saulteaux band governments. It covers most of present southern Saskatchewan and small parts of western Manitoba and southeastern Alberta. Further signings and adhesions continued until September 1877, the last by Stony and Assiniboine bands at Fort Walsh, and Chief Paskwa made a pictograph of the treaty in 1874.

events.title: Treaty 6 signed at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt
events.statement: Lt. Gov. Alexander Morris negotiated Treaty 6 at Fort Carlton and Fort Pitt in August and September 1876 with Plains and Woods Cree, Assiniboine and other bands; Mistawasis and Ahtahkakoop represented the Carlton Cree. Poundmaker questioned its intent, wanting farming instruction and aid once the buffalo had gone. Big Bear stayed away from Carlton and arrived at Fort Pitt after the ceremonies. New terms included a medicine chest and protection from famine and pestilence.

events.notes: Big Bear signed in 1882, per Wikipedia's Frog Lake article. Replaced The Canadian Encyclopedia (403) with the Dictionary of Canadian Biography. The earlier card's Poundmaker pemmican quotation was from the unreadable page and is dropped.

events.title: Treaty 7 signed at Blackfoot Crossing
events.statement: Treaty 7 was concluded on 22 September 1877 at Blackfoot Crossing on the Bow River, now the Siksika Nation reserve, with a second signing on 4 December for absent leaders. It involved the Siksika, Kainai, Piikani, Stoney-Nakoda and Tsuut'ina, whose buffalo were vanishing. The Canadian Encyclopedia says First Nations testimony shows each took it primarily as a peace treaty allowing settlement; none thought it a land surrender. Translation was a serious problem, and the written text met an oral tradition.

events.notes: The Canadian Encyclopedia was read through an archived copy, the live page refusing the fetch (403). Crowfoot had first been approached in 1875 (Wikipedia). The Treaty 7 Elders' The True Spirit and Original Intent of Treaty 7 was not read. The Tsuut'ina (Sarcee) are not catalogued separately here.

events.title: Frog Lake Massacre
events.statement: Hearing of the Métis victory at Duck Lake and rumours that soldiers were coming, Wandering Spirit, war chief of Big Bear's band, began gathering supplies at Frog Lake. Agent Thomas Quinn, controlling the inadequate rations, stood in the way. On 2 April 1885 Wandering Spirit shot Quinn and, despite Big Bear's attempt to stop it, his group killed eight more, two of them priests. Tried without counsel, he and seven others, some for killings at Battleford, were hanged that November.

events.title: Battle of Cut Knife
events.statement: Against General Middleton's orders, Lt. Col. William Otter gained leave to "punish Poundmaker" and led a flying column of 350 or 392 men, as Wikipedia variously gives it, against the Cree and Assiniboine camp. On 2 May 1885 the First Nations fighters forced his retreat. Poundmaker came into the fort on 26 May and was imprisoned. Tried for treason at Regina, he protested that he had done everything to stop bloodshed; he was sentenced to three years.

events.title: The Battle of Batoche
events.statement: Fifteen years after Red River, Louis Riel led a second rising, the North-West Resistance or Rebellion, decided at Batoche, the capital of his Provisional Government of Saskatchewan. From 9 to 12 May 1885 General Frederick Middleton's 916 regulars and militia attacked its trenches and rifle pits, held under Gabriel Dumont, until greater numbers and firepower overwhelmed the Métis. Middleton reported 51 Métis dead, a priest 16, and historians commonly accept 12. Riel surrendered on 15 May, and his government collapsed.

A plaque quoted on the same page says 800 attackers against the infobox's 916. Poundmaker's surrender (26 May, Battleford) moved off the card: he is not explained on this tour.

events.title: Louis Riel hanged at Regina
events.statement: Louis Riel led two resistance movements against the Government of Canada. Defeated at Batoche in 1885, he was imprisoned in Regina and convicted of high treason. Despite protests, popular appeals and the jury's call for clemency, he was hanged there on 16 November 1885. French Canadians saw him as a heroic victim, and the execution polarised Canada along ethno-religious lines; to the Métis he is a hero.

events.title: The Manitoba Act

place.name: Fort Garry (The Forks, Red River Settlement)

events.statement: While the fort was held, representatives of Red River's provisional government negotiated with the federal government. The resulting Manitoba Act received royal assent on 12 May 1870 and, from 15 July, made Manitoba Canada's fifth province. It set out language and school rights and set aside roughly 1.4 million acres for the Métis. Those protections were not fully realized: many Métis were cheated out of the land meant for them and left for the North-West Territories.

events.title: Treaty 8: first signing at Lesser Slave Lake
events.statement: As prospectors and settlers drawn by the Klondike Gold Rush moved north of Treaty 6, Canada extended the treaty process; the Geological Survey had also reported petroleum in the Athabaska region. Treaty 8 was signed on 21 June 1899 with First Nations of the Lesser Slave Lake area, near present-day Grouard. The most comprehensive Numbered Treaty, it covers about 841,000 km2 and thirty-nine communities, and by the official Treaty 8 account was accepted for "reasons of peace and friendship".

citations.title: Treaty 8 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: as prospectors and settlers—inspired by the Klondike Gold Rush—travelled to unceded territories that were north of Treaty 6, the Canadian government extended the treaty process north

citations.title: Treaty 8 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Geological Survey of Canada had also published reports that there was petroleum in the Athabaska region.

citations.title: Treaty 8 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: which concluded with the June 21, 1899, signing by representatives of the Crown and various First Nations of the Lesser Slave Lake area, is the most comprehensive of the eleven Numbered Treaties.

events.notes: Further adhesions at Fort Chipewyan and elsewhere (Wikipedia, per the earlier note) are not re-read. The Canadian Encyclopedia's Treaty 8 page refused the fetch (403), so the earlier claim that Cree representatives signed first is dropped. The point is the lake, about 45 km from Grouard, where the page puts the signing.

events.title: Champlain and Anadabijou at Tadoussac: alliance proposed
events.statement: Three days after reaching Tadoussac on 24 May 1603, Champlain and François Gravé Du Pont sought out the Montagnais (Innu) chief Anadabijou, celebrating with some 80 or 100 of his people a victory over the Iroquois. They shared the ceremonial pipe. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls it the first recorded meeting where an alliance was suggested against the Iroquois, a policy resulting in a century of French-Iroquois conflict.

citations.title: Anadabijou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: seek out his cabin “à la poincte de Sainct Matthieu” three days after their arrival at Tadoussac 24 May 1603.

citations.title: Anadabijou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: With some 80 or 100 of his people, Anadabijou was celebrating a recent victory

citations.title: Anadabijou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: a policy which was pursued by the French, resulting in a century of French-Iroquois conflict.

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Innu (Montagnais)

events.notes: Dated three days after the arrival of 24 May 1603 (DCB), which suggests rather than records an alliance, and names the Algonkins and Etchemins too. Replaced The Canadian Encyclopedia (403) with DCB. Innu oral tradition, per Wikipedia's Innu article, recalls early encounters with Champlain's men as fraught with distrust.

events.title: Founding of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy (Great Law of Peace)
events.statement: In Haudenosaunee tradition the Peacemaker, with Aionwatha (Hiawatha), united the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca under the Great Law of Peace, an oral constitution kept on wampum belts. Its date is contested. The Confederacy says it is unknown, time immemorial; the Onondaga Nation places it over a thousand years ago on the shores of Onondaga Lake. Many archaeologists and anthropologists say about 1450; other proposals include about 1142 and about 1190, with little agreement.

citations.title: Who We Are (Haudenosaunee Confederacy)
citations.quote: The confederacy was founded by the prophet known as the Peacemaker with the help of Aionwatha, more commonly known as Hiawatha.

citations.title: Who We Are (Haudenosaunee Confederacy)
citations.quote: The exact date of the joining of the nations is unknown and said to be time immemorial

citations.title: History (Onondaga Nation)
citations.quote: Over a thousand years ago on the shores of Onondaga Lake, in present day central New York, democracy was born.

citations.title: Great Law of Peace (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: is the oral constitution of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy

citations.title: Great Law of Peace (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the law was represented by symbols on wampum belts

citations.title: Great Law of Peace (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The exact date of the events is not known, but it is thought to date back to the late 12th century (c. 1190).

citations.title: Iroquois (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: likely between 1142 and 1660

events.notes: Dated as a range, since no single year is agreed. Wikipedia's Iroquois infobox has between 1142 and 1450, its lead 1142 to 1660 with little agreement, and its text puts many archaeologists and anthropologists at about 1450 and gives the eclipse proposal of 31 August 1142. Haudenosaunee sources reject a precise date. The date lies before the catalogue's window, as background.

events.title: Tuscarora join the Confederacy; the Five Nations become the Six Nations

place.name: Onondaga Nation territory (council fire of the Confederacy)

events.statement: Defeated by British colonists and their Indian allies in the Tuscarora War of 1711 to 1715, considered the bloodiest colonial war in North Carolina, most surviving Tuscarora left the state over some ninety years, migrating to Pennsylvania and New York. They aligned with the Haudenosaunee through linguistic and cultural ties. In 1722, sponsored by the Oneida, they were accepted as the Confederacy's sixth nation.

citations.title: Tuscarora War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: This was considered the bloodiest colonial war in North Carolina.

citations.title: Tuscarora (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Tuscarora (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Wikipedia's Tuscarora people article dates the war 1711 to 1713; its war article runs to February 1715, and says the Tuscarora signed a further treaty with colonial officials in 1718. Replaced The Canadian Encyclopedia (403). The point stands for the Confederacy's council fire: nothing read places the admission at Onondaga.

events.title: Beaver Wars (Iroquois Wars; French and Iroquois Wars)
events.statement: From 1609 to 1701 intermittent wars around the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence pitted the Haudenosaunee, backed by the Dutch and later the English, against the French-allied Wendat and others. The traditional view blames a drive to monopolise the fur trade; other theories cite replenishing populations after epidemics in the 1630s and imposing the Great Law of Peace. Devastating attacks in 1648 and 1649 broke the Wendat, and the wars ended at the Great Peace of Montreal.

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: were a series of intermittent conflicts fought in the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence River regions of North America from 1609 to 1701.

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The wars pitted the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois), supported by the Dutch and later the English, against neighboring Indigenous nations such as the Wendat (Huron), who were allied with the French.

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: While the traditional view is that the Haudenosaunee wanted to expand their territory in order to monopolize the North American fur trade, two other theories have gained acceptance

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: a need for the Haudenosaunee to replenish their population after catastrophic epidemics in the 1630s, and a desire to impose the Great Law of Peace on other Iroquoian-speaking people.

citations.title: Beaver Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The war against the Wendat culminated in the devastating attacks of 1648 and 1649.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a peace treaty between New France and 39 First Nations of North America that ended the Beaver Wars.

events.notes: Start date varies: Wikipedia dates the wars 1609 to 1701; many accounts date the intense phase to the 1640s. Place is a representative anchor (Montreal). The Canadian Encyclopedia's Iroquois page refused the fetch (403). Montreal did not exist in 1609; it stands for the Peace of 1701 that ended the wars. The first fight, Champlain's at Ticonderoga in July 1609, is named in Wikipedia's infobox.

events.title: Great Peace of Montreal
events.statement: In the north, the Beaver Wars, the fight over the fur trade between the Haudenosaunee and the French with their Huron and Algonquin allies, ended on 4 August 1701, when Louis-Hector de Callière, governor of New France, and 1,300 representatives of 39 Indigenous nations signed a peace at Montreal. All-out war did not return, though within three years Odawa warriors attacked a Haudenosaunee village near present-day Kingston and planted a Huron club on a dead warrior to provoke new fighting.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was signed on August 4, 1701, by Louis-Hector de Callière, governor of New France, and 1300 representatives of 39 Indigenous nations.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The French, allied to the Hurons and the Algonquins, brokered a peace agreement between their allies and the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The peace was fragile, however; although all-out war did not break out, within only three years the Odawa attacked a Haudenosaunee village near a French fort in present-day Kingston, Ontario.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The warriors planted a Huron club on a dead Haudenosaunee warrior to try to provoke new fighting.

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Beaver Wars saw the Hurons and Algonquins, supported by the French, pitted against the Haudenosaunee of the powerful League of Five Nations

citations.title: Great Peace of Montreal (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Control over the fur trade became a high-stakes game among the Native American tribes

events.notes: The same article also says over 1,300 people from over 40 nations; it writes 'Six Nations', though the Tuscarora joined in 1722. The Haudenosaunee also made a separate treaty at Albany with the British in 1701, per the earlier note, not re-read. One Wikipedia source; The Canadian Encyclopedia refused the fetch (403).

events.title: Albany Congress
events.statement: From 19 June to 11 July 1754 representatives of seven British colonies met at Albany to discuss relations with Native nations and defence against the French, with a treaty with the Mohawk and other Haudenosaunee as their mission. They approved Benjamin Franklin's Plan of Union, which the colonial legislatures rejected. At the congress the Haudenosaunee sold Pennsylvania a huge tract west of the Susquehanna without consulting the western Lenape living there, whose anger helped bring raids on Pennsylvania's frontier.

citations.title: Albany Congress (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Representatives met daily at the City Hall (Dutch: Stadt Huys) in Albany, New York, from June 19 to July 11, 1754, to discuss better relations with the Native American tribes and common defensive measures against the French threat

citations.title: Albany Congress (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: they were colonists with the more limited mission of pursuing a treaty with the Mohawks and other major Iroquois tribes.

citations.title: Albany Congress (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The delegates passed the plan unanimously. They submitted it with their recommendations, but the legislatures of the seven colonies rejected it, as it would have removed some of their existing powers.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: agreed to the sale without consulting the western Lenape whose villages on the Allegheny River and its tributaries lay within the territory sold.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: contributed to the western Lenape's decision to attack Pennsylvania's frontier settlements.

citations.title: Albany Congress (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a meeting of representatives sent by the legislatures of seven of the British colonies in British America

citations.title: Albany Congress (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Albany delegates spent most of their time debating Benjamin Franklin's Albany Plan of Union

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1754, at the Albany Congress, the Haudenosaunee agreed to sell to Pennsylvania a huge tract of land west of the Susquehanna River.

events.notes: Anger over the purchase is given alongside the July 1755 defeat of the Braddock Expedition as a cause of the Lenape attacks. The Haudenosaunee claimed authority over the Lenape by right of conquest.

events.title: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix
events.statement: The line moved within five years. At Fort Stanwix the British negotiator Sir William Johnson and the Haudenosaunee agreed a Line of Property down the Ohio to the Tennessee River, signed on 5 November 1768 with one signatory for each of the Six Nations. It ceded Kentucky and most of present-day West Virginia, lands occupied mainly by the Shawnee and Lenape, who attended but did not sign. Rather than ending frontier violence, it helped set the stage for Dunmore's War.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The final treaty was signed on November 5 with one signatory for each of the Six Nations

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The line ran near Fort Pitt and followed the Ohio River as far as the Tennessee River, effectively ceding the Kentucky portion of the Virginia Colony to the Crown, as well as most of what is now West Virginia.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Although representatives of the Indian nations who occupied these lands, primarily the Shawnee and Lenape, were present at the negotiations in 1768, they were not signatories.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Rather than secure peace, the Fort Stanwix treaty helped set the stage for the next round of hostilities between Native Americans and American colonists along the Ohio River, which would culminate in Dunmore's War.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The British government hoped a new boundary line might bring an end to the rampant frontier violence between Native Americans and American colonists.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was negotiated between Sir William Johnson, his deputy George Croghan, and representatives of the Haudenosaunee.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty established a Line of Property following the Ohio River

events.notes: The source also says the Shawnee did not agree and contested Virginian settlement until the 1774 Treaty of Camp Charlotte. The Haudenosaunee claimed these lands by conquest and hoped to ease pressure on their own home territories.

events.title: The Sullivan Expedition
events.statement: After Haudenosaunee and Loyalist raids in 1778, Washington ordered the destruction of the settlements of the four British-allied Haudenosaunee nations. From June to October 1779 a Continental force under John Sullivan and James Clinton fought one major battle, at Newtown, and razed 40 villages with their crops. Over 5,000 refugees reached Fort Niagara, and several hundred are thought to have died that winter. Some scholars call the campaign a genocide, a term that is disputed.

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some scholars argue that it was an attempt to annihilate the Haudenosaunee and describe the campaign as a genocide, although this term is disputed.

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: While the campaign had only one major battle at Newtown on the Chemung River

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: She suggests that the overall death toll may have been a high as 55.5 percent or roughly 5,000 individuals

citations.title: Sullivan Expedition (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Taylor and Koehler are known as Wikipedia reports them, not read directly; the page calls Koehler's assumption questionable. Rachel Herrmann also reports several hundred. The Buffalo Creek Reservation article says the British 'were reported to be feeding and housing over 5000 refugees'. Date is the march from Easton, 18 June; the battle of Newtown was 29 August 1779, and the point is Newtown. Calloway's several hundred comes first on the page; Taylor follows him. Koehler's doubt moved into the statement. Rhiannon Koehler's roughly 5,000 rests on an assumption the page calls questionable; Calloway and Taylor have several hundred.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784)
events.statement: On 22 October 1784 delegates of the Six Nations signed a treaty with the United States at Fort Stanwix, giving up all claims to the Ohio territory, a strip along the Niagara River and all land west of the mouth of Buffalo Creek. Joseph Brant had said the delegation lacked authority to cede land, but he left early. The Six Nations council at Buffalo Creek refused to ratify it, and the Shawnee, Lenape and other Ohio nations rejected it.

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Treaty of Fort Stanwix was a treaty finalized on October 22, 1784, between the United States and Native Americans from the six nations of the Haudenosaunee League.

citations.quote: the Haudenosaunee Confederacy ceded all claims to the Ohio territory, a strip of land along the Niagara river and all land west of mouth of Buffalo creek.

events.title: Haldimand Proclamation (Grand River grant)

place.name: Six Nations of the Grand River (Haldimand Tract)

events.statement: On 25 October 1784, three days after the Fort Stanwix treaty, Governor Frederick Haldimand granted the Mohawk and such other Five Nations as wished to join them land six miles deep on each side of the Grand River, chosen by Joseph Brant and bought from the Mississaugas of the Credit that May. Its extent was disputed: the Crown held to a limit near Elora, surveyed in 1821 at 674,910 acres, though John Brant had contested it in 1819.

The Crown and Brant also differed over whether the grant was for all the Six Nations or only those living on it. The decree was given at Quebec; the point is the land granted.

events.title: Treaty of Canandaigua (Pickering Treaty)
events.statement: On 11 November 1794 Timothy Pickering, President Washington's agent, and Haudenosaunee royaner and war chiefs (counted as fifty or fifty-nine) signed the Treaty of Canandaigua, as the United States feared the Confederacy might join the Ohio war. It promised perpetual peace and friendship, acknowledged Haudenosaunee lands and promised $4,500 a year in goods. That payment, which Haudenosaunee leaders insist be made in cloth, is still honoured, but the guarantee of Oneida, Onondaga and Cayuga land rights was not.

citations.title: Treaty of Canandaigua (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Treaty of Canandaigua (Wikipedia)

events.title: Treaty of Big Tree (Seneca land sale)
events.statement: At Big Tree (Geneseo), after nearly a month of often heated negotiation from 20 August 1797, the Seneca Nation signed away on 16 September nearly all their homeland, nearly 3.5 million acres west of the Genesee River, keeping twelve small tracts and hunting and fishing rights. The $100,000 price went not to the Seneca but into Bank of the United States stock, its annual earnings paid to them. The sale opened western New York to settlement.

events.title: Treaties of Buffalo Creek (1838, 1842): Seneca removal treaties
events.statement: Beginning in 1837, by one account, agents of the Ogden Land Company bribed, intimidated and deceived 43 of more than 80 Seneca chiefs into the Treaty of Buffalo Creek, requiring the Seneca to give up all their New York reservations and move west of the Mississippi within five years. After the land sale fell through, a new treaty was ratified in 1842. Only Buffalo Creek was dissolved; the Seneca kept Cattaraugus, Oil Springs, Allegany and Tonawanda after 1850s legal battles.

citations.quote: Second Treaty of Buffalo Creek (1838)

events.title: French expedition against the Seneca (Denonville, 1687)
events.statement: In June 1687 the Marquis de Denonville led an army from Canada against the Seneca, to eliminate them as fur-trade rivals dealing with the English. Near Ganondagan on 13 July, Denonville says, a Seneca force of 800 attacked and fled; a British report from Seneca warriors says 450, and L'Abbé de Belmont that they came to reconnoitre. The Seneca burned Ganondagan themselves, by the British report. The French destroyed corn at four villages, 1.2 million bushels by French reckoning.

citations.title: Ganondagan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: to eliminate the Seneca as competitors in the international fur trade.[11] The Seneca had been dealing with the English, and the French wanted to keep control of the lucrative fur trade.

citations.title: Ganondagan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: were attacked by a Seneca force of 800, but after a short engagement "they soon resolved to fly."

citations.title: Ganondagan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: a British report, based on interviews of Seneca warriors, states that the Seneca force consisted of 450 people

citations.title: Ganondagan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Upon the French arrival at the village on the 14th, Denonville reports, "we found it burned" and a nearby fort abandoned.

citations.title: Ganondagan (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: from the four Seneca villages they visited, destroyed 1.2 million bushels of stored and standing corn.

events.notes: Denonville also claimed 45 Seneca dead and 60 wounded against 5 or 6 French dead and 20 wounded; those are his figures alone and are left off the card. The corn figure's footnote is O'Callaghan's Documentary History of New York, which prints the French expedition papers; not read directly. The army is given as 832 regulars, over 900 militia and some 400 allies; the author of that count was not seen. The source's 450 breaks down inconsistently (350 boys, 100 men and 5 women).

events.title: Treaty of Shackamaxon (Penn's Treaty)
events.statement: By historical tradition William Penn, who arrived in late October 1682, soon made a treaty of peace with the Lenape chief Tamanend under an elm at Shackamaxon. The Delaware Nation says Penn 'allegedly' made it: no paper survives, though a wampum belt is believed to have been made for it. Francis Jennings argues that Penn very likely signed and that his sons destroyed the document. The Delaware Nation adds that Penn's aim was still to take Lenape land.

citations.title: Treaty of Shackamaxon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: arrived in North America in late October 1682. According to historical tradition, he soon made a treaty with the Lenni Lenape under an ancient elm tree.

citations.title: Treaty of Shackamaxon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Francis Jennings argues that William Penn very likely signed a treaty, but that his less scrupulous sons, William Jr., John, and Thomas, destroyed the original document.

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)
citations.quote: Penn allegedly made the Treaty of Shackamaxon in what would become Philadelphia, PA with Lenape Chief Tamanend to solidify peaceful relations.

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)
citations.quote: Penn’s intention was ultimately still to dispossess the Lenape of large swaths of their homelands for his own profit or settlement

events.notes: Year-level date follows the tradition; the event itself is not documented. The site is in present-day Kensington and Fishtown, Philadelphia. Delaware Nation page read from the project's cached copy, since a live fetch returned HTTP 508. The Oklahoma encyclopedia dates Penn's land purchase and peace treaty with the Delaware to 1683, and Wikipedia's Tamanend article has their first document in 1683.

events.title: Peach War: Munsee Lenape occupy New Amsterdam
events.statement: At daybreak on 15 September 1655, with Stuyvesant's soldiers away conquering New Sweden, several hundred Munsee landed on Manhattan and ransacked houses without killing anyone; a skirmish that evening left three dead on each side. Raids on Pavonia and Staten Island followed, and Stuyvesant reported 40 colonists killed and 100 taken captive. The cause is debated: the killing of a Munsee woman picking peaches in a Dutch orchard, or, as some historians speculate, Susquehannock prompting.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: At daybreak on September 15, 1655, about 500 Munsee in 64 canoes landed near the southern end of Manhattan. They proceeded to break down doors, ransack houses, and threaten or beat some of the occupants

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the ensuing skirmish, three Munsee and three colonists were killed.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Stuyvesant later reported that in the attacks "40 Christians" were killed and 100, mostly women and children, taken captive.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The armed protest and raids may have been triggered by the murder of a Munsee woman who was stealing peaches from the orchard of Dutch colonist Hendrick van Dyck.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A number of historians have speculated that the Susquehannock were behind the armed protest.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In late August 1655, Stuyvesant with seven armed vessels and 317 soldiers sailed from New Amsterdam for Delaware Bay.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: One group of Munsee then crossed the Hudson River and attacked Pavonia while a second group raided Staten Island.

citations.title: Peach War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Dutch West India Company ordered Director-General Peter Stuyvesant to conquer the colony of New Sweden.

events.notes: The lead of the same source gives forty-three colonists killed and 'several hundred' Munsee; its body gives 'about 500'. Tom Arne Midtrød, quoted there, doubts it was meant as a military attack. Author of the 500 not seen.

events.title: First Esopus War
events.statement: The First Esopus War ran from 20 September 1659 to 15 July 1660, after Dutch settlers at Wiltwijck (Kingston) opened fire on Esopus gathered round a campfire. Esopus reinforcements raided outside the stockade, destroying crops and burning buildings, and besieged the settlement. The outnumbered colonists held out, burned Esopus fields and were reinforced from New Amsterdam. The war ended when the Esopus agreed to trade land for food, but tensions led to a second war.

citations.title: Esopus Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The First Esopus War was a short-lived conflict between Dutch settlers and the Esopus Natives from September 20, 1659 and July 15, 1660.

citations.title: Esopus Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: An incident occurred where a group of Dutch settlers opened fire on a group of Esopus around a campfire, who had been celebrating with brandy given as payment for farm work.

citations.title: Esopus Wars (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Single source. The source describes the Esopus as a Lenape tribe, 'instigated by settlers' for this first conflict.

events.title: Walking Purchase
events.statement: In 1737 William Penn's sons presented the Lenape with a deed of 1686, which the Delaware Nation calls illegitimate, ceding land as far as a man could walk in a day and a half. On 19 September James Logan's hired runners took a prepared trail; only Edward Marshall finished, some 70 miles north. The resulting line claimed about 1.2 million acres. The Haudenosaunee refused the Lenape's appeal for aid, and the Lenape were forced out.

citations.title: Walking Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Penn family and proprietors produced a deed to claim that a 1686 treaty with the Lenape ceded an area of 1,200,000 acres

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)
citations.quote: In 1737 Penn’s sons met with the Lenape and presented an illegitimate treaty supposedly signed with William Penn decades earlier

citations.title: Walking Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Provincial Secretary Logan hired the three fastest runners in the colony, Edward Marshall, Solomon Jennings, and James Yeates, to run on a prepared trail.

citations.title: Walking Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The walk occurred on September 19, 1737; only Marshall finished,[2] reaching the modern vicinity of present-day Jim Thorpe, Pennsylvania, 70 miles (113 km) to the north.

citations.title: Walking Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Lenape appealed to the Haudenosaunee to their north for aid on the issue, but the Haudenosaunee refused their request, ultimately siding with the Penn interests.

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)
citations.quote: As a result of the Walking Purchase and increasing settler occupation, dispossession, and violence, the Lenape are forced out of their homelands into Ohio territory.

citations.title: Walking Purchase (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: which included a western land boundary extending as far west as a man could walk in a day and a half

events.notes: The source also says James Logan's map misrepresented the Lehigh River as Tohickon Creek. In 2004 the Delaware Nation sued over 314 acres; the court dismissed the case as nonjusticiable, even if the fraud allegations were accurate. The walk began near Wrightstown; the place field is the Forks of the Delaware, the disputed land.

events.title: Treaty of Easton (1758)
events.statement: From 7 to 26 October 1758 Pennsylvania's lieutenant governor William Denny and New Jersey's governor Francis Bernard met representatives of the Haudenosaunee, Lenape and other nations at Easton. On 20 October Denny announced the return to the Haudenosaunee of the part of the 1754 Albany Purchase west of the Alleghenies, removing a major cause of raiding. As a result the western Lenape did not oppose the British capture of Fort Duquesne that November, though Pontiac's War later showed its limits.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A much larger conference was held at Easton from 7 to 26 October 1758. In attendance were Denny, Governor Francis Bernard of New Jersey, and representatives of numerous Indigenous nations.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: met with the new lieutenant governor William Denny.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: As a result, the western Lenape did not intervene to prevent the British capture of Fort Duquesne in November 1758.

citations.title: Treaty of Easton (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The outbreak of Pontiac's War in 1763 demonstrated the limits of the arrangements reached at Easton

events.notes: Charles Thomson, Teedyuscung's secretary, reported just over 500 Indigenous people present. The source elsewhere also says Pennsylvania agreed to return the land; Denny announced it in the Proprietors' name. The conference ran to 26 October, dated here by its opening; the source says it did not end in the formal signing of a written treaty.

events.title: The Treaty of Fort Pitt
events.statement: An American march on British Detroit had to cross Lenape country. On 17 September 1778 White Eyes, Captain Pipe and John Killbuck signed at Fort Pitt the first formal treaty between the United States and any Native nation, securing passage and military aid. It recognized Lenape sovereignty and held out a state with representation in Congress, never fulfilled. White Eyes soon died, allegedly of smallpox; the Delaware Nation holds that American militiamen murdered him. The alliance collapsed.

citations.quote: it was the first formal treaty between the new United States of America and any Native American groups, in this case the Lenape

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)
citations.quote: White Eyes was instrumental in establishing the Fort Pitt Treaty, which he signed on September 17th, 1778 along with Lenape leaders Gelelemund, a.k.a. Captain John Killbuck Jr., and Captain Pipe.

citations.quote: The treaty also recognized the Lenapes as a sovereign nation, guaranteed their territorial rights

citations.title: History (Delaware Nation)

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Pitt (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Treaty of Fort Pitt (Wikipedia)

citations.quote: The United States was planning to attack the British fort at Detroit, and Lenape assistance was essential for success.

events.notes: The Delaware Nation calls it the first treaty both signed with and broken with a Native Nation. Daniel K. Richter (via Wikipedia, not read directly) says the Lenape understood it as free passage only.

events.title: The Gnadenhutten massacre
events.statement: The killing went on in the Ohio country after Yorktown. In February 1782 Moravian Christian Indians, pacifists, primarily Lenape and Mohican, returned from Captive Town to harvest their old villages' crops. Pennsylvania militia under David Williamson falsely promised them protection, then on 8 March killed 96 at Gnadenhutten, infants among them, with mallet blows and scalping cuts in two 'killing houses'. Some militiamen refused to take part. William Crawford, who had not been there, was later killed in retaliation.

events.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians relocate to the Cherokee Nation (1867)
events.statement: In 1867 the main body of the Delaware, driven west over decades through Ohio, Indiana and Missouri and then living in Kansas, bought land in northeast Oklahoma from the Cherokee Nation, in two payments totalling $438,000. As Registered Delaware they became partial members of the Cherokee with limited autonomy. Whether the sale included citizenship rights went to court, and the Tribe's separate status stayed in dispute until an agreement with the Cherokee Nation in 2008.

citations.title: Delaware, Eastern (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: The main body of dispersed bands, living in Kansas at the time, bought land in northeast Oklahoma from the Cherokee in an 1867 treaty.

citations.title: Delaware, Eastern (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: became partial members of the Cherokee tribe and had limited autonomy.

citations.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Lenape were forced to cede their Eastern lands and moved first to Ohio and later to Indiana (Plainfield), Missouri, Kansas, and Indian Territory.

citations.title: Delaware Nation (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: they made two payments totaling $438,000. A court dispute followed over whether the sale included citizenship rights for the Delaware within the Cherokee Nation.

citations.title: Delaware Tribe of Indians (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: After years of negotiations, the two tribes resolved their differences through an agreement in October 2008.

citations.title: Delaware, Eastern (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: These Delaware, which the federal government termed Registered Delaware because they lived in Indian Territory

events.notes: Wikipedia's Delaware Tribe page quotes the BIA as dating the removal to Oklahoma with the Cherokees to 1879; every other source read has 1867, so 1879 looks like a slip. The $438,000 author is not named on that page. The Tribe's status was revoked in 1979, restored in 1996 (Oklahoma encyclopedia; 1991 per Wikipedia), overturned in 2004.

events.title: Jamestown founded within Powhatan territory
events.statement: In May 1607 the Virginia Company's colonists built James Fort on a swampy river island, chosen to evade Spanish patrols, inside the territory of the Powhatan. Their leader Wahunsenacawh, whom the English called Chief Powhatan, by then governed more than 30 nations, and the island was used by the Paspahegh. Conflict began at once, with deaths inside two weeks. Wahunsenacawh wanted the colonists out of the swamp and living in one of his towns.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The settlement at Jamestown, Virginia, was established in May 1607 within the territory of the Powhatan, who were led by Chief Wahunsunacawh, known to the colonists as Chief Powhatan.

citations.title: Jamestown, Virginia (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was established by the Virginia Company of London as "James Fort" on May 4, 1607 O.S. (May 14, 1607 N.S.).

citations.title: Jamestown, Virginia (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A river island was selected to evade Spanish naval patrols; however, it was infested with mosquitoes, lacked potable water, and was used by the Paspahegh people.

citations.title: Powhatan (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Powhatan (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Powhatan (Wikipedia)

events.notes: The Jamestown article also says, deeper in, that the site was uninhabited because nearby leaders thought it too poor and remote for farming; its lead says the Paspahegh used it.

events.title: First Anglo-Powhatan War
events.statement: The first of three wars between Virginia's colonists and the Powhatan Confederacy began in 1609; that November Powhatan's men killed John Ratcliffe and 32 others sent to buy corn. On 9 August 1610 Governor De La Warr's men burned the Paspahegh town, killing villagers, and shot captive children in the water. The capture of Pocahontas brought a ceasefire, and in 1614 peace was sealed by her marriage to John Rolfe.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In November, Powhatan ambushed and killed Captain John Ratcliffe and 32 other colonists, who had gone to Orapax to buy corn

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: De La Warr sent George Percy and James Davis with 70 men to attack the Paspahegh town on August 9, 1610, burning houses and cutting down cornfields. They killed between 15 and 75 villagers

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Returning downstream, the colonists threw the children overboard and shot them in the water.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Start date: the source says 1609; many accounts date the war 1610-1614. It gives the capture of Pocahontas as December 1612, left out of the card because the year is often given as 1613. Wikipedia's 'between 15 and 75' killed at Paspahegh is left off: the passage's footnotes are Alfred Cave (2013) and Howard Zinn (2003), neither read and neither clearly tied to that figure.

events.title: Powhatan attack of 22 March 1622 (Second Anglo-Powhatan War begins)
events.statement: On 22 March 1622 Opechancanough's warriors, placed among the English settlements, struck without warning along both shores of the James River, killing 347 by the historian Betty Wood's figure, a quarter of the colony; Wikipedia's article also has about 400, a third. Warnings from Christian Indians limited the toll. The militia then marched almost every summer for ten years against Powhatan towns, and in 1623 colonists poisoned the wine at a peace meeting. The war ran until 1632.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: his warriors struck without warning on March 22, 1622, from where they had been planted among the settlements, and killed hundreds in the Indian massacre of 1622.

citations.title: Opechancanough (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: during a series of coordinated attacks along both shores of the James River, extending from Newport News Point, near the mouth of the river, to Falling Creek

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

events.title: Third Anglo-Powhatan War
events.statement: On 18 April 1644 Opechancanough and what remained of the Powhatan Confederacy tried again to drive the settlers from Virginia, and a London newsbook reported several hundred colonists killed. The colony built frontier forts in 1645-46. In August 1646 Governor William Berkeley stormed Opechancanough's village and captured him, and the males over 11 were deported to Tangier Island. Paraded through Jamestown, the aged leader was shot in the back by a settler guarding him.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

The Opechancanough article calls him believed to be between 90 and 100 at capture. Death dated October 1646 in the Anglo-Powhatan Wars article. The point at Jamestown is an anchor.

events.title: Treaty of 1646 (Necotowance and Virginia)

place.name: Virginia Peninsula, between the York and James

events.statement: In October 1646 Virginia's General Assembly made peace with Necotowance, Opechancanough's successor, ending the Third Anglo-Powhatan War. The nations of the confederacy became tributaries of the English king. Necotowance gave up the peninsula between the York and James rivers, any Indian found there liable to death, and a frontier was set that could be crossed only by special pass. His people could keep living north of the York, though colonists went on encroaching on the lands the treaty set aside.

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Anglo-Powhatan Wars (Wikipedia)

events.title: Treaty of Middle Plantation (1677)
events.statement: On 29 May 1677, after Bacon's Rebellion, Cockacoeske of the Pamunkey signed first, with her son John West, in a treaty with Governor Jeffreys. The signatory nations accepted status as subjects of the Crown and gave up remaining claims to ancestral land in return for protection and reserved land, hunting and fishing rights. Article 12 acknowledged nations' subjection to her, which some Chickahominy and Rappahannock soon resisted. At Pamunkey Neck it created a zone of 18,000 acres.

events.title: Epidemic devastates the Wampanoag and the New England coast (c. 1614-1620)
events.statement: Between about 1614 and 1620 epidemics swept New England and the Maritimes. Alfred Crosby estimates losses as high as 90% among the Massachusett and mainland Pokanoket. All the Patuxet died except Tisquantum, who was abroad. Long thought to be smallpox, the disease is suggested by John Marr and John Cathey to be leptospirosis, from rats on European ships. The Narragansett escaped the worst, and the depopulation eased English colonization.

citations.title: Wampanoag (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Alfred Crosby has estimated population losses to be as high as 90 percent among the Massachusett and mainland Pokanoket.

citations.title: Patuxet (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: When the Pilgrims landed in 1620, all the Patuxet except Tisquantum had died.

Crosby is known through the Wampanoag article, whose footnote is Neal Salisbury, Manitou and Providence (1982), not read directly. The Patuxet article's mortality of 100% in many villages is left off, with no name behind it.

events.title: Wampanoag treaty with Plymouth Colony (Massasoit)
events.statement: On 1 April 1621 (22 March Old Style) Massasoit, whose Wampanoag had been weakened by epidemic and made to pay tribute by the Narragansett, made a treaty with Plymouth's governor John Carver. He sought an alliance against the Narragansett; the terms bound each side to surrender offenders and to aid the other in war. The peace helped Plymouth survive its first years, and collapsed after Massasoit's death in 1661, ending in King Philip's War.

citations.title: Wampanoag treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: was a treaty signed on April 1 [O.S. March 22], 1621[1] between the Wampanoag, led by Massasoit, and the English settlers of Plymouth Colony, led by Governor John Carver.

citations.title: Wampanoag treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Narragansett people capitalized on this decimation of the Wampanoag and forced them to pay tribute.

citations.quote: If any did unjustly war against him, we would aid him; if any did war against us, he should aid us.

citations.title: Wampanoag treaty (Wikipedia)

events.notes: The Massasoit article credits the view that he saved Plymouth to 'English sources'. The Wampanoag treaty article says both that the treaty lasted over fifty years and that it did not last long beyond 1661; the card follows the latter.

events.title: King Philip's (Metacom's) War begins at Swansea
events.statement: According to Benjamin Church, a band of Pokanokets attacked isolated homesteads at Swansea on 20 June 1675, likely against Philip's approval, days after Plymouth hanged three Wampanoags for the murder of John Sassamon. A full attack on Swansea followed on 24 June, and on 28 June a colonial expedition destroyed the Wampanoag town at Mount Hope. A coalition of Wampanoags, Pocomtucs, Nipmucs and Narragansetts then fought New England's colonists and their Native allies.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: According to Benjamin Church, a band of Pokanokets attacked several isolated homesteads in the small Plymouth colony settlement of Swansea on June 20, 1675, likely against Phillip's approval.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Wikipedia)

citations.quote: on June 28, they sent a punitive military expedition that destroyed the Wampanoag town at Mount Hope in Bristol, Rhode Island.

citations.quote: a coalition of Algonquian tribes of the Northeastern Woodlands—the Wampanoags, the Pocomtucs, the Nipmucs, and the Narragansetts—fought against the Puritan settlers of the New England Colonies and their Indian allies

citations.title: King Philip's War (Roger Williams National Memorial, NPS)
