events.notes: The war is dated 1675-1676 (NPS, Encyclopedia.com) or 1675-1678 (Wikipedia, which includes the northern theatre). The Great Swamp Fight article says only 'several Wampanoag men'. The Narragansett were officially neutral until the attack of December 1675.

events.title: Metacom (King Philip) killed at Mount Hope
events.statement: On 12 August 1676 Metacom, the son of Massasoit whom settlers called King Philip, was tracked to Mount Hope by a Plymouth militia team under Benjamin Church and Josiah Standish, and shot by an Indian named John Alderman. His corpse was cut up and his head displayed at Plymouth for a generation; Wampanoag memory holds that the skull was secretly buried. Hundreds of Wampanoags and their allies were executed or enslaved, and the Wampanoags were left effectively landless.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Massasoit's younger son Metacom (c. 1638–1676), named King Philip by the settlers, became the sachem in 1662

citations.title: King Philip's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: when Captain Benjamin Church and Captain Josiah Standish of the Plymouth Colony militia tracked him to Mount Hope in Bristol, Rhode Island. He was shot and killed by an Indian named John Alderman on August 12, 1676.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Hundreds of Wampanoags and their allies were publicly executed or enslaved, and the Wampanoags were left effectively landless.

events.notes: Title and kind treat this as a battle; the source describes a pursuit and killing. Left as they are.

events.title: Narragansett sachems grant land to Roger Williams (Providence)
events.statement: Ordered banished by Massachusetts Bay in October 1635, the minister Roger Williams, who had spoken against taking Native land by force, slipped away in January 1636. The Narragansett sachems Canonicus and Miantonomi let him settle on land that became Providence Plantations. For decades afterwards Williams's diplomacy helped keep the Narragansett on friendly terms with the English, until the attack of December 1675 pushed them into King Philip's War.

citations.title: Narragansett (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: Colonial officials forced Williams to leave the colony because he spoke out against taking Native American land by force

citations.title: Narragansett (Encyclopedia.com)

events.notes: Sources differ on the transaction: Wikipedia has Williams 'acquire' land, Encyclopedia.com has the Narragansett 'give' it. The card says 'let him settle'. Encyclopedia.com dates the banishment to 1636.

events.title: Great Swamp Fight (Great Swamp Massacre)
events.statement: In King Philip's War, Boston demanded that the Narragansett hand over Wampanoag refugees, and they would not. On 19 December 1675 militia from Plymouth, Connecticut and Massachusetts Bay, with Pequot and Mohegan allies, attacked their main settlement, overran it after a fierce fight and burned it. About 70 of the militia were killed. Estimates of the Narragansett dead run from about 400 to over 1,000, many of them women and children.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Four days later, the Great Swamp Battle took place on the bitterly cold and stormy day of December 19, 1675.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Roger Williams National Memorial, NPS)
citations.quote: cost the lives of three hundred Native American men and almost four hundred women and children.

citations.title: King Philip's War (Roger Williams National Memorial, NPS)
citations.quote: The Narragansett would not turn over these refugees.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It is believed that at least 97 Narragansett warriors and 300 to 1,000 non-combatants were killed, though exact figures are unknown.

citations.title: Narragansett (Encyclopedia.com)
citations.quote: One participant of the battle estimated that between six hundred and one thousand Narragansett warriors died.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: about 70 of their men were killed and nearly 150 more wounded.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: including about 150 Pequot and Mohegan Indians, against the Narragansetts

citations.title: King Philip's War (Roger Williams National Memorial, NPS)
citations.quote: the authorities in Boston demanded that the Narragansett turn over Wampanoag refugees as hostages.

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The colonial militia from Plymouth Colony, Connecticut Colony, and Massachusetts Bay Colony were led to the main Narragansett settlement

citations.title: Great Swamp Fight (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Date: 19 December (Wikipedia) against 16 December (Encyclopedia.com). Drake's estimate (King Philip's War, 1999, p. 119) is known only through Wikipedia's footnote in the infobox; not read directly. The colonial 70 has a footnote nearby to Axelrod, p. 104, not read directly. Wikipedia's lead says 150 Pequots; its body says about 150 Pequot and Mohegan. Confidence set to high: the attack is established, only its toll is rough. Figures moved from the card: National Park Service 300 men and almost 400 women and children; James Drake at least 97 warriors and 300 to 1,000 non-combatants; a participant 600 to 1,000 warriors.

events.title: Pequot War begins
events.statement: The Pequot War of 1636-1638 grew from rivalry over the fur trade among the Pequot, Mohegan, Narragansett, Dutch and English. Its proximate cause was the killing of the trader John Oldham off Block Island on 20 July 1636, by Narragansett-allied Indians by one account, by Pequots by another. In August John Endecott's roughly 90 men, by Wikipedia's account, burned Niantic villages there, then a Pequot village. Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Saybrook, the Narragansett and Mohegan fought the Pequot.

citations.title: Pequot War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A more proximate cause of the war was the killing of a trader named John Oldham, who was attacked on a voyage to Block Island on July 20, 1636.

citations.title: Pequot War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Several of his crew and he were killed and his ship was looted by Narragansett-allied Indians, who sought to discourage settlers from trading with their Pequot rivals.

citations.title: Pequot War (Wikipedia)

events.title: The Mystic massacre

place.name: Mystic Fort (Pequot fort near the Mystic River)

events.statement: During the Pequot War, on 26 May 1637, a Connecticut force under Captain John Mason, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, reached the palisaded Pequot village near the Mystic River while the sachem Sassacus was away with several hundred warriors. After stiff resistance Mason ordered it set ablaze and its two exits blocked. Those who ran were shot or killed by Narragansett fighters. Between 300 and 700 Pequot, mostly women, children and the elderly, were trapped inside.

citations.title: Mystic massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: took place on May 26, 1637 during the Pequot War, when a force from the Connecticut Colony under Captain John Mason and their Narragansett and Mohegan allies set fire to the Pequot Fort near the Mystic River.

The earlier citation to mptn-nsn.gov is dropped because that page could not be fetched (empty in the cache and 403 live). Moved from the card: John Underhill, who was there, wrote of about four hundred in the fort.

events.title: Treaty of Hartford (1638)
events.statement: On 21 September 1638 English colonists in Connecticut, the Mohegan and the Narragansett concluded a treaty at Hartford after the Pequot War. Surviving Pequot prisoners were divided, 80 each to the two nations and 20 to the Niantic sachem Ninigret, and Pequot lands went to the Connecticut River towns. The Pequot name itself was outlawed and no Pequot town allowed. Massachusetts Bay, not a party, disputed it. In 2025 a Connecticut legislative committee approved a resolution condemning the treaty.

citations.quote: concluded between English colonists in Connecticut, the Mohegan nation and the Narragansett nation on September 21, 1638, following the Pequot War, in Hartford, Connecticut.

citations.quote: each tribe received 80 captives, with 20 captives being awarded to Ninigret, a sachem of the Eastern Niantic who were allied with the Narragansett.

events.title: Narragansett siege of Fort Shantok
events.statement: After the Mohegan captured the Narragansett sachem Miantonomo in 1643 and Uncas's brother killed him with colonial leave, the Narragansett attacked from June 1644. In 1645 Uncas and the Mohegan were besieged at Fort Shantok and nearly defeated when colonists, in Wikipedia's account led by Thomas Tracy and Thomas Leffingwell, brought supplies and lifted the siege. The New England Confederation sent troops and threatened invasion, and the Narragansett signed a peace that lasted about thirty years.

events.title: Wabanaki Confederacy formed at the Caughnawaga Council
events.statement: By the Passamaquoddy wampum record, Eastern Algonquian peoples formed their own confederation at one of the three-yearly councils at Caughnawaga, with the aid of an Ottawa sakom; it is dated to the 1680s, after King Philip's War and the First Abenaki War. Member nations were to see each other as brothers, and the union helped challenge Haudenosaunee hostilities along the St Lawrence and English colonial expansion.

events.title: First Treaty of Casco (1678)
events.statement: On 12 April 1678 the provincial government of New York, which then controlled Maine, signed a treaty at Casco with Penobscot representatives under Chief Madockawando, closing the First Abenaki War. Captives were to be returned without ransom. English property rights were recognized, but settlers owed a peck of corn a year per family, a land tax that symbolized continuing Abenaki sovereignty. No copy survives; historians use Jeremy Belknap's 1784 summary. English settlers refused to abide by the terms.

events.title: Treaty of Portsmouth (1713)
events.statement: On 13 July 1713, after Queen Anne's War, eight sachems signed with totemic pictographs at Portsmouth, ending hostilities between the Eastern Abenaki and Massachusetts Bay and New Hampshire. The written text allowed English settlers back and restricted trade to approved posts. Wabanaki later claimed articles were at odds with verbal agreements, especially on British sovereignty. They had not been consulted on the Treaty of Utrecht.

events.title: Dummer's War (Father Rale's War; Lovewell's War)
events.statement: Dummer's War (1722-1725) set the New England colonies against the Wabanaki Confederacy of Mi'kmaq, Wolastoqiyik, Penobscot and Abenaki, allied with New France, as New England settlement spread along Maine and at Canso. After rangers raided Norridgewock, the Wabanaki burned Brunswick and took hostages to trade for their own people held at Boston, and Massachusetts declared war on 25 July 1722. Sébastien Rale was killed at Norridgewock in 1724, and New England took over much of Maine.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the winter of 1722, New England rangers raided Norridgewock, trying to capture Râle. While he escaped, the rangers destroyed the church and mission house.

events.notes: End dates vary: 1725 (Wikipedia lead), 1726 (Annapolis Royal) or 1727 (Dummer's Treaty final). The point is Norridgewock, a principal target and a stand-in; Shute's declaration was presumably at Boston, which the sources read don't state. The date of 25 July 1722 appears in the infobox and the Norridgewock article.

events.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Norridgewock massacre)
events.statement: On 22-23 August 1724 New England rangers under Jeremiah Moulton and Johnson Harmon went to the Abenaki village of Norridgewock on the Kennebec to kill the Jesuit Sébastien Râle, on whose head Massachusetts had set a £100 bounty, and destroy the settlement. Râle and Chief Mog were killed, and the rangers massacred, by John Grenier's account, nearly two dozen women and children; accounts of the dead vary. Survivors abandoned the village for St Francois (Odanak).

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On August 22, 1724, Captains Jeremiah Moulton and Johnson Harmon led 200 rangers to the main Abenaki village on the Kennebec River, Norridgewock, Maine, to kill Father Sébastien Râle and destroy the settlement.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Other motivations for the raid included the special £100 scalp bounty placed on Râle's head by the Massachusetts provincial assembly

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Casualties, depending on the sources consulted, vary, but most accounts record about eighty Abenaki being killed.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Lieutenant Richard Jacques killed Râle in the opening moments of the battle; Chief Mog was killed, and the rangers massacred nearly two dozen women and children.

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: those who had escaped were forced to abandon their village and moved northward to the Abenaki village of St Francois (Odanak, Quebec).

citations.title: Battle of Norridgewock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On the 23rd, there were 160 Abenaki, many of whom were killed as they tried to escape.

events.notes: The source says 160 Abenaki were there on the 23rd, that at least 31 fought so others could escape, and that the English lost two militiamen and one Nauset. Grenier, The Far Reaches of Empire (2008), is known through the Wikipedia footnote, not read directly. The page's 200 rangers and 'about eighty' dead have no footnote that names a giver, so they are off the card.

events.title: Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1726 (ratified at Annapolis Royal)
events.statement: On 4 June 1726 Mi'kmaw, Wolastoqiyik and Passamaquoddy leaders gathered at Annapolis Royal to ratify a treaty with the British Crown, based on one negotiated at Boston in 1725 after war with New England. Seventy-seven delegates signed the articles of peace; Lawrence Armstrong and John Doucett signed the British promise not to molest fishing, hunting and planting. Parks Canada calls it the first treaty between these peoples and any European state in the region, and the basis of later ones.

citations.title: The Peace and Friendship Treaty of 1726 (Parks Canada)
citations.quote: On 4 June 1726, Mi’kmaw, Wəlastəkokewiyik, and Peskətəmohkatewey leaders gathered at Annapolis Royal, Nova Scotia, to ratify a treaty with the British Crown. This treaty was based on a treaty negotiated in Boston in 1725

events.title: Membertou baptized at Port-Royal
events.statement: On 24 June 1610, weeks after the French returned to Port-Royal, the missionary priest Jessé Fléché baptized the Mi'kmaq chief Membertou and 20 of his extended family, by the Dictionary of Canadian Biography's account the first First Nations people baptized by the French. Membertou took the name Henri. The Dictionary suggests he may have seen baptism as a diplomatic ritual consolidating the alliance with the French, or as akin to the resurrection ceremony of the chiefs.

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: Scarcely a few weeks after their return, a number of the French organized Membertou’s baptism

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: on 24 June 1610, the feast day of Saint John the Baptist, the missionary priest Jessé Fléché heard the great chief’s confession and baptized him, along with 20 members of his extended family

citations.quote: they became the first people of the First Nations to be baptized by the French.

citations.quote: Membertou became Henri.

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: with baptism seen as a diplomatic ritual that would consolidate the union.

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: For Membertou, perhaps it represented a variation of the resurrection ceremony of the chiefs

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: until the French came back at the beginning of June 1610.

citations.title: Membertou (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: the Micmac chief again took care of the habitation at Port-Royal

events.notes: The earlier Canadian Encyclopedia citation is dropped: the page can't be read by the fetcher (403 live, empty in the project cache), so the Concordat-of-1610 note and the 'first Indigenous person' wording are unconfirmed here. The earlier notes also gave other relative counts (21 or 24) that were not re-checked.

events.title: Halifax founded by the British
events.statement: On 21 June 1749, on King George II's order, Edward Cornwallis arrived with 13 transports and 1,176 settlers and founded Halifax as the new capital of Nova Scotia, at the harbour the Mi'kmaq call K'jipuktuk. The Mi'kmaq viewed it as violating an earlier treaty, and most of their communities refused a peace treaty that year in anger over it. The founding marked the beginning of Father Le Loutre's War with the Mi'kmaq and Acadians.

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cornwallis founded the Town of Halifax on what is now known as the Halifax Peninsula, on June 21, 1749.

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: in 1749, King George II ordered Edward Cornwallis to establish Halifax as a new capital.

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The establishment of Halifax marked the beginning of Father Le Loutre's War, as the Mi'kmaq viewed it as violating a treaty they signed with British colonial authorities in 1727

citations.title: Halifax, Nova Scotia (Wikipedia)

events.title: Treaty of 1752 (Mi'kmaq of Shubenacadie)
events.statement: On 22 November 1752 Governor Hopson and Jean-Baptiste Cope, chief sakamow of Shubenacadie, signed a treaty at Halifax reaffirming the 1726 treaty and formalizing commercial relations. Accounts differ on whether the war had ended in 1751; scholars disagree on whether Cope signed for all Mi'kmaq. Cope burned it on 23 May 1753. R. v. Simon (1985) held it protected hunting rights for those from Shubenacadie but found too little evidence on whether hostilities ended it, as Stephen Patterson later testified.

citations.title: Peace and Friendship Treaties (Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada)
citations.quote: This treaty was signed in Halifax on 22 November by Governor Hopson and Jean-Baptiste Cope, chief sakamow of Shubenacadie

CIRNAC says intermittent war ended in 1751; the Treaty of 1752 page says the treaty fell 'during' Father Le Loutre's War and the Cope page has the war continuing at the burning, so the statement no longer follows CIRNAC alone. The same page says Marshall's lawyers then turned to the Halifax Treaties of 1760-61.

events.title: Siege of the Susquehannock fort at Piscataway Creek
events.statement: In 1675 the Susquehannock, weakened by epidemics and war, moved to a palisaded fort on Piscataway Creek: most historians credit a Haudenosaunee defeat, Francis Jennings coercion by Maryland. After Virginians mistakenly killed several and raids were blamed on them, a large militia under John Washington and Thomas Truman besieged the fort in September and executed five sachems summoned to a parley. In early November the Susquehannock escaped by night, and survivors scattered.

citations.quote: By the 1670s, epidemics and years of war with the Haudenosaunee had taken their toll on the Susquehannock.

citations.title: Susquehannock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Most historians believe that the Haudenosaunee inflicted a major defeat on the Susquehannock c. 1674

citations.quote: a thousand-man expedition against the Susquehannock was mounted by militia from Virginia and Maryland led by John Washington and Thomas Truman.

citations.title: Susquehannock (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Truman and Washington summoned five sachems to a parley but then had them summarily executed.

citations.title: Susquehannock (Wikipedia)

events.title: Conestoga massacre (Paxton Boys)

place.name: Conestoga Indian Town (Manor Township, Lancaster County)

events.statement: At dawn on 14 December 1763 about fifty armed colonists from Paxton rode into Conestoga Indian Town, burned the homes and killed the six people they found. Those away took refuge in Lancaster, where officials locked them in the workhouse; on 27 December the Paxton Boys broke in and killed the fourteen inside, men, women and children. No one was ever arrested or tried. In early 1764 the Paxton Boys marched on Philadelphia until Benjamin Franklin turned them back.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town (ExplorePAHistory)
citations.quote: On December 14, 1763, about fifty armed colonists from Paxton (near modern Harrisburg) rode into Conestoga. In a dawn attack reminiscent of the Kittanning raid, they burned the homes and murdered the six Indians they found there.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town (ExplorePAHistory)
citations.quote: sought refuge in Lancaster, where the city officials locked them inside the workhouse, supposedly the most defensible building in town.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town (ExplorePAHistory)
citations.quote: On December 27, the Paxton Boys returned, broke into the workhouse, and murdered the fourteen Indian men, women, and children inside.

citations.title: Conestoga Indian Town (ExplorePAHistory)
citations.quote: Benjamin Franklin rode over to them and convinced the Paxton Boys to return home without further violence, but no one was ever arrested or tried for the crimes committed at Conestoga and Lancaster.

citations.quote: In February 1764, the Paxton Boys marched on Philadelphia with the intent of murdering the Moravian Lenape and Mohican who had been moved to that city for their protection.

events.notes: Wikipedia gives 20 Conestoga killed in all (6 + 14); the earlier note records one Historical Society of Pennsylvania source counting 21, not re-read. ExplorePAHistory says the town was formed by Susquehannock, Seneca, Delaware, Shawnee and Conoy.

events.title: Beothuk leader Nonosabasut killed and Demasduit captured at Red Indian Lake
events.statement: On 1 March 1819, with the governor's leave to recover property the Beothuk had taken the previous fall, John Peyton Jr. and eight armed men went up to Beothuk (Red Indian) Lake. They seized Demasduit, and Peyton's party killed her husband Nonosabasut, the group's leader, as he tried to negotiate her release; her infant son died two days later. Demasduit died of tuberculosis in January 1820, and the couple's remains came back from Scotland in 2020.

citations.title: Demasduit (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On March 1, 1819, John Peyton Jr. and eight armed men went up the Exploits River to Beothuk Lake in search of the Beothuks and their equipment.

citations.title: Demasduit (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The governor of the colony, Sir Charles Hamilton, authorized an attempt to recover the stolen property.

citations.title: Demasduit (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Nonosabasut, her husband and the leader of the group, was killed while attempting to negotiate for Demasduit’s release. Her infant son died two days after she was taken.

citations.quote: She observed the kidnapping of Demasduwit and the killing of Nonosbawsut by Peyton’s party in March 1819

citations.title: Demasduit (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 2020, the remains of Demasduit and her husband Nonosabasut were repatriated from Scotland after years of advocacy.

citations.title: Demasduit (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: she was taken ill and died of tuberculosis at Ship Cove (now Botwood) aboard Buchan's vessel Grasshopper, on 8 January 1820.

events.notes: Names are spelled variously (Demasduit/Demasduwit, Nonosabasut/Nonosbawsut). Wikipedia's grand jury absolving Peyton carries a citation-needed tag and is left off. The earlier Canadian Encyclopedia citation is dropped because that page could not be read (403). The Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls the event a kidnapping and killing. The 1 March date is when the party set out.

events.title: Shanawdithit, the last known Beothuk, dies at St. John's
events.statement: Shawnadithit (Shanawdithit, Nancy April) died of tuberculosis in St John's on 6 June 1829. She had witnessed Demasduit's capture in 1819 and, starving, was taken with her mother and sister by the furrier William Cull in 1823. Her accounts to William Cormack and her drawings are a chief record of Beothuk language and customs. The Dictionary of Canadian Biography calls her the last known survivor, while oral histories suggest a few Beothuk lived on.

citations.title: Shawnadithit (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)

Wikipedia also notes Santu Toney, recorded in 1910, as possible evidence of later survival. Spelling differs by source.

events.title: Nanticoke move to Fort Niagara and the Six Nations (1778 onward)
events.statement: In 1778 two hundred Nanticoke, allied with the British, moved north to Fort Niagara during the Revolutionary War, and the British later resettled them with Haudenosaunee peoples at the Six Nations Reserve near Brantford, Ontario. From the Chesapeake Bay homeland, some Nanticoke had moved to Pennsylvania in 1744 with the Haudenosaunee's permission. Adopted into the Confederacy, their descendants still live on the Grand River reserve, while others live in Oklahoma among the Delaware.

citations.title: Nanticoke people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: During the American Revolution, they allied with the British.

citations.title: Nanticoke people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1778, two hundred Nanticoke moved north to Fort Niagara in present-day Canada because of their alliance. Later the British resettled them at the Six Nations Reserve with Iroquois peoples, near Brantford, Ontario, Canada.

citations.quote: Some Nanticoke moved up to Pennsylvania in 1744, where they gained permission from the Iroquois Confederacy to settle near Wyoming, Pennsylvania

citations.quote: Others now live on the Six Nations of the Grand River reserve in Ontario, Canada where some ancestors resettled after the Revolutionary War, as they had been adopted as members of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy.

citations.quote: Today their descendants continue to live in Oklahoma among the Delaware Nation and the Delaware Tribe of Indians.

citations.title: Nanticoke people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: whose traditional homelands are in the Chesapeake Bay area

events.notes: Single source. It says Fort Niagara is in present-day Canada, but the place field's Fort Niagara is on the American side (Youngstown, New York); the card doesn't repeat that.

events.title: Epidemics devastate the Wendat and neighbours (1634-1640)
events.statement: From 1634 to about 1640 epidemics of measles and smallpox, which have been linked to contact with French traders and missionaries, devastated the Wendat and Petun. McMillan and Yellowhorn put the Wendat at 20,000-30,000 falling to about 9,000 by 1640, and the Petun at around 8,000 falling to 3,000. So many died that they abandoned villages and fields, and their society's structure was disrupted.

citations.quote: A number of epidemics were documented in Huron–Petun societies between 1634 and 1640, which have been linked to the arrival of French missionaries and traders.

citations.title: Petun (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: One modern estimate places the Petun population at around 8000, dropping to 3000 by 1640 following waves of disease epidemics.

citations.title: Petun (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: there were an estimated 18–25 Wendat villages with an overall population of 20,000–30,000; this had dropped to about 9000 by 1640.

citations.title: Huron people (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Huron people (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Huron people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Such losses had a high social cost, devastating families and clans, and disrupting their society's structure and traditions.

events.notes: McMillan and Yellowhorn (First Peoples in Canada, 2004) are known here only through the Petun article's footnote 2, not read directly. Wikipedia's Huron people article has half to two-thirds dying, leaving about 12,000; no giver could be tied to that, so it is left off. The Canadian Encyclopedia's figure (20,000-25,000 to about 9,000 by 1642), cited on the earlier card, couldn't be read by the fetcher (403).

events.title: Haudenosaunee destroy Wendake; Sainte-Marie burned
events.statement: In March 1649 a large Haudenosaunee war party entered Wendake and burned the mission villages of St Ignace and St Louis, capturing Jean de Brébeuf and Gabriel Lalemant at St Louis. By 1 May the Wendat had burned 15 of their villages and fled, many to Gahoendoe (Christian Island), where most starved that winter. On 16 June the Jesuits burned their mission of Sainte-Marie rather than risk it being overrun. Some Wendat later settled near Quebec; others became the Wyandot.

citations.title: Sainte-Marie among the Hurons (Wikipedia)

The article's 'about 10,000' to Gahoendoe has no giver either, so the card says 'many'. The Canadian Encyclopedia citation on the earlier card couldn't be read (403).

events.title: Pontiac's attempt on Fort Detroit
events.statement: The nations of the Great Lakes, among them the Odawa, Ojibwe, Potawatomi and Wyandot, were alarmed by the policies of the British general Jeffery Amherst. On 7 May 1763 the Odawa leader Pontiac entered Fort Detroit with about 300 men carrying concealed weapons, hoping to take it by surprise, but the British were ready. He laid siege instead as war spread across the region, and lifted it on 31 October, convinced the French would not come.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On May 7, Pontiac entered Fort Detroit with about 300 men carrying concealed weapons, hoping to take the stronghold by surprise. The British had learned of his plan, however, and were armed and ready.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The conflict is named after its most well-known participant, the Odawa leader Pontiac.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The first group was composed of tribes of the Great Lakes region: Odawas, Ojibwes, and Potawatomis, who spoke Algonquian languages, and Wyandot, who spoke an Iroquoian language.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The war began in May 1763 when Native Americans, alarmed by policies imposed by British General Jeffery Amherst, attacked a number of British forts and settlements.

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Pontiac lifted the siege on October 31, 1763, convinced that the French would not come to his aid at Detroit

citations.title: Pontiac's War (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Nester (2000, pp. 77-78) is known only through Wikipedia's footnote on the 300; not read directly. Wikipedia's lead says nine forts destroyed; its body says eight taken; the card avoids a count. The date is the failed surprise; the siege followed.

events.title: The Royal Proclamation of 1763

place.name: Indian Reserve west of the Appalachians (Ohio River)

events.statement: With the siege still on, George III issued the Royal Proclamation on 7 October 1763. It forbade new settlement, at least for the time being, west of a line along the Appalachians, marked as an Indian Reserve, and allowed land purchases only by Crown officials at a public meeting. The line was meant to move west in an orderly way. The proclamation remains legally important to First Nations in Canada as the first legal recognition of Aboriginal title.

events.title: Treaty of Camp Charlotte ends Lord Dunmore's War

events.statement: After Virginia's victory over Cornstalk's Shawnee at Point Pleasant on 10 October 1774, the Virginians under Lord Dunmore marched into the Ohio Valley and compelled Cornstalk to a peace at Camp Charlotte near the Scioto towns on 19 October. The Shawnee agreed to stop hunting south of the Ohio and harassing travellers on the river, honouring the 1768 Stanwix cession of Kentucky. The Mingo leader Logan said he would cease fighting but refused to attend.

events.title: Harmar's campaign against Kekionga
events.statement: In autumn 1790 General Josiah Harmar marched from Fort Washington against Kekionga with regulars and, mostly, militia. Blue Jacket and Little Turtle gathered warriors and evacuated the towns. John Hardin's advance party reached Kekionga on 15 October and spent days looting and burning; then on 19-22 October Harmar's divided detachments were ambushed in turn. With more than 200 casualties by Colin Calloway's count, he ordered a hasty retreat.

events.title: St. Clair's Defeat

place.name: Fort Recovery, Ohio (site of St. Clair's defeat)

events.statement: At dawn on 4 November 1791, in the Northwest Territory, about 1,000 warriors under Little Turtle of the Miami, Blue Jacket of the Shawnee and Buckongahelas of the Lenape encircled General Arthur St. Clair's camp. In under three hours the Americans lost 630 killed and almost 300 wounded, against about 25 Native dead. Proportionately, the historian Colin Calloway writes, it was the biggest US military disaster ever. Washington forced St. Clair to resign, and Congress investigated.

The infobox gives 656 Americans killed or captured and 21 Native dead. Confidence set to high: the battle is established. Moved from the card: Landon Jones's 'most decisive defeat' (through a Wikipedia footnote).

events.title: The Battle of Fallen Timbers
events.statement: Three years later the United States came back. On 20 August 1794 General Anthony Wayne's Legion, with Kentucky militia, defeated Shawnee under Blue Jacket, Ottawa under Egushawa and others near the Maumee in little more than an hour. Fleeing warriors reached the British Fort Miami to find its gates shut against them. Wayne lost 33 men; estimates of the Native dead run from 19 to about 40. It was the last battle of the Northwest Indian War.

events.title: The Treaty of Greenville
events.statement: The peace was signed at Fort Greenville on 3 August 1795. For goods worth $20,000 and annual payments, the nations of the Western Confederacy ceded large parts of modern Ohio, and the United States kept posts inside Indian Country, among them the future site of Chicago. Blue Jacket urged acceptance while Little Turtle led the opposition. Settlers went on encroaching, and the Shawnee chief Tecumseh charged that the peace chiefs had given away land they did not own.

events.title: Treaty of Fort Wayne (Ten O'clock Line Treaty)
events.statement: In September 1809 Governor William Henry Harrison, against President Madison's wishes, met the Potawatomi, Lenape, Eel River and Miami at Fort Wayne, promising subsidies and using willing sellers to press holdouts. Signed on 30 September, the treaty sold over 3,000,000 acres, mostly along the Wabash. The Miami, Wea and Kickapoo had been opposed; the Shawnee were excluded. It led to the war begun by Tecumseh.

events.title: The Battle of Tippecanoe
events.statement: The Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother Tenskwatawa had built a confederacy of nations opposed to American settlement, based at Prophetstown. In 1811 Governor William Henry Harrison marched on the town with about 1,000 men while Tecumseh was away recruiting allies. Before dawn on 7 November warriors under Tenskwatawa attacked; Harrison's men held for over two hours, then burned the abandoned town and its winter food. The confederacy never fully recovered, and the victory won Harrison the nickname 'Tippecanoe'.

events.title: The Battle of the Thames and the death of Tecumseh
events.statement: In 1813, with the Americans at war with Britain, General Henry Procter abandoned Detroit and Amherstburg and retreated up the Thames valley, Tecumseh and his followers reluctantly going with him. On 5 October they made a stand a few miles west of Moraviantown in Upper Canada. Harrison's mounted infantry overran the British line, the warriors fell back once Tecumseh was killed, and his confederacy collapsed. The Americans regained control of Detroit, and Procter was later court-martialled.

events.title: Bad Axe Massacre; end of the Black Hawk War
events.statement: On 1-2 August 1832 US Army regulars and militia, with the steamboat Warrior on both days, attacked Black Hawk's band of Sauk and Meskwaki as it tried to recross the Mississippi near present-day Victory, Wisconsin; Black Hawk and most leaders had fled by the second day. Historians have called it a massacre since the 1850s, and the Oklahoma encyclopedia a slaughter of the unarmed. It ended the war, and in September the tribes sold about 6 million acres of Iowa.

events.title: Treaty of Chicago (1833)
events.statement: On 26 September 1833 the United States and the Chippewa, Odawa and Potawatomi agreed an initial version of the Treaty of Chicago, with supplementary articles the next day. It required them to cede 5,000,000 acres in Illinois and Michigan Territory and move west of the Mississippi within three years, for presents, annuities, payment of their debts and an equal tract on the Missouri, between the Boyer and Nodaway rivers. It was one of the removal treaties, ratified in 1835.

events.title: Potawatomi Trail of Death
events.statement: After Chief Menominee's band refused to leave Twin Lakes by the removal deadline of 1838, General John Tipton's militia surprised the village on 30 August. On 4 September they began marching 859 Potawatomi on the rolls to Kansas. The journey of about 660 miles ended on 4 November near Osawatomie; 756 arrived, 42 were recorded dead, 28 of them children, by Arville Funk's count, and the rest escaped. The chiefs had protested that signatures on the 1836 treaty were forged.

events.title: Forced removal of the Miami from Indiana
events.statement: Having ceded their Indiana land by treaties between 1818 and 1840, the Miami faced forced removal in 1846. On 6 October, the Myaamia Center records, people boarded canal boats near Peru, loading finishing near Fort Wayne next day; they went on by ship to Kansas Landing and 50 miles overland, reaching the reservation by 9 November. Counts run from 300 on the Peru marker and 327 in a Miami Nation timeline to the Oklahoma encyclopedia's five hundred.

events.title: Robinson Superior and Robinson Huron Treaties
events.statement: On 7 September (Superior) and 9 September 1850 (Huron), at Sault Ste. Marie, Ojibwa chiefs of the north shores of Lake Superior and Lake Huron made treaties with the Crown through William Benjamin Robinson, ceding their territory while keeping listed reserves and annuities. An augmentation clause promised higher annuities if the land proved productive, but they stayed capped at $4 per person from 1874. In 2024 the Supreme Court of Canada ruled unanimously against the Crown's failure to raise them.

events.title: Battle of Mabila (de Soto expedition)

place.name: Mabila (site uncertain; Marengo County, Alabama region)

events.statement: On 18 October 1540 Hernando de Soto reached Mabila, a fortified town under Tuskaloosa, whom the Spanish had taken hostage. A fight broke out, warriors emerged from the houses, and the Spanish burned the town and killed most of them. Spanish accounts at the time put the Native dead at 2,500 to 3,000; the chronicler Elvas has about 2,500; Tony Horwitz gives 2,000 to 6,000. The site remains unfound, though 2021 finds in Marengo County point to the province.

events.title: Battle of Ayubale in Moore's raid on Apalachee

place.name: Apalachee Province missions (Ayubale and San Luis), Florida

events.statement: On 25 January 1704 James Moore's expedition of Carolina colonists and Muscogee allies reached Ayubale, a large Apalachee mission town. While most Muscogee raided the surrounding villages, Moore entered the town with his colonists. Father Angel Miranda and 26 men held the church compound for nine hours, surrendering with 58 women and children when their arrows ran out. The scholar John Hann says the raids sent 2,000 into exile; Governor Bienville wrote of 2,000 Apalachee killed.

events.title: Tuscarora War begins
events.statement: The Tuscarora War began in September 1711, when Chief Hancock's Lower Towns, pressed by small coastal nations harassed by settlers, staged what NCpedia calls an evidently intended warning attack on settlements from 22 September, after John Lawson, taken hostage, was put to death. Tom Blount's northern Tuscarora stayed out at first. Expeditions of colonists and Native allies from South Carolina followed in 1712 and 1713, and many Tuscarora migrated north to join the Haudenosaunee as the sixth nation.

citations.title: Tuscarora War (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Point moved from Fort Neoheroka, built after the first attacks, to New Bern, standing for the settlements attacked. Date: Wikipedia's lead gives 10 September 1711; both sources date the attacks to 22 September. Lawson: NCpedia has him taken hostage in September 1711 and put to death; Wikipedia has him killed in the raids, and its 'hundreds of settlers' names no giver. Richard White and Rebecca Seaman, cited on Wikipedia, suggest the war grew out of misunderstandings.

events.title: Siege of Fort Neoheroka

place.name: Fort Neoheroka (Tuscarora), Greene County, North Carolina

events.statement: From 20 to 23 March 1713 colonel James Moore, with a force of colonists and nearly 1,000 Native allies by Jim Shamlin's count, took Fort Neoheroka, the last great Tuscarora stand. A tunnel charge failed; fire and three days of hand-to-hand fighting won the fort. Baron von Graffenried wrote of about 200 burned in a redoubt and about 900 dead and captured, women and children among them; NCpedia has Moore losing 47 killed. It ended Tuscarora war-making capacity.

The Tuscarora War article has Hancock captured by Blount and executed in 1712, with a citation-needed tag.

events.title: Yamasee War begins

place.name: Pocotaligo (Yamasee town), near Yemassee, South Carolina

events.statement: On the evening of 14 April 1715 a South Carolina delegation came to the Yamasee town of Pocotaligo, promising redress of grievances. In the night the Yamasee debated and chose war; at dawn on Good Friday, 15 April, they attacked, killing Thomas Nairne, John Wright and two others. The war, driven by abusive trade and the Indian slave trade, drew in the Muscogee, Cherokee, Catawba and others until 1717. The Yamasee moved south but raided into the 1720s.

events.title: Natchez revolt at Fort Rosalie
events.statement: On 28 November 1729, provoked when commandant Sieur de Chépart demanded land from a Natchez village for his plantation, the Natchez attacked Fort Rosalie and its homesteads. They killed about 230 colonists, by a tally made a year later, reported by James Barnett: 138 men, 35 women and 56 children; hundreds were captured. The French and Choctaw retaliated in 1730, enslaving hundreds; campaigns through 1731 ended the Natchez as a unified nation, and survivors joined other nations.

citations.quote: Natchez leaders were provoked to revolt when the French colonial commandant, Sieur de Chépart, demanded land from a Natchez village for his own plantation near Fort Rosalie.

The tally is footnoted nearby to James Barnett (2007), not read directly; who first made it is not stated on the page. The revolt article says most women and enslaved Africans were spared. The French also ordered the massacre of the uninvolved Chaouacha. Barnett, The Natchez Indians (2007), p. 105, is known through the footnote, not read directly.

events.title: Battle of Ackia (French attack on Chickasaw)

place.name: Ackia and Ogoula Tchetoka (Chickasaw villages), Tupelo area, Mississippi

events.statement: On 26 May 1736 a force from Lower Louisiana under Governor Bienville, of French and Choctaw, stormed the fortified Chickasaw village of Ackia near present Tupelo. Under mantelets that proved ineffective, it was pinned down on the hillside by 'a shower of balls' and fell back with heavy losses, about 200 by a school history of Alabama by William Garrott Brown and Albert Pickett. A force from Upper Louisiana had already been crushed in March, and Bienville retreated.

events.title: Anglo-Cherokee War
events.statement: Settlers encroaching on Cherokee towns brought open war in 1758, when Virginia militia attacked Moytoy over an alleged horse theft. After the garrison of Fort Prince George killed Cherokee hostages, Cherokees besieged Fort Loudoun until it surrendered in August 1760, then attacked the departing garrison, killing, by Carroll Van West's account, more than two dozen. Archibald Montgomerie razed ten Lower Towns before defeat at Echoee Pass; in 1761 James Grant destroyed homes and food. Treaties ended it in late 1761.

Wikipedia's Anglo-Cherokee War says the garrison was massacred; its Fort Loudoun article, followed here, is fuller. The army sizes (1,200 and 2,800) and the 5,000 people have no named author on the page and are left off. Van West's Tennessee Encyclopedia entry is known through the Fort Loudoun article's footnote, not read directly. The 16 hostages have no giver on the page, so that figure is off the card.

events.title: Treaty of Augusta confirms Catawba reservation
events.statement: In return for their alliance in the French and Indian War, the 1763 Treaty of Augusta gave the Catawba a tract 'fifteen miles square', about 144,000 acres in South Carolina. Within a few years settlers had leased almost all the most fertile land. In 1840, by the Treaty of Nation Ford with South Carolina, the Catawba sold all but one square mile of it, though only the federal government had that power and the Senate never ratified it.

citations.quote: In 1763, the colonial government of South Carolina confirmed a reservation for the Catawba of 225 square miles (580 km2; 144,000 acres), on both sides of the Catawba River

events.title: Treaty of Hopewell with the Cherokee

place.name: Hopewell on the Keowee (near Pendleton), South Carolina

events.statement: On 28 November 1785 US representative Benjamin Hawkins and Cherokee leaders signed the first Treaty of Hopewell at Andrew Pickens's plantation on the Keowee. It set much of the Cherokee Nation's northern and eastern boundary, ceded a wedge of land south of the Cumberland around Nashville, and barred settlement on Cherokee land. An article providing for a Cherokee delegate to Congress has yet to be fulfilled. The Cherokee, despite signing, did not recognize US sovereignty over their ancestral lands.

events.title: The Battle of Horseshoe Bend (Tohopeka)
events.statement: In the South the Creeks were split by a war of their own, and the Red Sticks, the faction opposing American expansion, held out at Tohopeka on the Tallapoosa. On 27 March 1814 Andrew Jackson's militia and regulars, with Cherokee and Lower Creek allies, attacked. The Cherokee crossed the river to strike from the rear as Jackson charged the barricade. By nightfall at least 800 of the 1,000 Red Sticks under Chief Menawa had died, against 49 of Jackson's men.

events.title: The Treaty of Fort Jackson
events.statement: The peace that followed Jackson's victory was signed on 9 August 1814 at Fort Jackson near present-day Wetumpka, concluding the Creek War. The Creeks were forced to cede between 21 and 23 million acres, much of it in central and southern Alabama. The Indian agent Benjamin Hawkins thought the terms too harsh, for nearly eight million of those acres were taken from allied Indians.

Wikipedia's treaty article also places the signing on the Tallapoosa near Alexander City; the Encyclopedia of Alabama and NPS put it at Fort Jackson near Wetumpka, matching the place field. Article IX of the Treaty of Ghent nominally required restoring such lands; the Encyclopedia says the US ignored it.

events.title: The Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek

place.name: Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty site (southwest Noxubee County), near Macon, Mississippi

events.statement: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 set out to move the eastern nations west of the Mississippi. On 27 September, at Dancing Rabbit Creek, Choctaw negotiators led by Greenwood LeFlore and Mosholatubbee signed with John Eaton and John Coffee, giving up their remaining homeland, 10 to 11 million acres, for land in Indian Territory. It was the first removal treaty carried into effect under the Act. Article 14 let Choctaw who chose to stay in Mississippi become citizens.

events.title: Choctaw removal begins
events.statement: The first wave of Choctaw removal from the Mississippi homeland began in October 1831, with later waves in 1832-1834, 1838 and 1844-1855, by the Choctaw Nation's own history. The Oklahoma Historical Society counts more than six thousand arriving in Indian Territory in the fall and winter of 1831-32 and about five thousand more in 1832-33. The Nation describes catastrophic losses, falling hardest on elders and children, which cost it knowledge keepers.

citations.title: A new Chahta homeland: a history by the decade, 1830-1840 (Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma)
citations.quote: The first wave of removals began in October 1831. Later waves occurred throughout 1832-1834, 1838, and throughout 1844-1855.

citations.quote: Removal caused catastrophic losses within the numerous Choctaw communities. The removal journey was particularly devastating to elders and children

citations.title: Choctaw (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)

events.notes: Place = Nanih Waiya as the homeland the Choctaw left. A death toll is left off the card: Wikipedia gives about 2,500 in its Choctaw Trail of Tears article and 2,000-4,000+ in its Trail of Tears table, neither with an author I could confirm on the page.

events.title: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek

place.name: Pontotoc, Chickasaw council house area, Mississippi

events.statement: On 20 October 1832, after Mississippi declared jurisdiction over the Chickasaw and outlawed tribal self-governance, Chickasaw leaders including Ishtehotopa, Tishominko and Levi and George Colbert signed at their Council House on Pontotoc Creek. They ceded the remaining homeland east of the Mississippi, 6,283,804 acres, for a promise of suitable land in the west. The historian Arrell Gibson calls it the basic Chickasaw removal document; further arrangements ran on to 1837.

citations.title: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1832 (Chickasaw.tv, Chickasaw Nation)
citations.quote: signed at the Chickasaw Council House on October 20, 1832, relinquished Chickasaw lands east of the Mississippi River in exchange for a promise to find suitable land west of the Mississippi River.

citations.title: Treaty with the Chickasaw, 1832 (Chickasaw.tv, Chickasaw Nation)

citations.quote: The treaty ceded the 6,283,804 acres of the remaining Chickasaw homeland in Mississippi

citations.title: Treaty of Pontotoc Creek (Wikipedia)

events.notes: I know Gibson's wording only as Wikipedia quotes it. The acreage has no named author on the Wikipedia page, so it stands as the treaty article's figure.

events.title: The Treaty of New Echota
events.statement: The Cherokee treaty was made by a minority. On 29 December 1835 at New Echota, US officials and the Treaty Party, a political faction, signed terms for the Cherokee Nation to cede its southeastern territory and move west. The National Council did not approve it, Principal Chief John Ross did not sign, and the Cherokee Nation holds that the signers lacked authority under its law. Despite Ross's pleas the Senate passed it in May 1836 by a single vote.

citations.title: Treaty of New Echota (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: by officials of the United States government and representatives of a minority Cherokee political faction, the Treaty Party.

citations.title: Treaty of New Echota (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Although the treaty was not approved by the Cherokee National Council nor signed by Principal Chief John Ross , it was amended and ratified in March 1836, and became the legal basis for the forcible removal

events.notes: Wikipedia's lead says ratified March 1836, its body and infobox May 1836 (23 May per the infobox); May used. The Oklahoma Historical Society calls the signers the Ridge Party. Ross's petition with almost 16,000 signatures was delivered in spring 1838, after ratification, so it is left off this card.

events.title: Second Seminole War begins (Dade battle)

place.name: Dade battle site, near Bushnell, Florida

events.statement: On 28 December 1835 Seminole and Black Seminole warriors ambushed two US Army companies under Major Francis Dade just south of present-day Bushnell, on their march from Fort Brooke to reinforce Fort King. Only three soldiers and their guide Louis Pacheco were reported to have survived, one soldier dying the next day. The Seminoles were resisting removal under the Treaty of Payne's Landing, and the fight officially started a war that ended in 1842 without a peace treaty.

citations.title: Dade battle (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: were ambushed by approximately 180 Seminole and Black Seminole warriors as they marched from Fort Brooke on Tampa Bay to reinforce Fort King

citations.title: Second Seminole War (Wikipedia)

events.notes: Numbers differ within Wikipedia's article: 103 men in the lead, 110 in the background section; its warrior count of about 180 has no named author and is left off. The article's infobox gives Seminole losses of 3 killed and 5 wounded and quotes a Seminole account with the same figures. The infobox of the war's article dates it from 23 December 1835, when Dade left Fort Brooke.

events.title: The Trail of Tears begins
events.statement: That treaty became the legal basis for removal. Forced expulsion began in May 1838, when General Winfield Scott received President Van Buren's final order; about 2,000 Cherokee had already gone west. Nearly 14,000 were driven from their homes and held in stockades before the journey to Oklahoma and Arkansas, and over 4,000 died of cold, disease and hunger, more than a quarter of the nation. In Cherokee the event is called 'the place where they cried'.

citations.title: Trail of Tears (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Trail of Tears (Wikipedia)

citations.quote: In 1838, nearly 14,000 Cherokees were forced from their homes and held in stockades before beginning a grueling journey westward to Oklahoma and Arkansas. Over 4,000 died from cold, disease, and hunger on the six-month march

citations.title: Cherokee (Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture)
citations.quote: In 1838–39 more than one-fourth of the tribe died on the trek from the Southeast to the Indian Territory.

citations.title: Trail of Tears (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the Cherokee language , the event is called nu na da ul tsun yi ( ' the place where they cried ' )

citations.title: Treaty of New Echota (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: became the legal basis for the forcible removal known as the Trail of Tears

events.notes: Estimates differ: removed nearly 14,000 (NPS) or 16,000 (Wikipedia's table); deaths over 4,000 (NPS), about 4,000 in Wikipedia's text, 4,000-8,000 in its table. A footnote in Wikipedia quoting the historian Ostler says the majority of removal deaths came in internment camps and the first years after arrival rather than on the journey, against the NPS 'on the march' wording; not put on the card because I saw it only as a footnote quotation. The card no longer says the deaths came 'on the march', given Ostler's point below.

events.title: Muscogee (Creek) removal
events.statement: The Creek War of 1836 ended with about 2,500 Muscogee people, including several hundred warriors in chains, marched to Montgomery and crowded onto barges in the July heat. Between the summer of 1836 and early 1837, by the National Park Service's account, over 14,000 made the three-month journey to Indian Territory, over 800 miles by land and 400 by water. It counts 21,792 Muscogee in Georgia and Alabama in 1832, and only 13,537 in Oklahoma twenty years after removal.

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation (Ocmulgee Mounds, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Creek War of 1836 ended when about 2,500 people, including several hundred warriors in chains, were marched on foot to Montgomery, Alabama, and crowded onto barges during the extreme heat of July.

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation (Ocmulgee Mounds, National Park Service)
citations.quote: During the summer and winter of 1836-early 1837, over 14,000 Muscogee Indians made the three-month journey to Oklahoma, a trip of over 800 land miles and another 400 by water.

citations.title: The Muscogee Nation (Ocmulgee Mounds, National Park Service)
citations.quote: 21,792 Muscogee Indians lived in Georgia and Alabama in 1832. Twenty years after the "removal" ended, only 13,537 Muscogee remained in Oklahoma.

events.notes: Place = Tukabatchee as an Alabama Muscogee town; removal covered all of Muscogee territory. Wikipedia's Trail of Tears table gives 19,600 removed over 1834-1837 and 3,500-4,500 deaths, a broader count than the NPS one for 1836-37. NPS adds that as a percentage of population the Muscogee suffered more deaths than the Cherokee; not used.

events.title: Cherokee Nation adopts a written constitution
events.statement: In 1827 the Cherokee Nation, governed from New Echota, adopted a written constitution modeled on that of the United States, with legislative, executive and judicial branches. Georgia responded the next year by declaring the Cherokee government abolished and its citizens subject to Georgia law. Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) failed on jurisdiction, but in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), a missionary's case, the Supreme Court held that Georgia had no power to impose its laws in the Nation.

events.title: Treaty of Medicine Creek
events.statement: On 26 December 1854 at Medicine Creek, members of the Puyallup, Nisqually, Steilacoom and Squaxin Island tribes ceded nearly all their lands to Governor Isaac Stevens, the first of his treaties, keeping three tiny reservations and access to hunting and fishing grounds, for $32,500. The treaty's marks purport to record 62 leaders, but not all signed. Dissatisfaction led to armed conflict; in 1856 Stevens agreed larger Puyallup and Nisqually reservations.

citations.quote: members of the Puyallup, Nisqually, Steilacoom, and Squaxin Island tribes enter a treaty with the United States in which they cede nearly all their lands, retaining three tiny reservations and access to traditional hunting and fishing grounds.

events.title: Treaty of Point Elliott
events.statement: On 22 January 1855 at Point Elliott, now Mukilteo, Chief Seattle joined 81 other leaders of Puget Sound tribes in signing with Governor Isaac Stevens; tribes including the Duwamish and Suquamish surrendered their lands for cash, reservations and access to fishing and hunting grounds. The treaty set up the Port Madison, Tulalip, Swinomish and Lummi reservations, but none for the Duwamish, Skagit, Snohomish or Snoqualmie. Fighting broke out in the region before ratification in 1859.

events.title: Treaty of Point No Point
events.statement: On 26 January 1855 at Hahdskus, or Point No Point, on the Kitsap Peninsula, Governor Isaac Stevens concluded a treaty with the S'Klallam, Chimakum and Skokomish, who ceded their land for small reservations along Hood Canal and $60,000. Leaders argued against his terms before being persuaded on the second day; the Skokomish leader Hool-hol-tan said he was not ready to sign. The treaty also required them to free their slaves and trade only with the United States.

events.title: 1862 Pacific Northwest smallpox epidemic (begins at Victoria)
events.statement: Smallpox reached Victoria on the steamship Brother Jonathan from San Francisco on 12 March 1862. HistoryLink says officials vaccinated as many whites as possible and very few Indians, though about 500 Songhees were vaccinated in April and 3,400 on the lower Fraser in May. Infected Indigenous camps were forced out, spreading the disease north to Alaska and south to Puget Sound. Robert Boyd estimates 14,000 deaths from April to December 1862, about half the coast's Native people.

citations.quote: It was carried from San Francisco on the steamship Brother Jonathan and arrived at Victoria, British Columbia, on March 12, 1862. White officials vaccinated as many whites as possible and very few Indians.

citations.title: Smallpox Epidemic of 1862 among Northwest Coast and Puget Sound Indians (HistoryLink, Greg Lange)
citations.quote: Vancouver Island authorities forced them to leave. The Indians returned to their homelands, causing the disease to spread north from Vancouver Island to southern Alaska, and south into the Puget Sound region.

citations.quote: During May, 3,400 Indians along the lower Fraser River were reportedly vaccinated

events.notes: Wikipedia's two-thirds of British Columbia First Nations, around 20,000, is left off: its footnote is Boyd 1999, p. 172, the chapter's first page, and a search did not find the figures there. Wikipedia gives over 70% among the Haida and 60% among the Tlingit, unattributed; omitted. Wikipedia's account of police burning the Northern Encampment on 11 May is tagged 'citation needed' and HistoryLink dates a similar removal to June and has Tsimshian torching their own dwellings, so the burning is dropped. The Haida people article says the epidemic began 26 March; both epidemic-specific sources say 12 March.

events.title: Kiks.ádi destruction of Redoubt Saint Michael (Old Sitka)

place.name: Redoubt Saint Michael / Old Sitka (Starrigavan Bay)

events.statement: In June 1802 Tlingit warriors of the Kiks.ádi clan, led by Skautlelt and Kotleian, attacked the Russian-American Company's Redoubt Saint Michael near Sitka at mid-day, aiming to drive out the colonizers. They killed many of the Russians, British deserters and Aleuts there, took the sea otter pelts and burned the settlement. A few who were away or fled reached safety; the British ship Unicorn rescued others and extracted a ransom.

events.title: The Battle of Sitka

place.name: Shís'gi Noow, Kiks.ádi fort site (Sitka National Historical Park)

events.statement: Russia's fur traders were pressing into Alaska, and in 1802 Tlingit warriors burned their post at Sitka. Alexander Baranov came back in late September 1804 with the sloop Neva, fur traders and hundreds of Aleuts. His landing party assaulted Shís'gi Noow, the Kiks.ádi sapling fort, and was driven off by gunfire. After days of bombardment, with supplies dwindling, the clan withdrew; the Kiks.ádi elder Herb Hope called it a planned survival march. The Russians fortified Sitka.

events.title: Russia sells Alaska
events.statement: After an all-night session, William Seward and Eduard de Stoeckl signed the treaty ceding Russian America in Washington at 4 a.m. on 30 March 1867, for $7.2 million, and the Senate ratified it on 9 April. Only Russia and the United States were parties. Article III excepted 'uncivilized native tribes' from citizenship, leaving them subject to whatever laws the United States adopted, though most of the territory's roughly 60,000 inhabitants lived outside Russian jurisdiction.

events.title: Alaska handed over at Sitka
events.statement: The transfer came at Fort Sitka on 18 October 1867, 6 October in the Russian calendar. Some 250 US Army troops marched to the governor's house on Castle Hill, the Russian flag came down and the American flag went up, and Captain Peshchurov handed the territory to General Lovell Rousseau. American soldiers then replaced Russian ones at the gates of the fence around the Tlingit village. American sovereignty took legal effect across the territory that day.

events.title: The Nootka Crisis
events.statement: On the far Pacific coast, Spain and Britain collided on Nuu-chah-nulth land. In July 1789 Esteban José Martínez, commander of Spain's outpost at Nootka Sound, seized the British ships Argonaut and Princess Royal and arrested James Colnett. On 13 July the Nuu-chah-nulth leader Callicum, brother of Maquinna, went to confront him and was shot dead; accounts differ over how. Outcry in Britain mobilized the Royal Navy, and three conventions followed, the last, in 1794, providing for mutual abandonment of Nootka.

citations.title: Nootka Crisis (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Later in the day the Argonaut arrived and Martínez seized the ship and arrested Colnett, his crew, and the Chinese workers Colnett had brought.

citations.title: Nootka Crisis (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: who was on board the newly captured Princess Royal . Callicum's attitude and angry calls alarmed the Spanish and somehow Callicum ended up shot dead. Sources differ over exactly how this happened.

citations.title: Nootka Crisis (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Nootka Crisis (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Nootka Convention (Wikipedia)
