events.notes: Martínez had already seized Iphigenia (May, released) and North West America (June); the title's July date fits the Argonaut and Princess Royal. The earlier version cited the Canadian Encyclopedia, which refused my scripted fetch (403), so its quotes were not re-read and were replaced. Its claim that Maquinna hosted the negotiations is tagged 'citation needed' on Wikipedia and is dropped.

events.title: Capture of the trading ship Boston in Nootka Sound
events.statement: On 22 March 1803, the day before the American ship Boston was to sail, Maquinna's Nuu-chah-nulth people came aboard at Nootka Sound to trade and dine, and at a signal attacked; all but two of the crew were killed. Maquinna spared the armourer John Jewitt and the sailmaker John Thompson as slaves, and told Jewitt the attack answered depredations by earlier American and Spanish visitors. Jewitt, freed in 1805 by the brig Lydia, published the account of it.

citations.title: John R. Jewitt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On 22 March 1803, the day before Boston intended to set sail, Nootka came aboard to trade and were given dinner. At a signal, the Nootka attacked, and all but two of the white men were killed.

citations.title: John R. Jewitt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: One other man—the Boston's sailmaker, John Thompson—was in hiding until the next day, when Jewitt pretended to be his son and begged Maquinna to spare his "father".

citations.title: Maquinna (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: told him that the ship Boston was taken in response to several depredations committed by earlier American and Spanish visitors. Jewitt was rescued in 1805 by Samuel Hill , captain of the brig Lydia .

citations.title: Nuu-chah-nulth (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He and his men killed the captain and all the crew but two, whom they kept as slaves.

citations.title: John R. Jewitt (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: his life was saved by Maquinna, who saw how useful it would be to have an armourer

events.notes: Wikipedia's Jewitt article has the Boston anchored at Woody Point in Nootka Sound, 'a few miles from any habitation', so the point at Yuquot is near rather than exact; Jewitt's Narrative was not checked. Almost all of this rests on Jewitt's own Narrative (1815), the only account, written from captivity; Wikipedia's summary is the source read.

events.title: Destruction of the trading ship Tonquin in Clayoquot Sound
events.statement: In June 1811 Captain Jonathan Thorn of the American ship Tonquin struck the Tla-o-qui-aht elder Nookamis in the face with a fur skin during a trade dispute. On 15 June warriors led by Wickaninnish returned to trade, then killed all but four of the crew. The next day the wounded clerk James Lewis allegedly detonated the magazine as they looted the ship; the blast may have killed many of them. The only account comes from the interpreter Joseachal, who survived.

citations.title: Tonquin (1807 ship) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: taking one of Nookamis' fur skins and hitting him on the face with it.

citations.title: Tonquin (1807 ship) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Violence immediately erupted as warriors led by Wickaninnish attacked the crew on board, killing all but four of the men.

citations.title: Tonquin (1807 ship) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Lewis allegedly destroyed Tonquin by lighting a fuse that detonated the ship's powder magazine when the Tla-o-qui-aht returned to loot the ship; the explosion may have killed more than 100 natives.

citations.title: Tonquin (1807 ship) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The only known survivor of the crew was Joseachal

citations.title: Tonquin (1807 ship) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: His account is the only one detailing the fate of the Tonquin

events.notes: Wikipedia only, resting on Joseachal's report as written down by Duncan McDougall at Fort Astoria. Dated to the attack of 15 June. Wikipedia has no named authority for its 'more than 100' dead, so the figure is off the card. Thorn's blow is reported by the interpreter through McDougall.

events.title: Potlatch ban enacted in the Indian Act
events.statement: An amendment to the Indian Act signed on 19 April 1884, in force from 1885, made celebrating the potlatch or the Tamanawas dance a crime punishable by two to six months' imprisonment. Missionaries and agents urged it; so did a 1883 petition from Coast Tsimshian and Nisga'a chiefs, while other First Nations saw it as an instrument of injustice. Arrests stayed few until 1921, when a raid on Dan Cranmer's potlatch sent 20 people to prison. It lasted until 1951.

citations.title: Potlatch ban (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the third section of the Indian Act , signed on April 19, 1884, it was declared that

citations.title: Potlatch ban (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: is guilty of a misdemeanor, and liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than six nor less than two months

citations.title: Potlatch ban (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some First Nations saw the law as an instrument of intolerance and injustice

citations.title: Potlatch ban (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1883 the department of Indian affairs received a petition from the Coast Tsimshian and Nisga'a Chiefs at Port Simpson, Kincolith, Green Ville

citations.title: Potlatch ban (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Arrests for charges under the Act were few until 1921, when a raid on the village of Memkumlis held by Chief Dan Cranmer saw the arrest and charges laid against 45 people

citations.title: Potlatch (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: To some extent, this was at the urging of missionaries and government agents who considered it "a worse than useless custom"

citations.title: Potlatch (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The potlatch ban was repealed in 1951.

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the ban both 1884 (Act) and 1885 (begun, in force). The earlier version's Canadian Encyclopedia citations refused my scripted fetch (403) and were replaced. 20 sent to Oakalla Prison is from the Potlatch ban article's lead.

events.title: Founding of New Metlakatla on Annette Island, Alaska
events.statement: In 1887, after William Duncan's doctrinal split with Church authorities at Metlakatla, British Columbia, he and about 800 Tsimshian followers travelled by canoe to Annette Island in Alaska and built New Metlakatla in a grid, with a church, school, cannery and sawmill. A Tsimshian search committee had chosen the site, on Tongass Tlingit territory. Duncan lobbied Congress, which created the reservation in 1891, still Alaska's only Indian reservation.

citations.title: William Duncan (missionary) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: then led approximately 800 Tsimshians in a canoe voyage from "Old" Metlakatla to "New" Metlakatla, Alaska , in 1887.

citations.title: William Duncan (missionary) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: on the territory of the Tongass tribe of Tlingit

citations.title: William Duncan (missionary) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: still Alaska's sole Indian reservation

citations.title: Metlakatla, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: had a doctrinal dispute with the Church authorities in Metlakatla, B.C. He and a devoted group of Tsimshian followers decided to leave Metlakatla.

citations.title: Metlakatla, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: after a Tsimshian search committee in seagoing canoes discovered its calm bay, accessible beaches, nearby waterfall, and abundant fish.

citations.title: Metlakatla, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: lobbied the U.S. Congress for an Indian reserve on Annette Island. Although the reservation system had not been used in Alaska, Congress granted his request in 1891.

citations.title: Metlakatla, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They laid out the town in a European-style grid pattern.

citations.title: Metlakatla, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It contained a church, a school, a cannery, and a sawmill.

events.notes: The Canadian Encyclopedia (cited earlier, about 825 Ts'msyen) refused my scripted fetch (403), so its quote was not re-read; Wikipedia's approximately 800 is used. Wikipedia's Metlakatla article says the Tlingit chief Johnson granted the Tsimshian permission to occupy the land. Duncan's sexual misconduct charges (never convicted, per Wikipedia) are left off the card.

events.title: Pacific Fur Company founds Fort Astoria at the Columbia mouth
events.statement: On 12 April 1811, 33 men of John Jacob Astor's Pacific Fur Company landed from the Tonquin at the mouth of the Columbia, eleven of them Hawaiian labourers, and by the end of May had built Fort Astoria of bark-covered logs. The lower Chinook leader Comcomly greeted them warmly and profited as their trade intermediary. With the War of 1812 the company folded; the North West Company bought it out in 1813 and renamed the post Fort George.

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: 33 men disembarked on 12 April 1811.

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Among the PFC men were eleven Kanaka laborers from the Hawaiian Kingdom

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the end of May 1811, company employees built Fort Astoria out of bark-covered logs

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The onset of the War of 1812 caused the PFC to fold

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: bought out the assets of the PFC in 1813, including Fort Astoria. They renamed it Fort George

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Comcomly 's mercantile skills as an intermediary gained him significant profits in deals with Fort Astoria.

citations.title: Comcomly (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Comcomly was regarded as the leader of the lower Chinooks, with multiple wives and many slaves as proof of his prominence. He greeted the Americans warmly

citations.title: Fort Astoria (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the primary fur trading post of John Jacob Astor 's Pacific Fur Company (PFC).

events.notes: Site was on Chinookan land, south side of the river from Comcomly's village. HistoryLink says some Astorians at first suspected him of plotting to seize the post. Astor's ownership appears on Wikipedia's Tonquin article and earlier in Fort Astoria.

events.title: Intermittent fever epidemic on the lower Columbia (c. 1829-1833)

place.name: Cape Disappointment, mouth of the Columbia River

events.statement: In the summer of 1830 an epidemic known as intermittent fever or fever and ague swept the lower Columbia. David Douglas wrote that it had depopulated the country and that villages once fielding one to two hundred warriors were totally gone. The Chinook leader Comcomly was among the dead. Presumed to be malaria, called 'cold sick', it brought what one account calls a tremendous loss of Native lives in the Willamette Valley through 1833.

citations.title: Comcomly (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: In the summer of 1830, a terrible epidemic known as "intermittent fever" or "fever and ague" swept across the lower Columbia.

citations.title: Comcomly (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: which has depopulated the country. Villages, which had afforded from one to two hundred effective warriors, are totally gone; not a soul remains

citations.title: Comcomly (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: He died in 1830, one of the many victims of an intermittent fever epidemic that swept the region.

citations.title: Comcomly (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Comcomly died in 1830 after an "intermittent fever" epidemic, also called "cold sick" and presumed to be malaria

citations.title: Comcomly (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A malaria epidemic that occurred in 1830-33 in the Willamette Valley resulted in a tremendous loss of Native American lives.

events.notes: Wikipedia also gives an estimate of 150,000 deaths from several diseases near the Willamette-Columbia confluence, 1829-1833, without naming the estimator on the page; omitted as far above what the sources I read support. Year is 1830 (Comcomly's death); the title's range is 1829-1833.

events.title: Unangan resistance to Russian fur traders on Unalaska (1763-1766)
events.statement: Between 1763 and 1766 Unangan of the Fox Islands rose against Russian fur traders, who took families hostage to force labour and fur tribute; they destroyed Russian ships and killed hunters and traders. Reprisal followed: Stepan Glotov's men destroyed the villages of southern Umnak, killing many. The National Library of Medicine's timeline has Ivan Solovief's workers killing and enslaving on Umnak, Unalaska and Kodiak, in retaliation for resistance to sexual exploitation.

citations.title: Unalaska, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Between 1763 and 1766, a conflict between the Russian fur traders and the Unalaska Natives occurred; the Aleuts destroyed four Russian ships and killed 175 hunters/traders.

citations.title: Stepan Glotov (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: pursued a policy of forcing natives to work and pay the Yasak (tax paid in furs) by taking their families hostage.

citations.title: Stepan Glotov (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Glotov and his men destroyed all the Aleut villages on the southern part of Umnak, and with the assistance of other forces the revolt was ended, with several hundred Aleuts being killed directly

citations.title: 1766: Armed Russian fur traders massacre Unangan (Aleut) (Native Voices, US National Library of Medicine)
citations.quote: arms his workers to murder Unangan (Aleut) men, women, and children in retaliation for their resistance to the sexual exploitation of Unangan women.

citations.title: 1766: Armed Russian fur traders massacre Unangan (Aleut) (Native Voices, US National Library of Medicine)
citations.quote: The workers go to Umnak, Unalaska, and Kodiak Islands, where they systematically kill people and enslave young women and men.

citations.title: Stepan Glotov (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: suppressed a revolt of the Aleut natives of the Fox Islands

events.notes: Wikipedia's 4 ships and 175 killed, and 'several hundred' Aleuts killed, name no giver; search results of low weight ran from 188 to over 375 Russians. Lydia Black's Russians in Alaska was not read. The National Library of Medicine dates its entry 1766 and also says Solovief vowed to cut the population from 25,000 to 2,500, unattributed; omitted. Glotov's article cites Veniaminov as relying on eyewitnesses.

events.title: Russian colonization of the Aleutian Islands
events.statement: By the National Park Service's account, Russians colonized the entire Aleutian chain by 1760 and reached Kodiak and Southeast Alaska by 1800. They forced many Unangax̂ to hunt sea otter for them, often violently, and families diverted to that work could not procure their own food. It estimates 15,000-18,000 Unangax̂ before contact and 2,500 by the end of Russian presence.

citations.title: Unangax History and Culture (Aleutian World War II, National Park Service)
citations.quote: colonizing the entire island chain by 1760 and expanding to Kodiak and Southeast Alaska by 1800.

citations.title: Unangax History and Culture (Aleutian World War II, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Russians forced many Unangax̂ to hunt for them, often using violence in the process. Unangax families, diverted to working for the Russians, were unable to procure subsistence foods for themselves.

citations.title: Unangax History and Culture (Aleutian World War II, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Before Russian contact, the Unangax̂ population was estimated to be 15,000-18,000; by the end of Russian presence in the Aleutian Islands, only 2,500 Unangax̂ residents remained.

events.notes: Britannica (earlier citation, first contact 1741) refused my scripted fetch (403) and was dropped, so first contact is off the card. 'By 1760' is the NPS wording; the raiding and colonising continued well after, as the Unalaska card shows. Wikipedia's Aleuts article has about 25,000 reduced to under a tenth, with no giver; left off.

events.title: Awa'uq (Refuge Rock) massacre of Koniag Alutiiq
events.statement: In 1784 Grigory Shelikhov sent boats with small cannon and 130 armed men against Koniag Alutiiq sheltering at Refuge Rock (Awa'uq), off Sitkalidak Island; he insisted he was outnumbered and attacked first. The ship's physician Miron Britiukov, denouncing him to the czar, estimated 500 killed and more drowned; other accounts say 200 to 300. The anthropologist Lydia Black says neither extreme is entirely accurate. Hostage-taking followed, and the Alutiiq were forced to hunt sea otters for the traders.

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre (Seattle Times, 1992)
citations.quote: Shelikhov sent several boats with 2 1/2-pound cannons and 130 armed men to Refuge Rock.

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre (Seattle Times, 1992)
citations.quote: He insisted in his reports that he had been badly outnumbered and was attacked first. Ship physician and eyewitness Miron Britiukov, in a scathing account to the czar, cited numerous atrocities and denounced Shelikhov's action.

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre (Seattle Times, 1992)
citations.quote: Britiukov estimated 500 were killed and more drowned, including those who threw themselves off the seaside cliffs 10 stories high to escape the onslaught.

citations.title: Archaeologist may have found site of Alaska massacre (Seattle Times, 1992)
citations.quote: Other accounts put the death toll at 200 to 300 villagers. Lydia Black, a Russian-born anthropologist at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, says her studies indicate neither extreme view is entirely accurate.

citations.title: Refuge Rock, Partition Cove (CoastView)
citations.quote: the Russian traders enslaved men to hunt sea otters year-round, while women and children were held hostage.

events.notes: Month conflict: Wikipedia August 1784 (infobox 14 August); CoastView April 1784; the Seattle Times says 'that August afternoon'; the date field keeps the year. Other tolls: CoastView at least 300, Wikipedia 200-500 and 'some sources' up to 2,000-3,000 with no authority named on the page. Shelikhov claimed over 1,000 captured and 400 held hostage.

events.title: Thule (early Inuit) migration from Alaska across the Canadian Arctic to Greenland
events.statement: Thule people, ancestors of the Inuit, developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and spread east across northern Canada, reaching Greenland by the 13th century. By the 15th century they had replaced the Dorset in the eastern Arctic; one genetic reading finds virtually no interaction between them, while Inuit legend recalls earlier people called the Tuniit. Their name comes from Thule in northwest Greenland, where remains were first found at Comer's Midden.

citations.title: Thule people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE and expanded eastward across northern Canada , reaching Greenland by the 13th century.

citations.title: Thule people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the 13th or 14th century, the Thule had occupied an area inhabited until then by the Dorset, and by the 15th century, the Thule had replaced the Dorset.

citations.title: Thule people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: in northwest Greenland, facing Canada, where the archaeological remains of the people were first found at Comer's Midden

citations.title: Dorset culture (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some modern genetic studies show the Dorset population were distinct from later groups and that "there was virtually no evidence of genetic or cultural interaction between the Dorset and the Thule peoples."

citations.title: Dorset culture (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Inuit legends recount them encountering people they called the Tuniit

events.notes: The point is the old Thule site, now Pituffik, where Comer's Midden is; Qaanaaq is the settlement relocated in 1953. The migration has no single place. Dates vary by study; the Canadian Encyclopedia's ca. 1200 CE (earlier citation) refused my scripted fetch (403) and is not re-read; Wikipedia's Dorset article has the Thule moving east from the 11th century.

events.title: Martin Frobisher meets Inuit in Frobisher Bay and takes a man captive
events.statement: In August 1576 Martin Frobisher's ship reached the bay that bears his name on Baffin Island, where Inuit came to trade meat and furs. One agreed to pilot the ship; the five seamen who rowed him ashore landed out of sight, against orders, and were never seen again. Frobisher then seized a man who came to trade by kayak and took him to England. Inuit oral tradition holds that the five lived among them for some years.

citations.title: Frobisher, Sir Martin (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: In late August, natives came to the ship to trade meat and furs for trinkets and clothing. One native agreed, by signs, to pilot the ship

citations.title: Frobisher, Sir Martin (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: Contrary to Frobisher's orders, the five men who rowed the native ashore landed out of sight of the ship.

citations.title: Frobisher, Sir Martin (Dictionary of Canadian Biography)
citations.quote: he captured a native who had come to the ship in his kayak to trade and took him to England.

citations.title: Martin Frobisher (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Inuit oral tradition tells that the men lived among them for a few years of their own free will until they died attempting to leave Baffin Island in a self-made boat.

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the first meeting to 18 August 1576 and says the five were 'taken captive'; the Dictionary of Canadian Biography says 'late August' and only that none was seen again, so the card uses the latter. Month precision used.

events.title: Hans Egede founds Hope Colony (Haabets Koloni) in Greenland
events.statement: On 3 July 1721 the Norwegian priest Hans Egede, his wife, four children and forty other colonists reached Nuup Kangerlua and established Hope Colony with a portable house on Kangeq Island. Searching for descendants of the old Norse colonists, he found only Kalaallit, and began studying their language. Scurvy drove most colonists home after the first winter, but the mission revived Danish-Norwegian interest after about 300 years, and a smallpox epidemic later reached the Inuit from a ship.

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: bearing Egede, his wife and four children, and forty other colonists.

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On 3 July they reached Nuup Kangerlua and established Hope Colony

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: with the erection of a portable house on Kangeq Island

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the end of the first winter, many of the colonists had been stricken with scurvy and most returned

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: credited with revitalizing Danish-Norwegian interest in the island after contact had been broken for about 300 years.

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The ship also returned one of Egede's convert children with a case of smallpox .

citations.title: Hans Egede (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: By the next year, the epidemic was raging among the Inuit

events.notes: Wikipedia only. Wikipedia's Greenlandic Inuit article says in 1814 the Treaty of Kiel confirmed Greenland as a territory of Denmark. Egede's mission also founded what became Nuuk. The quote 'On 3 July they reached' has a footnote marker after 'July' on the page.

events.title: Dena'ina attack on Fort St. Nicholas ('battle of Kenai')
events.statement: In 1797 Dena'ina attacked the Lebedev-Lastochkin Company's fort of St. Nicholas at Kenai, in what was later called the Battle of Kenai; the same year Tyonek Dena'ina under Quq'ey destroyed the Russian post at North Foreland, and the Iliamna post fell too. By the anthropologist Alan Boraas's account, anger at economic exploitation and sexual slavery drove them, and they killed the roughly 100 Russians in the fort; another count has over one hundred dead on all sides.

citations.title: Kenai, Alaska (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: culminating in an incident in which the Dena'ina attacked Fort St. Nicholas, later dubbed the battle of Kenai. Over one hundred deaths occurred from all involved parties.

citations.title: A Dena'ina Chronology (Anchorage Museum)
citations.quote: Tyonek Dena'ina under Quq'ey destroy Russian post at North Foreland; Russian post at Iliamna also destroyed; Dena'ina attack Russian fort in the Battle of Kenai

citations.title: Kenai Peninsula historical conference sheds light on Russian-Native history (Peninsula Clarion)
citations.quote: Dena'ina angered by the economic exploitation and sexual slavery that Russians practiced upon Alaska Native women, killed the roughly 100 Russians living in the fort.

citations.title: Kenai Peninsula historical conference sheds light on Russian-Native history (Peninsula Clarion)
citations.quote: the Russian mercantile militiamen of the fur-trading Lebedev-Lastochkin Company erected the palisades of St. Nicolas Redoubt

events.notes: Boraas's view is known through a newspaper report of his conference talk, which also credits the attack with deterring Baranov from making Kenai the mainland capital. The fort's founding differs: 1786 in Wikipedia's Kenai article, 1791 in the Clarion and Wikipedia's Russian America list. No Russian account was read. The Clarion quote may overstate: 'the roughly 100 Russians' sits against Wikipedia's all-sides count, so both are given.

events.title: Ahtna kill the Serebrennikov party at Batzulnetas
events.statement: In 1847-48 the Russian-American Company sent Ruf Serebrennikov to traverse from the mouth of the Copper River to the Yukon. By the National Park Service's account the Ahtna killed him and his entire party near the village of Batzulnetas in the summer of 1848, and the Russians appear to have made no further efforts to explore the region. Earlier Russian advances had been pushed back by the Ahtna, and a post of 1819 was destroyed.

citations.title: Human History (Wrangell-St. Elias, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Assigned the task of traversing from the mouth of the Copper to the Yukon River, Ruf Serebrennikov and his entire party was killed by the Ahtna near the village of Batzulnetas in the summer of 1848.

citations.title: Human History (Wrangell-St. Elias, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Russians appear to have made no further efforts to explore the region.

citations.title: Human History (Wrangell-St. Elias, National Park Service)
citations.quote: In 1847-48, the Russian American company tried to examine the rest of the Copper Basin.

citations.title: Ahtna (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Russians would try to go up the river only to be pushed back by the Ahtna. In 1819 the Russians built a post at the confluence of the Copper and Chitina Rivers , which was destroyed.

events.notes: No source read gives the cause or an Ahtna account of the killing. Year precision kept; the page says summer 1848. Wikipedia does not say who destroyed the 1819 post, and neither does the card.

events.title: Lewis and Clark meet the Nez Perce at Weippe Prairie
events.statement: In mid-September 1805, crossing the Bitterroots, William Clark went ahead with a few hunters for food and came out on Weippe Prairie, where the Nez Perce gathered in summer for roots, berries and game. They met three frightened boys hiding in the grass and gave them small presents. The Nez Perce, nervous of these strangers, accepted them, and after the expedition reunited on 22 September its leaders traded gifts and passed the pipe with the head man Twisted Hair.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Unprepared for the arduous trek over the Bitterroot Mountains, Captain Clark and a small group of hunters went ahead of the main party in search of food.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: they encountered three frightened Nez Perce boys hiding in the grass. Clark gave them small presents

citations.title: Weippe Prairie (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Nez Perce people were nervous over the intentions of these strangers but accepted them onto their land.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: After Lewis and Clark reunited on September 22, 1805, they spoke with a Nez Perce head man known as Twisted Hair: trading gifts, passing the pipe, and acquiring information about the country.

citations.title: Weippe Prairie (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Historically, in the summer months the Nez Perce would come to the prairies to harvest roots and berries and to hunt.

events.notes: A first contact; no treaty was made here. Single source (NPS), which draws on the expedition journals; no Nimíipuu oral account was read. The NPS page says 'the Nez Perce'; the catalogue's participant is nimiipuu.

events.title: Nez Perce Treaty of 1855 (Walla Walla Council)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: At the Walla Walla Council of 29 May to 11 June 1855, Governor Isaac Stevens met the Nez Perce, Yakama, Umatilla, Cayuse and Walla Walla. After more than a week of tense talks the Nez Perce treaty was made, dated 11 June. By the Tribe's account its leaders kept about 7.5 million acres as an exclusive reservation, with the right to hunt and fish in their usual and accustomed places. The Senate ratified in 1859.

citations.title: Walla Walla Council (1855) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: between the United States and sovereign tribal nations of the Cayuse , Nez Perce , Umatilla , Walla Walla , and Yakama .

citations.title: Walla Walla Council (1855) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: council occurred on May 29 – June 11

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1863 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: supplementary and amendatory to the treaty made between the United States and said tribe on the 11th day of June, 1855

citations.title: The Treaty Period (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Treaty of 1855 was ratified by the US Senate in 1859.

citations.title: History (Nez Perce Tribe)
citations.quote: Tribal leaders negotiated retention of approximately 7.5 million acres to be protected as the Tribe's exclusive reservation.

citations.title: The Treaty Era (Nez Perce National Historical Park, NPS)
citations.quote: After more than a week of tense negotiations

citations.title: The Treaty Era (Nez Perce National Historical Park, NPS)
citations.quote: while still retaining the right to hunt and fish in their "usual and accustomed places"

events.notes: Wikipedia's council article says the treaties were signed on 9 June, but the 1863 treaty's own text dates the Nez Perce treaty 11 June, matching the date field. NPS says the nimíipuu 'agreed to cede 7.5 million acres'; that looks an error for the land kept, since NPS itself has the 1855 reservation cut by 90% and the Tribe has 750,000 acres after 1863.

events.title: Nez Perce Treaty of 1863 ("Thief Treaty")
events.statement: After gold was found on the reservation in 1860, the US called a second council rather than stop the trespass, and at Lapwai on 9 June 1863 cut the reservation by 90 percent, to about 750,000 acres by the Tribe's count. Bands outside the new lines walked out and refused to endorse it, but 51 headmen from inside made their marks. The Senate ratified it in 1867. Nimíipuu called it the Thief Treaty; it set up the war of 1877.

citations.title: The Treaty Period (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: In 1860, gold was discovered within the boundaries of the reservation. Rather than stop the newcomers from trespassing on reservation land, the U.S. government instead initiated another treaty council that would shrink the 1855 reservation by 90%

citations.title: The Treaty Period (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The bands that lived outside of the proposed reservation boundaries walked out of the proceedings and refused to endorse this land grab. Nevertheless, 51 headmen who lived within the proposed reservation boundaries affixed their marks to the new treaty.

citations.title: The Treaty Period (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The 1863 Treaty became known amongst nimíipuu as the 'Thief Treaty' or 'Steal Treaty' and created the conditions that would eventually lead to the armed clash

citations.title: History (Nez Perce Tribe)
citations.quote: the federal government forced the Tribe into a second treaty in 1863, which reduced the reservation to about 750,000 acres.

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1863 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: at the council-ground, in the valley of the Lapwai, W. T., on the ninth day of June, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three

events.notes: Wikipedia's Chief Joseph article gives 760,000 acres and says Chief Lawyer and allied chiefs signed. The Senate ratified in 1867 per NPS.

events.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (opening battle of the Nez Perce War)
events.statement: On 17 June 1877, days after young warriors' revenge raids killed settlers on the Salmon River, Captain David Perry's cavalry entered White Bird Canyon. A Nez Perce party came out under a white flag, but the volunteer Ad Chapman, for reasons not fully explained, opened fire. Warriors under Ollokot and White Bird then routed Perry's command, at a cost of 34 US dead and 3 Nez Perce wounded by the National Park Service's count, opening the Nez Perce War.

citations.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: entered the Salmon River area to seek revenge for the 1875 murder of Wahlitits' father

citations.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: At least 18 settlers were killed by the Nez Perce.

citations.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Six Nez Perce warriors waited with a white flag to discuss a truce with the approaching soldiers.

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: for reasons that cannot fully be explained, opened fire on the peace party. The nimíipuu responded and bullets began to fly.

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The die was cast and the first battle of the Nez Perce War began.

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Chapman, a volunteer came up to Theller's position or close by

citations.title: White Bird Battlefield (NPS)
citations.quote: he left behind thirty-four dead. An additional two soldiers and two volunteers were wounded. Three nimíipuu suffered wounds, but no one was killed.

citations.title: Battle of White Bird Canyon (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Ollokot and White Bird led roughly equal numbers of warriors.

events.notes: Wikipedia gives about 70 warriors, 106 soldiers and 11 volunteers, leaving out 13 Nez Perce scouts; no giver named, so left off. Wikipedia's six warriors under the flag differ from Yellow Wolf's five, as quoted there. It also says many warriors were too drunk to fight that morning, from whiskey taken in the raids; left off as its authority wasn't traced. The NPS names the shooter as Chapman in the sentence the quote continues.

events.title: The Bear Paw and the surrender of Chief Joseph
events.statement: War in Idaho sent about 800 Nez Perce fleeing the US Army in summer 1877. From 30 September Colonel Nelson Miles besieged them forty miles short of Canada, and cannon fire targeted the families' shelters. On 5 October, told they would return to Idaho, Joseph surrendered; the words recorded as his, in translation, end 'I will fight no more forever'. The promise was overruled, and those who surrendered or were captured, over 400, were sent to Kansas and Indian Territory.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: approximately 800 nimíipuu (Nez Perce) spent a long and arduous summer fleeing U.S. Army troops

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: a mere forty miles short of the Canadian border. Following a five-day battle and siege, the nimíipuu ceased fighting at Bear Paw on October 5th, 1877

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: remembered October 2 as the day Chief Looking Glass was killed.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The fighting continued. The army targeted the area where the families were sheltered with cannon fire.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Joseph and Whitebird were told that they would be returned to Idaho, the leaders will not be killed, and, most importantly, that the army wanted to quit fighting. White Bird mistrusted the army's promises and refused to surrender.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: At 2pm Joseph met with Miles and Howard, handed over his rifle, and made his now famous speech

citations.title: Battle of Bear Paw (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: White Bird and about 50 followers, however, slipped through the army lines and continued on to Canada

citations.title: Battle of Bear Paw (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The total number of Nez Perce who surrendered or were captured was 431, including 79 men, 178 women, and 174 children.

citations.title: Battle of Bear Paw (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever.

citations.title: Battle of Bear Paw (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: an oral message from Joseph which was translated as follows

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)

events.notes: Counts differ: 431 (Wikipedia's battle article, footnoted to Mark H. Brown's The Flight of the Nez Perce (1967), p. 410, known only through that footnote, not read directly), 418 (Wikipedia's war article), over 400 (NPS). NPS says 30 to 50 left with White Bird, Wikipedia about 50, and 200 to 300 reached Canada in all. Wikipedia says 42 miles from the border. The speech's text is as the NPS gives it; Lt. Wood also left an account of the surrender. Moved from the card: Looking Glass's death on 2 October, White Bird's escape, and the place name C'aynnim Alikinwaaspa. The speech's setting differs: the NPS has it at the surrender to Miles and Howard, Wikipedia as an oral message carried by two Nez Perce men, translated by Ad Chapman, so the card says only 'recorded as his, in translation'.

events.title: Captured Nez Perce sent to Fort Leavenworth and Indian Territory
events.statement: Though Joseph and White Bird were told at Bear Paw they would return to Idaho, the prisoners were marched 265 miles to the Tongue River, sent on to Fort Buford, and in November carried by train to Fort Leavenworth, where they lived in swampy bottomland over its commander's protests. Next came Indian Territory, near Tonkawa. Joseph pleaded in Washington in 1879; only in 1885 did he and 268 survivors return to the Northwest, he to Colville.

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Miles marched his captives 265 miles (426 km) to the Tongue River Cantonment in southeast Montana Territory

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 23, the Nez Perce prisoners had their lodges and equipment loaded into freight cars and themselves into eleven rail coaches for the trip via train to Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Over the protests to Sherman by the commander of the Fort, the Nez Perce were forced to live in a swampy bottomland.

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Joseph and the Nez Perce were sent to Oklahoma and eventually located on a small reservation near Tonkawa, Oklahoma .

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1885, Joseph and 268 surviving Nez Perce were finally allowed to return to the Pacific Northwest.

citations.title: Bear Paw Battlefield (Nez Perce National Historical Park, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Joseph and Whitebird were told that they would be returned to Idaho

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The able-bodied warriors were marched out to Fort Buford

citations.title: Nez Perce War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Conditions in "the hot country" were hardly better than they had been at Leavenworth.

citations.quote: Chief Joseph went to Washington in January 1879 to plead that his people be allowed to return to Idaho

events.title: Yakama Treaty of 1855 (Treaty of Yakama)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: On 9 June 1855 at Walla Walla, the Yakama, Umatilla, Cayuse and Walla Walla treating with Governor Stevens were forced, says HistoryLink, to cede over 6 million acres, partly as punishment for the Whitman killings; the Yakama Nation counts over 12 million. Fishing, hunting and gathering rights stayed reserved. Kamiakin refused, then signed under duress, for $200,000 over years. Stevens promised no trespass before ratification, but a month later, the Nation says, opened the lands. The Senate ratified in 1859.

citations.title: Yakama Nation History & Treaties (Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation)
citations.quote: Lands ceded to the federal government during the 1855 Treaty signing included over 12 million acres of land.

citations.title: Yakama Nation History & Treaties (Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation)
citations.quote: Tribal leaders reserved the right to fish, hunt and gather all of the tribe's traditional foods on the reservation as well as the ceded area.

citations.title: Yakama Nation History & Treaties (Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation)
citations.quote: Although the Treaty was signed on June 9, 1855 it did not become valid until ratified March 8, 1859

citations.title: Yakama Nation History & Treaties (Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakama Nation)
citations.quote: just one month after the treaty was signed Governor Stevens through northwest newspapers declared all ceded lands open and available for white settlement.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: The tribes were paid $200,000 over a number of years in exchange for their land. Kamiakin first refused to sign the treaty, but later did so under duress.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: assured the Native people that white miners and colonizers would not be allowed to trespass on tribal lands during the time before the treaty could be ratified

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: were forced to cede in excess of 6 million acres to the United States government, partly as punishment for the killing by a group of young Cayuse of Methodist missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman

events.notes: The reservation is given as 1,130,000 acres on the Yakama Nation's page, in a passage from another author. 'Allied bands' reflects the participants field and the Yakama Nation's 'tribes and bands'. HistoryLink lumps the Yakama, Umatilla, Cayuse and Walla Walla tribes in its 6 million acres. The Nation's page also carries 'a mere twelve days' from another author; its own text says one month.

events.title: Yakama War begins (fight at Toppenish Creek)
events.statement: On 5 October 1855, by HistoryLink's count, gunfire broke out across the ford at Toppenish Creek between Kamiakin's 300 warriors and Major Granville Haller's 84 soldiers, who had marched after the Indian sub-agent Andrew Bolon was killed investigating attacks on miners. Yakama elder Alex Saluskin's account has miners raping and murdering a woman, her daughter and the daughter's baby, and warriors retaliating. HistoryLink counts two Yakama and five soldiers dead. Haller retreated by night; the war lasted to 1858.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: gunfire erupts between Yakama Chief Kamiakin's 300 warriors and Major Granville O. Haller's 84-man troop of soldiers. The two groups have been at a standoff across the ford at Toppenish Creek.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: told by Yakama tribal elder Alex Saluskin, miners raped and murdered a Yakama woman, her teenage daughter, and the daughter's baby in the Wenas Valley

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Andrew J. Bolon, the Indian sub-agent at The Dalles, was shot and killed while investigating these incidents. It was for this reason that Major Haller and his troops set out

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Kamiakin had two dead, four wounded, one captured. Haller had five dead, 17 wounded.

citations.title: Yakama War begins on October 5, 1855 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: they slipped away under cover of night and retreated toward The Dalles.

citations.title: Yakima War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Yakima War (1855–1858)

events.notes: HistoryLink prints the date of the Wenas Valley killing as 'September 1955', evidently 1855. Wikipedia's account differs in detail: Qualchan killing the prospectors after a rape, and Bolon intercepted on 20 September. Saluskin's account dates from 1967.

events.title: Killing of Marcus and Narcissa Whitman at Waiilatpu
events.statement: On 29 November 1847, during a measles outbreak that killed hundreds of Cayuse while leaving settlers comparatively unscathed, a small group of Cayuse men killed the missionaries Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and eleven others at Waiilatpu. They suspected Whitman, a physician, of poisoning those in his care; five later pleaded tribal law on killing a medicine man who gives bad medicine. More than forty-five whites were held captive, and Oregon raised a militia, beginning the Cayuse War.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and eleven others at Waiiletpu, the Whitmans' mission near present-day Walla Walla, Washington, on November 29, 1847.

citations.title: Whitman massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They were killed by a small group of Cayuse men who suspected that Whitman had poisoned the 200 Cayuse in his medical care during an outbreak of measles

citations.title: Whitman massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Cayuse in at least three villages held Whitman responsible for the widespread epidemic that killed hundreds of Cayuse while leaving settlers comparatively unscathed.

citations.title: Whitman massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: they used the defense that it was tribal law to kill the medicine man who gives bad medicine.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: authorize the creation of a volunteer militia force of five hundred men to apprehend the Whitmans' killers and rescue the more than forty-five white captives

events.notes: Also called the Whitman massacre, the Whitman killings and the Tragedy at Waiilatpu; the Oregon Encyclopedia spells the place Waiiletpu. Wikipedia adds earlier disputes over land and pay between Tiloukaikt and Whitman. No Cayuse account of the day itself was read.

events.title: Cayuse War ends with the hanging of five Cayuse men

place.name: Oregon City, Oregon (site of trial and hanging)

events.statement: Oregon's volunteer militia ran out of money by late summer 1848 without taking the men it wanted; its pursuit that March fought only Palouse with no connection to the Whitman killings. Governor Joseph Lane then persuaded friendly Cayuse to offer five for trial: Chief Teloukaikt, Tomahas, Clokamas, Isaiachalakis and Kiamasumkin. After a brief trial at Oregon City all five were publicly hanged on 3 June 1850. The war, says the Oregon Encyclopedia, ended as it began, with violence.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the militia's only fight was with Palouse who had no connection to the Whitman killings.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The militia's military campaign ended in late summer 1848.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: he persuaded friendly Cayuse to offer five individuals for trial. By April 1850, Oregon officials had Chief Teloukaikt, Tomahas, Clokamas, Isaiachalakis, and Kiamasumkin in custody.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: After conferring for just over an hour, the jury brought in a verdict of guilty for the five Cayuse, and the judge sentenced all to a public hanging on June 3, 1850.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The Cayuse War ended as it had begun, with violence.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: the Provisional Government ran out of appropriations and loans to sustain the volunteers in the field.

citations.title: Cayuse Indian War (Oregon Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: The brief trial was held in late May in Oregon City

events.notes: Wikipedia dates the Cayuse War 1847-1855. The page title of the Oregon Encyclopedia uses 1847-1855 in its URL while the narrative ends in 1850. The same page has the column slowed earlier by two brief fights with Cayuse. It quotes the New York Tribune doubting the policy of the hanging. The source does not say the five were the actual killers; it says they were offered.

events.title: Treaty with the Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla (1855)

place.name: Walla Walla Valley (Camp Stevens treaty ground), Washington

events.statement: On 9 June 1855 at the Walla Walla Council, Isaac Stevens and Joel Palmer concluded a treaty with the confederated Walla Walla, Cayuse and Umatilla. By the Tribes' own account they ceded 6.4 million acres for a reservation homeland of 250,000 acres, and reserved perpetual off-reservation rights to fish at usual and accustomed sites, to hunt, gather medicines and pasture livestock. Federal legislation in the late 1800s reduced the reservation to its present 172,000 acres.

citations.title: History & Culture (Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation)
citations.quote: In 1855, the Cayuse, Umatilla and Walla Walla tribes and the U.S. Government negotiated a treaty in which 6.4 million acres were ceded in exchange for a reservation homeland of 250,000 acres.

citations.title: History & Culture (Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation)
citations.quote: also reserved perpetual off-reservation rights to fish at usual and accustomed sites and to hunt, gather medicines such as roots and berries, and pasture livestock on unclaimed lands.

citations.title: History & Culture (Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation)
citations.quote: As a result of federal legislation in the late 1800s that reduced its size, the Umatilla Reservation is now 172,000 acres

citations.title: Treaty of June 9, 1855 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: by and between Isaac I. Stevens, governor and superintendent of Indian affairs for the Territory of Washington

citations.title: Walla Walla Council (1855) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the treaties signed at this council on June 9

citations.title: Walla Walla Council (1855) (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: were ratified by the U.S. Senate four years later, in 1859

events.notes: Palmer appears in the treaty text as 'Superintendent Palmer', for those residing in Oregon. Treaty text also secures the exclusive right of taking fish in reservation streams.

events.title: Hellgate Treaty

place.name: Council Grove State Park (Hell Gate treaty ground), Montana

events.statement: On 16 July 1855 at Hell Gate, Governor Isaac Stevens obtained a treaty from the Salish, Pend d'Oreille and Kootenai, who had come expecting to talk of intertribal peace. When Stevens called chief Victor 'an old woman' and 'dumb as a dog', Victor walked out; a compromise, Article 11, promised a survey of the Bitterroot Valley. Believing that protected his people, Victor signed. The Jesuit Adrian Hoecken said not a tenth of what was said was understood by either side.

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty was signed at Hellgate on 16 July 1855.

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They were pleased at Stevens's invitation to the treaty council and expected to talk about intertribal peace.

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: When Stevens lashed out, calling Victor "an old woman" and "dumb as a dog," Victor walked out of the council.

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: He inserted Article 11 into the treaty, providing for a survey of the Bitterroot Valley.

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: said the translations were so poor that "not a tenth of what was said was understood by either side

citations.title: Treaty of July 16, 1855 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: under the name of the Flathead Nation, with Victor, the head chief of the Flathead tribe, as the head chief of the said nation

citations.title: Treaty of Hellgate (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: between the United States and the Bitterroot Salish , Upper Pend d'Oreille , and Lower Kutenai tribes.
