Point moved from Hellgate Canyon, about 38 km to the east-southeast, to Council Grove, where the page has the council and its monument.

events.title: Removal of the Bitterroot Salish to the Flathead Reservation
events.statement: After drought in 1889 left the Bitterroot Salish short of food, Chief Charlo signed retired general Henry Carrington's removal agreement that November. Earlier, officials had forged his mark on the 1872 Garfield agreement. On 15 October 1891 the remaining people left the valley; Charlo insisted on no military escort, though Salish oral histories and newspaper accounts say troops were present. Elders remembered the three-day, sixty-mile journey to the Flathead Reservation as a funeral march.

citations.title: Bitterroot Salish (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They had some success with agriculture until an unprecedented drought in 1889.

citations.title: Bitterroot Salish (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Finally, Charlo signed Carrington's agreement on November 3, 1889.

citations.title: Bitterroot Salish (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: When Chief Charlo refused to sign, U.S officials forged Charlo's "x" onto the official copy of the agreement that was sent to the Senate for Ratification.

citations.title: Bitterroot Salish (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: They left the valley on October 15, 1891. Charlo organized the march himself and insisted that it take place without a white military escort. However, Salish oral histories and newspaper accounts indicate that troops were present during the removal.

citations.title: Bitterroot Salish (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Elders later remembered the three-day, sixty-mile journey as a funeral march.

citations.title: Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes of the Flathead Nation (New World Encyclopedia)
citations.quote: In October 1891, Chief Charlot and the remaining tribal members left the Bitterroot and marched sixty miles to the Flathead Reservation.

events.notes: Wikipedia's lead says they were 'forcibly moved', while its body has the agreement and the march Charlo organized; the card gives the sequence. Some historians call it Montana's or the Salish Trail of Tears (Wikipedia). Charlot/Charlo spellings both occur.

events.title: Battle of Tohotonimme (Pine Creek; Steptoe Disaster)

place.name: Pine Creek (Tohotonimme) battlefield near Rosalia, Washington

events.statement: On 17 May 1858 a column under Lieutenant Colonel Edward Steptoe, each soldier issued about 40 rounds, was attacked near present-day Rosalia, after entering Spokane land against Governor Stevens's promise to respect it while the tribe stayed peaceful. Schitsu'umsh, joined by Palouse and Spokane, fought it all day; by the Tribe's account Steptoe's men were down to their last rounds before they slipped away under cover of dark. It brought Wright's punitive campaign.

citations.title: History (Coeur d'Alene Tribe)
citations.quote: Known as the Battle of Tohotonimme by Tribes, the Battle of Steptoe was a conflict between several Tribes and the United States Army under Colonel Edward Steptoe.

citations.title: History (Coeur d'Alene Tribe)
citations.quote: The battle lasted all day, and brought the Colonel's men to within their last few rounds of ammunition, before they were able to slip away under cover of dark.

citations.title: Battle of Pine Creek (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Leaving the fort, Steptoe's command of 159 soldiers were each issued about 40 rounds of ammunition.

citations.title: Battle of Pine Creek (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It was at this time a group of Coeur d'Alenes, joined by some Palouses, attacked.

citations.title: Battle of Pine Creek (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It took place on May 17, 1858, near what is present-day Rosalia, Washington .

citations.title: Columbia Plateau Indian War 1858 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Seeking retribution, the army responded with a brutal punitive strike.

citations.title: Battle of Pine Creek (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: contrary to the promise of Governor Isaac Stevens that whites would respect Spokane land as long as the tribe agreed to remain peaceful.

events.notes: Wikipedia also has a figure of 164 riflemen in its infobox against 159 in the text; warrior estimates (800-1,000) and losses are unattributed there and omitted. HistoryLink and NPS give fighting on 17-18 May. Wikipedia's infobox adds Yakama, Cayuse and Kamiakin, outside the participants field; not used. The Tribe's page calls Steptoe Colonel; Wikipedia a brevet lieutenant colonel.

events.title: Battle of Four Lakes
events.statement: On 1 September 1858, by HistoryLink's count, more than 700 troops under Colonel George Wright overwhelmed somewhat fewer than 500 Yakama, Palouse, Spokane and Schitsu'umsh at Four Lakes, the first battle of the punitive campaign after Steptoe's defeat. The warriors meant to lure the cavalry onto the plains, but Wright's rebored rifles had a range of 1,000 yards. Four days later he won again at Spokane Plains.

citations.title: Columbia Plateau Indian War 1858 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: On September 1 more than 700 troops led by Colonel George Wright overwhelmed somewhat fewer than 500 Indians at Four Lakes , finally defeating them four days later at Spokane Plains .

citations.title: Battle of Four Lakes (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: planned to lure Wright's cavalry over the ridge and onto the plains beyond

citations.title: Battle of Four Lakes (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Wright's troops were armed with rebored 1841 Harpers Ferry Rifles.

citations.title: Battle of Four Lakes (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: These had a range of 1,000 yards

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 1, 1858, Wright's troops defeated the allied tribes at the Battle of Four Lakes

events.notes: Strength differs: Wikipedia's war article says 601 men, its battle article about 700 including 200 civilian drovers. Its infobox gives no US losses and 17-20 Native dead, unattributed; omitted, as is its uncited claim of five times the range. HistoryLink 5144 calls Four Lakes a skirmish. Kamiakin and Qualchan led, per Wikipedia.

events.title: Battle of Spokane Plains
events.statement: On 5 September 1858 Colonel George Wright's column met warriors on the Spokane Plains, who set the prairie grass alight to stampede the pack train and hide their attack. Wright countered with infantry, cavalry and artillery together; the fighting ran over 14 miles and one soldier was wounded, by HistoryLink's account. It calls the battle a defeat for the warriors; Wikipedia's Coeur d'Alene War article says there was no decisive winner, though the tribes were greatly weakened.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains occurs on September 5, 1858 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: U.S. Army soldiers under Colonel George Wright (1803-1865) defeat Native Americans at the Battle of Spokane Plains.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains occurs on September 5, 1858 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: The soldiers and the warriors fight over a distance of 14 miles and one soldier is wounded.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains occurs on September 5, 1858 (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: The warriors set fire to prairie grass to stampede the pack train and to conceal their attack. Wright ordered a counterattack with combined arms -- infantry, cavalry, and artillery working in concert

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: where they set fire to the grass and shot at the troops through the smoke; while there was no decisive winner, the tribes were greatly weakened.

events.notes: Wikipedia's battle article gives 6 Native dead and 1 US wounded in its infobox, with 500-700 warriors; unattributed, omitted except for the wounded soldier that HistoryLink also gives.

events.title: Wright slaughters Palouse horses at Liberty Lake
events.statement: On 8 September 1858, by HistoryLink's account, Colonel George Wright ordered about 800 horses, the herd of a Palouse chief, slaughtered at Liberty Lake to deny them to enemy tribes; soldiers also destroyed lodges and grain stores. Wikipedia's Battle of Spokane Plains article dates it to 9-10 September, at 600 to 900 of nearly 1,000. Horses were the tribes' wealth and power. Wright regretted it, he wrote, but called the chastisement severe but well merited.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright slaughters 800 Palouse horses (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: orders his troops to slaughter 800 Native American horses (the herd of a Palouse chief) at Liberty Lake to deny their use by enemy tribes. Soldiers also destroy Native American lodges and storehouses of grain.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright slaughters 800 Palouse horses (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Horses represent both the wealth and military power of the tribes.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: between 9 and 10 September 1858, soldiers commanded by Col. George Wright captured a herd of nearly 1,000 Indian horses

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Numbers of horses killed vary between 600 and 900 animals.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: I deeply regretted killing these poor creatures, but a dire necessity drove me to it...The chastisement which these Indians have received has been severe but well merited

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: that were being guarded by tribal elders and children attempting to drive them to safety.

events.notes: Wikipedia's Coeur d'Alene War article says over 800. Date field 8 September follows HistoryLink; Wikipedia's 9-10 September is on the card.

events.title: Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (Hangman Creek)
events.statement: From 25 September 1858, at his camp on the Ned-Whauld River, Colonel George Wright hanged Yakama and Palouse prisoners he suspected of killing whites. He told Qualchan he would hang his father Owhi unless he surrendered; Qualchan came under a white flag and was hanged within 15 minutes, though HistoryLink says he had no part in Bolon's death, the charge officers used. Six Palouse followed, and the creek became Hangman's Creek. Wikipedia's Coeur d'Alene War article has seventeen hanged there.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Colonel George Wright (1803-1865), U.S. Army, hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners he suspects of killing whites.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: he sent word to Qualchan that if he did not surrender, Wright would hang his father.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Yakama warrior Qualchan is hanged 15 minutes after he surrenders to Wright carrying a white flag. The following day, six Palouse warriors are hanged after surrendering.

citations.title: U.S. Army Colonel George Wright hangs Yakama and Palouse prisoners (HistoryLink)
citations.quote: Army officers justified the summary execution by blaming Qualchan for the death of Indian Agent Andrew J. Bolon in 1855, but Qualchan had no involvement in this event.

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the army hanged seventeen Palouse along Latah Creek which was later called Hangman Creek as a result

events.notes: HistoryLink's own dates differ: summary says six Palouse hanged the day after Qualchan; body says 10 Palouse reported on 25 September and six were ordered hanged, four more killed 30 September. Wikipedia's 'seventeen Palouse' goes on to count Qualchan, a Yakama, among them. Exact site on the creek is not given, so the point is approximate. Wikipedia's Yakima War article tells a different story of the miners' killing in which Qualchan is involved; that is about the miners, not Bolon.

events.title: Treaty of Friendship ending the Coeur d'Alene War

place.name: Coeur d'Alene Mission (Sacred Heart, Cataldo, Idaho)

events.statement: On 17 September 1858 at the Coeur d'Alene Mission, by the Tribe's chronology, a treaty was negotiated to bring peace. George Wright's text is headed Preliminary Articles of a Treaty of Peace and Friendship; Wikipedia's Battle of Spokane Plains article calls it a document of surrender. His terms required the return of army property, the handing over of those responsible for the attack on Steptoe, and free passage for whites; in return he promised no more war against them.

citations.title: History (Coeur d'Alene Tribe)
citations.quote: Treaty of Friendship September 17th, 1858 After the Battle between the Tribes and Steptoe, later that year a Treaty was negotiated between the Tribal Nations and the U.S. Government to bring about a peaceful resolution

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty required that the Skitswish return army property and hand over the individuals responsible for the attack on Steptoe, and give permission for whites to pass through their lands without interference in the future.

citations.title: Coeur d'Alene War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In return, Wright promised that there would be no more war waged against the Skitswish people.

citations.title: Preliminary Articles of a Treaty of Peace and Friendship (Access Genealogy)
citations.quote: Done at the headquarters of the expedition against northern Indians, at the Coeur d’Alene Mission, Washington Territory, this 17th day of September, 1858.

citations.title: Battle of Spokane Plains (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On September 17, the Schitsu'umsh chiefs signed a document of surrender.

events.notes: The place follows Wright's own text, dated at the Mission; the point is the state park at Cataldo, by Wikidata, with the Mission's site approximate. Spokane removed from the participants: the articles are headed with the Coeur d'Alene, and the Spokane seem to have met Wright separately, later, at Latah Creek. Wikipedia says the tribes turned over Qualchan, which contradicts HistoryLink's account of his surrender on the Hangman Creek card; not used here.

events.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley
events.statement: On 1 October 1863 Governors James Nye of Nevada Territory and James Doty of Utah Territory signed a treaty of peace and friendship at Ruby Valley with twelve chiefs of the Western Bands of the Shoshone, all but one by mark. It allowed roads, telegraph, a railroad and mines, and promised twenty annual payments of $5,000, but did not say the Shoshone ceded their land. Many Western Shoshone councils were still refusing a $145 million settlement in 2006.

citations.title: Treaty of October 1, 1863 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: Treaty of Peace and Friendship made at Ruby Valley, in the Territory of Nevada, this first day of October, A. D. one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Governor James W. Nye of the Nevada Territory and Governor James Duane Doty of the Utah Territory signed the Treaty of Ruby Valley.

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Twelve chiefs signed for the "Western Bands of the Shoshonee Nation of Indians."

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In exchange, the Shoshone would receive twenty annual payments worth $5,000 each cattle and other goods.

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty did not state that the Shoshone were to cede their lands.

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: As of 2006, most of the Western Shoshone tribal councils had refused to settle for a payment of $145 million

citations.title: Treaty of Ruby Valley (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: maintain existing telegraph and stage lines, construct one railroad and engage in specified economic activities.

events.notes: Kappler dates the treaty 1 October 1863; ratified with amendments, proclaimed 21 October 1869. 'Mines' rests on Article IV of the treaty text. Wikipedia says US cavalry massacred 52 Goshute at Bahsahwahbee in May 1863, shortly before.

events.title: The Bear River Massacre (Massacre at Boa Ogoi)

place.name: Bear River Massacre site near Preston, Idaho

events.statement: Settlers had taken over Cache Valley's food sources; the final catalyst for Colonel Patrick Connor's expedition was a Shoshone attack on miners on the Montana Trail. On 29 January 1863 his California Volunteers struck Bear Hunter's winter encampment. Some 21 soldiers died. Estimates of the Shoshone dead run from 156, from the chief Sagwitch's son, to 493, counted by a settler among the bodies. Some call it the largest mass murder of Native Americans by the US military.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Colonel Patrick Edward Connor led a detachment of California Volunteers as part of the Bear River Expedition against Shoshone chief Bear Hunter .

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Connor estimated his forces killed more than 224 out of 300 warriors.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Danish immigrant Hans Jasperson said he walked among the bodies and counted 493 dead Shoshone people.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Some sources describe it as the largest mass murder of Native Americans by the US military

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In 1918, Sagwitch's son Be-shup , Frank Timbimboo Warner, said, "[H]alf of those present got away," and 156 were killed.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Historian Brigham D. Madsen estimated about 250 were killed in the massacre.

citations.title: Boa Ogoi: Restoring Sacred Land 150 years after the Bear River Massacre (Marley Madsen, Utah State University)
citations.quote: instigating the largest mass murder of Native Americans in the history of the United States

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The final catalyst for Connor's expedition was a Shoshone attack on a group of eight miners on the Montana Trail.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Around 250 to 400 Northern Shoshone children and adults were killed near their homes, and 21 US soldiers died.

citations.title: Bear River Massacre (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the settlers were consuming significant food resources and taking over areas that pushed the Shoshone increasingly into areas of marginal food production

events.notes: Warner, Madsen (Shoshoni Frontier) and Jasperson are as Wikipedia reports them, not read directly. Its lead says around 250 to 400 killed and 21 soldiers dead, and a footnote lists 350 and 400 too. Also called the Battle of Bear River and the Massacre at Boa Ogoi. The expedition followed a Shoshone attack on miners on the Montana Trail and Kinney's arrest warrants for Bear Hunter, Sanpitch and Sagwitch. Wikipedia's 'some sources' are footnoted to Madsen (read) and Dana Hedgpeth in the Washington Post (not fetchable, so not credited). Moved from the card: Connor claimed more than 224 of 300 warriors; Brigham Madsen about 250; Frank Timbimboo Warner gave 156 in 1918; Hans Jasperson 493.

events.title: Box Elder Treaty (Northwestern Shoshone)
events.statement: On 30 July 1863 at Box Elder, Utah Territory, General Patrick Connor and James Doty made a treaty with Northwestern Shoshone led by Pocatello, six months after the Bear River Massacre compelled many Great Basin groups to treat. It called for peace, promised $5,000 a year as compensation for 'utter destitution' and recognized Pocatello's claim between the Raft River and the Portneuf Mountains. It had little effect until 1968, when the United States paid about 50 cents an acre.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Box Elder Treaty is an agreement between the Northwestern Shoshone and the United States government, signed on July 30, 1863.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: This killing had a devastating effect on the indigenous people of the Great Basin, and compelled many groups to accept treaties in 1863.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: James Duane Doty and General Patrick Edward Connor were the lead negotiators for the United States. Pocatello was the lead negotiator for the Indian groups.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: It contains a promise by the U.S. to pay the Shoshone $5,000 yearly as compensation for the "utter destitution" inflicted by war.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The treaty had little effect until 1968, when the United States compensated the Northwestern band for their land claim at a rate of about 50¢ per acre.

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Articles of agreement made at Box Elder, in Utah Territory, this thirtieth day of July, A. D. one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It also recognizes the claim of Chief Pocatello and his people to the land "bounded on the west by the Raft River and on the east by the Porteneuf Mountains".

citations.title: Box Elder Treaty - Wikipedia
citations.quote: It was adopted after a period of conflict which included the Bear River Massacre on January 29, 1863.

events.notes: The treaty text says it was made at Box Elder, Utah Territory. Wikipedia only. Wikipedia's account has Bear Hunter captured and tortured before being killed, per Shoshone oral histories; that belongs to the massacre card. Added quotes for the Raft River and Portneuf boundaries and for the Bear River Massacre date. The treaty's spelling is Porteneuf.

events.title: Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868 (Eastern Shoshone and Bannock)
events.statement: On 3 July 1868 at Fort Bridger, Washakie and other Eastern Shoshone with Taggee and other Bannock made a treaty setting apart a Wind River reservation of around 3.2 million acres, less than a tenth of the 44 million acres or so recognized for Washakie's people five years before. The Bannock were promised a reservation in the Port Neuf country when the president thought it advisable; the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes say the treaty affirmed Fort Hall as their permanent home.

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: Articles of a treaty made and concluded at Fort Bridger, Utah Territory,on the third day of July

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: which shall embrace reasonable portions of the "Port Neuf" and "Kansas Prairie" countries

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: Wash-a-kie, his x mark

citations.title: Coming to Wind River: The Eastern Shoshone Treaties of 1863 and 1868 (WyoHistory.org)
citations.quote: The second treaty, signed in 1868, shrank this to a far smaller reservation—of around 3.2 million acres, with its heart in the Wind River Valley.

citations.title: Coming to Wind River: The Eastern Shoshone Treaties of 1863 and 1868 (WyoHistory.org)
citations.quote: The reservation covered less than a tenth of the area set aside for Washakie's bands just five years earlier.

citations.title: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes
citations.quote: the tribal leadership signed the Fort Bridger Treaty, which affirmed that the newly established Fort Hall Indian Reservation would become the permanent home for the Shoshone and Bannock people.

citations.title: Treaty of July 3, 1868 (Access Genealogy, text from Kappler)
citations.quote: Bannacks: Taggee, his x mark

events.notes: The treaty text says only that when the US deems it advisable a reservation shall be selected for the Bannock; the Tribes' page frames it as affirming Fort Hall (established by order of 14 June 1867). WyoHistory says the 1863 treaty specified around 44 million acres.

events.title: Pyramid Lake War begins (Williams Station incident and the first Battle of Pyramid Lake)
events.statement: Accounts of the Williams Station killings of 6 or 7 May 1860 conflict: the National Park Service has four white men attacking a Paiute woman, then burned in the house; others tell of a raid without cause, or of captured Paiute children, in one version sexually assaulted girls. On 12 May Northern Paiute warriors decisively defeated William Ormsby's volunteers; he died. Larger forces fought them on 2 June. An August cease-fire brought no treaty; accounts differ on who prevailed.

citations.title: The Pyramid Lake War (Pony Express National Historic Trail, National Park Service)
citations.quote: An old Paiute man and a younger Pauite woman went to a house owned by J.O. Williams, a white. Four white men in the house tied up the man and attacked the woman.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: One account claimed the raid was made without cause by a renegade band from the north.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Ultimately, the party killed the men and found the two children tied up.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Another account, given by a Paiute member in an 1880 interview

citations.title: The Two Battles of Pyramid Lake (Nevada State Historic Preservation Office)
citations.quote: On May 12, 1860, Northern Paiute warriors, fighting to retain their way of life, decisively defeated a volunteer army from Virginia City and nearby settlements.

citations.title: The Two Battles of Pyramid Lake (Nevada State Historic Preservation Office)
citations.quote: On June 2, 1860, a larger force of volunteers and regular U.S. Army troops engaged Numu warriors in battle

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Major William Ormsby (who later died in the First Battle of Pyramid Lake )

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Smaller raids and skirmishes continued until a cease-fire was agreed to in August 1860; there was no treaty.

citations.title: The Pyramid Lake War (Pony Express National Historic Trail, National Park Service)
citations.quote: On May 7, 1860, an incident at the Williams Station in Carson Valley, Nevada set off the Pyramid Lake War.

citations.title: The Pyramid Lake War (Pony Express National Historic Trail, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The house was burned with the men in it.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On May 6, a raiding party led by mixed-race Bannock warrior Mogoannoga attacked the station, killing five Americans and burning down the establishment.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: A third account claimed the kidnapped children were two 12-year-old girls who were sexually assaulted before being hidden.

citations.title: The Pyramid Lake War (Pony Express National Historic Trail, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Paiutes claimed a big victory when they defeated U.S. Major William Ormsby's force in Nevada, but the Indians eventually were defeated.

citations.title: The Two Battles of Pyramid Lake (Nevada State Historic Preservation Office)
citations.quote: fought with such courage and strategy that the attacking forces were held back during the day until the Numu could withdraw.

citations.title: Paiute War (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Result Stalemate

events.notes: Date of the station incident differs: NPS 7 May, Wikipedia 6 May, and Wikipedia has Mogoannoga leading the raid and five Americans killed, where NPS has four men burned in the house. Wikipedia gives 79 white and 25 Indigenous dead in the two battles, unattributed; omitted. Numaga had voted against war, per Wikipedia. Trimmed: dropped 'the station burned' (no quote supports it). Corrected after verification: restored the incident's date, the outcome of the NPS account, the third account and the disputed outcome of the war (NPS: Indians eventually defeated; infobox: stalemate; Nevada marker: Numu held the attackers until they could withdraw). 'Ormsby's volunteers' follows NPS 'Ormsby's force'; Wikipedia says the five companies never chose an overall commander.

events.title: Wovoka's vision and the Ghost Dance of 1889
events.statement: Wovoka, or Jack Wilson, a Paiute who worked for the rancher David Wilson near Yerington and learned Christian theology there, said he had a vision during the solar eclipse of 1 January 1889. It promised the resurrection of the Paiute dead and the removal of whites and their works; the Ghost Dance would bring it about, with righteous living and non-violence. Scholars disagree on the date, Tom Thatcher placing a first vision in 1887. It spread east, to the Lakota.

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Wovoka's vision entailed the resurrection of the Paiute dead, and the removal of whites and their works from North America .

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Anthropologists, historians, and theologians provide conflicting accounts of when and how Wovoka had his vision.

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Wovoka received his first vision while chopping wood for David Wilson in 1887.

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Wovoka often worked for David Wilson, a rancher in the Yerington, Nevada , area

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: it moved quickly beyond his local Paiute community by word of mouth to Native American tribes further east, notably the Lakota

citations.title: Wovoka (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Wovoka said he had a prophetic vision after falling into a coma during the solar eclipse of January 1, 1889

events.notes: Date kept: the card's vision is the one during the eclipse of 1 January 1889, a fixed date, and it says the date is disputed. Thatcher, citing Mooney, gives 1887 for a first vision, known only through Wikipedia. Wikipedia reports he also advocated non-violence in the Christian spirit.

events.title: Potato War (Honey Lake)
events.statement: In the Potato War of October 1857, by Wikipedia's Washoe article the last armed conflict between the Washoe and non-Indians, hungry Washoes were killed or wounded for taking three acres of potatoes from William Morehead's farm near Honey Lake. Tim Purdy's local history has Morehead and others confronting a band of Washo at the patch. Fariss and Smith's county history of 1882, naming settlers under Captain William Weatherlow with Winnemucca's Paiutes, says those punished were of the Pit River tribe.

citations.title: Washoe people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The last armed conflict with the Washoes and non-Indians was the Potato War of 1857

citations.title: Washoe people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: when hungry Washoes were killed or wounded for taking three acres of potatoes

citations.title: Washoe people (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The troublesome savages were of the Pit River tribe , and a company of the settlers, under Captain William Weatherlow, and accompanied by Winnemucca and a band of his Pah-Ute braves , went out against the savages

citations.title: Milford's Potato War (Tim Purdy)
citations.quote: It all began in October 1857 when a band of Washo Indians visited William Morehead’s potato patch, some two miles northwest of Milford.

events.notes: Purdy and Wikipedia's Washoe article support the Washoe in the participants; the Pit River attribution belongs to the old history quoted on Wikipedia, about Weatherlow's company. Counts differ (three in a Lassen Historical Society summary, eleven in a county curriculum page, both seen only in a search) and stay off the card. Date stays a year. Fariss and Smith are known through the block quote and footnote on the Washoe article, not read directly.

events.title: Modoc War begins (fight at Lost River)
events.statement: In April 1870 Captain Jack (Keintpoos) and 371 other Modocs left the Klamath Reservation for their Lost River homeland. On 28 November 1872 Captain James Jackson left Fort Klamath with troops and with Linkville militia reached the village on the 29th. The Modocs fled by boat across Tule Lake to the Stronghold. Skirmishes burned Jack's village and left a Modoc woman and child dead. By the National Park Service's account, enraged Modocs killed 14 settlers.

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: In April of 1870, Jack along with 371 other Modocs, left the reservation and returned to their Lost River homeland.

citations.title: Battle of Lost River (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: On November 28, Captain James Jackson , commanding 40 troops, left Fort Klamath for Captain Jack's camp.

citations.title: Battle of Lost River (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: Reinforced by citizen militia from Linkville (now Klamath Falls, Oregon ), the troops reached Jack's camp on the Lost River

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The ensuing battle, the Lost River Battle, caused the Modocs to flee by boat, crossing Tule Lake, to take refuge at the Stronghold

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: These skirmishes resulted in the burning of Captain Jack's village and the deaths of a Modoc woman and child. An enraged group of Modocs traveled east around Tule Lake and killed 14 male settlers.

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: an unauthorized attack on a Modoc village across the river was carried out by a group of civilians.

events.notes: NPS says the war began 28 November with Major Green leaving Fort Klamath, and gives 29 November elsewhere; Wikipedia says Green furnished the troops and Captain Jackson led them, with 40 men, 29 November for the fight. NPS spells the leader Keintpoos; Wikipedia Kintpuash.

events.title: Captain Jack (Kintpuash) and three Modoc leaders hanged at Fort Klamath
events.statement: On 3 October 1873, after conviction for attacking the peace commission that left General Canby and Reverend Thomas dead, Captain Jack, Schonchin John, Black Jim and Boston Charley were hanged before nearly 2,000 people; all Modocs were made to attend. Barncho and Slolux were sent to Alcatraz. An army surgeon cut off Jack's and Schonchin John's heads and sent them to Washington. Twelve days later, by the National Park Service's count, 163 Modocs went as prisoners of war to Oklahoma.

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: On October 3, 1873, Captain Jack, Schonchin John, Black Jim, and Boston Charley were hanged. Barncho and Slolux had their sentences commuted by President Grant and were sent to Alcatraz.

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: Nearly 2,000 people attended the hanging. The attendance of all Modocs was mandatory. Twelve days after the hanging, 163 Modocs were sent as prisoners of war to the Quapaw Agency in Oklahoma.

citations.title: The Modoc War (Lava Beds National Monument, National Park Service)
citations.quote: The Modocs who had attacked the peace commissioners were imprisoned at Fort Klamath, where they were tried and convicted of murder.

citations.title: Kintpuash (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: their bodies were removed from the scaffold, and an Army surgeon decapitated them. The severed heads were sent to Washington, D.C., for scientific purposes.

events.notes: A sentence carried out after a military trial. Wikipedia's war article gives 153 sent to Indian Territory against NPS's 163. NPS: the Modocs' population fell by one-third in exile.

events.title: Federal treaty commissioners negotiate unratified treaties with California tribes
events.statement: In 1851-52 three federal commissioners, Redick McKee, O. M. Wozencraft and George Barbour, negotiated 18 treaties with California peoples, promising 8.5 million acres for reservations; McKee, assigned the north, reached the Upper Klamath in September 1851. Settlers flooded Congress with complaints of excess land, and the Yurok Tribe says Congress rejected the treaties and failed to tell the tribes. For the Tongva, by one account, those who negotiated had no authority to cede their land.

citations.title: Redick McKee (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: O. M. Wozencraft and George W. Barbour were appointed as well and began negotiations in 1851.

citations.title: Redick McKee (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: McKee was assigned the task of creating treaties with natives of Northern California. His party arrived on the Upper Klamath river in September 1851.

citations.title: Tongva (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The US government signed 18 treaties between 1851 and 1852 promising 8.5 million acres (3.4 million ha) of land for reservations .

citations.title: Tongva (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The US had negotiated with people who did not represent the Tongva and had no authority to cede their land.

citations.title: Treaty Negotiations (Yurok Tribe)
citations.quote: which was inundated with complaints from settlers claiming the Indians were receiving an excess of valuable land and resources. The Congress rejected the treaties and failed to notify the tribes of this decision.

events.notes: Place is where McKee's party reached the Klamath; the 18 treaties were signed at many sites. Wikipedia's Tongva page says the Senate did not ratify.

events.title: Chumash revolt of 1824

place.name: Mission Santa Inés (Santa Ynez Valley), California

events.statement: Protesting treatment by guards, Chumash at three missions planned a rising, but a soldier beating a boy at Santa Inés on 21 February 1824 set it off early; by one account 19 Chumash and a soldier died as much of the mission burned. They seized La Purísima and Santa Barbara, leaving the latter for the hills. Troops retook La Purísima on 16 March; after a pardon, most returned by 28 June, ending California's largest organized resistance under Spain and Mexico.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Chumash planned a coordinated rebellion at all three missions. Due to an incident with a soldier at Mission Santa Inés on Saturday, February 21, the rebellion began early. Most of the Santa Inés mission complex was burned down.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: then attacked Mission La Purisima from inside, forced the garrison to surrender, and allowed the garrison, their families, and the mission priest to depart for Santa Inés in peace.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: the Chumash of Mission Santa Barbara captured the mission from within without bloodshed, repelled a military attack on the mission, and then retreated from the mission to the hills.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: until a Mexican military unit attacked people on March 16 and forced them to surrender.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: negotiated with the Chumash and convinced a majority to return to the missions by June 28.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: The Chumash revolt was the largest organized resistance movement to occur during the Spanish and Mexican periods in California.

citations.title: Mission Santa Inés (California Missions Foundation)
citations.quote: the Chumash revolt of 1824 when the Indians aggressively protested treatment by the military guards

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: a young Chumash boy from Mission La Purisima was severely beaten by a Mexican soldier

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: In the struggle at Mission Santa Ines on the first day, 15 Chumash women and children died, 4 men died in the fires, and one Mexican soldier was killed.

citations.title: Chumash revolt of 1824 (Wikipedia)
citations.quote: issued a general pardon to all who had participated in the revolt, other than those already convicted at military tribunals

events.notes: California was then under the Mexican Republic. Wikipedia's infobox gives 8 Mexican and 42 Chumash dead, unattributed, and says up to 2,000 Chumash and Yokuts took part; omitted. A general pardon was issued. Corrected after verification: the trim left 'without bloodshed' as the only word on violence and lost the flight to the hills, the pardon and the cause; those are restored. To stay at 80 words the garrison's release at La Purísima (held three days first) is left to its citation. The page also has two Chumash killed at Santa Barbara, four settlers killed at La Purísima, and sixteen Natives killed on 16 March; about 816 of 1,000 had returned by 28 June.

events.title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Dolores) founded among the Ohlone

place.name: Mission San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores), San Francisco

events.statement: Mission San Francisco de Asís is dated two ways: Father Francisco Palóu said the first Mass there on 29 June 1776, and he and Pedro Cambón dedicated a small chapel on 9 October. It was sited to evangelize the Ohlone. Ramaytush Ohlone are recorded entering from 1785 and later made 36,000 bricks for the adobe church finished in 1791. The mission was plagued by disease; the California Missions Foundation says more than 5,000 Native people had died there by 1832.

citations.title: Mission San Francisco de Asís (California Missions Foundation)
citations.quote: The mission was plagued by disease and high mortality rates among the Indian population.

events.title: Kumeyaay (Tipai) uprising at Mission San Diego

place.name: Mission San Diego de Alcalá (Kumeyaay Nipawai), California

events.statement: In 1775 hundreds of local Tipai attacked Mission San Diego, burning it and killing Father Luis Jayme and two others. The California Missions Foundation says they were discontented with rules and regulations; another account blames years of sexual assaults by Presidio soldiers and torture with metal-tipped whips. Jayme himself had complained that soldiers' abuse and rape of Indian women provoked attacks. The padres rebuilt the mission like an army fort.

events.title: Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded on Kumeyaay land
events.statement: On 16 July 1769 Junípero Serra founded Mission San Diego de Alcalá on a hill overlooking the bay, in an area long inhabited by the Kumeyaay, the beginning of the Alta California mission chain. Within weeks, says the California Missions Foundation, violence had killed both Indians and missionaries. Luis Jayme pressed for a move over water and the nearby Presidio soldiers, and in 1774 the mission went about six miles inland, toward the river and the Native villages.

citations.quote: Founded by Father Junipero Serra on July 16, 1769, it is here where the Spanish religious and political dream to begin an Alta California mission chain first became reality.

citations.quote: a drought in 1774 forced the mission fathers to move Mission San Diego about six miles inland to its present location, closer to the San Diego River, to gain access to more favorable agricultural lands and the local Indian villages.

events.notes: The point is the 1769 site on the hill, the Presidio of San Diego, about six miles from the present inland mission. Wikipedia calls it the second Franciscan-founded mission in the Californias (after San Fernando de Velicatá); the Foundation calls it the first of the twenty-one. Sources differ on why it moved: drought (Foundation), water and soldiers (Wikipedia on Jayme).

events.title: Bloody Island (Clear Lake) massacre of Pomo people

place.name: Clear Lake, Lake County (Bloody Island), California

events.statement: Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone enslaved and starved Pomo at Clear Lake until they rebelled and killed their captors. On 15 May 1850 US Dragoons under Lieutenants Nathaniel Lyon and J. W. Davidson came on Pomo at Badon-napoti, and killed old men, women and children. Wikipedia, crediting the National Park Service, has 60 of 400 killed; it notes other accounts of 200; a report by Major Sherman claimed about 800. Ni'ka, or Lucy Moore, survived underwater breathing through a reed.

events.title: Mariposa War: Mariposa Battalion enters Yosemite Valley
events.statement: In the Mariposa War of December 1850 to June 1851, a state militia battalion, authorised at two hundred men, raised after miners' land seizures and raids on James Savage's post, pursued the Ahwahnechee and Chowchilla. On 27 March 1851 it found a Yosemite Valley refuge, the earliest known non-Indigenous force to enter, burned villages and food stores, and forcibly moved people out. Tenaya's people were marched toward the Fresno Reservation; many fled back, and the militia killed his youngest son.

events.title: Three Knolls Massacre of the Yahi

place.name: Ishi Wilderness / Mill Creek country (Yahi homeland), California

events.statement: In 1865, near their special place Black Rock on Mill Creek, settlers attacked a sleeping group of Yahi and killed about forty, by Richard Burrill's account in retaliation for two white women and a man killed near Oroville. Robert Anderson, one of the attackers, wrote that many bodies floated downstream. Of 33 who escaped, a Mohican Press account says, cattlemen killed about half. The last survivors, among them Ishi, went into hiding.

events.title: Battle of the Big Hole (dawn attack on the Nimíipuu camp)
events.statement: On 9 August 1877 Colonel John Gibbon's men, 183 by his report, surprised the sleeping Nez Perce camp, which believed the war was behind it. Red Wolf recalled women running into water to hide their children, and 'many were killed as they ran'. Fighting continued into the 10th before the Nez Perce withdrew in good order. Jerome Greene puts their dead at probably 70 to 90, mostly women and children. Wikipedia has Gibbon losing 29, two more dying later.

events.title: Malheur Reservation closed; Northern Paiute interned at Yakima
events.statement: In November 1878, after the Bannock War, General Howard was ordered to move about 543 Paiute and Bannock prisoners from Malheur to the Yakama Reservation, 350 miles north. Agent Rinehart's report of August 1879 and settlers' pressure for the land brought the reservation's closure that year. Sarah Winnemucca then went to Washington to lobby for their release, and Interior Secretary Schurz allowed a return at their own expense, a permission the Yakama agent James Wilbur later said was soon revoked.

events.title: California 'Act for the Government and Protection of Indians'
events.statement: On 22 April 1850 California's first legislature enacted the Act for the Government and Protection of Indians, signed by Governor Peter Burnett and nicknamed the Indian Indenture Act. Any white person could post a bond for a Native person's court fine and take their labour; people arrested for 'strolling about' could be sold for up to four months. Gangs abducted and sold children. Parts were repealed after 1865, the rest in 1937; Governor Newsom apologized in 2019.

events.title: Governor Burnett predicts a 'war of extermination' against California Indians
events.statement: On 6 January 1851, in his State of the State address to the California Senate, Governor Peter Burnett said that a war of extermination between the races 'until the Indian race becomes extinct must be expected', with painful regret, as beyond human power to avert. He had signed the Act of 1850 and left office three days later. In the early 1850s the legislature authorized payment for expeditions against Native Californians.
